Oil and gas production in Texas’s Permian Basin has tripled since 2018. #1442. Jack Grealish can't turn down a good night out and his attitude is a problem. IAN HERBERT reveals how the magnetic maverick star sparked concern and now faces a tragedy of missed opportunity

By IAN HERBERT, DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 22:00 EDT, 29 October 2026 | Updated: 09:57 EDT, 2 November 2026

At the Pride of Britain awards a week back, we witnessed the brilliant and magnetic side of Jack Grealish, sprinkling stardust as he presented an award to a child of unimaginable courage who counts the Everton player as his hero. 'Footballers are classed as heroes – but these are the real heroes,' Grealish said that night. You could have heard a pin drop.

It was no different when he arrived back at Everton in September, to the delight of the kids awaiting him and his white Lamborghini in the country lane outside the club's Finch Farm training base. 'It feels so good. I think I'm at my best at everything in life when I feel loved,' Grealish said, articulating a very real sense that he was coming home.

He is popular around the club because it can be said without fear of exaggeration that he has a heart of gold.

Only on Thursday, an Everton-supporting father-of-three with a cancer diagnosis that gives him weeks to live disclosed that Grealish had put £10,000 his way. But within hours of that simple act of altruism coming to light, evidence of the other Grealish emerged, as Everton announced he had been excluded from the squad to face Newcastle in the Carabao Cup for failing to turn up for training last week.

It was by no means the first time. Everton sources say there had been similar causes for concern last season. Grealish reported sick ahead of last weekend's game at Arsenal, shortly after the Pride of Britain awards, and has breached Everton's disciplinary code through an unauthorised absence. The stated reason for his absence at Arsenal was illness.

Jack Grealish remains popular at Everton and has a heart of gold, shown by a £10,000 gift to a fan suffering from cancer, but he has since been dropped over a breach of discipline

There were similar causes for concern last season, with his return this summer going against David Moyes' better judgement

Everton's owners, looking for Grealish's glitz and glamour to gloss over their desperately poor and unambitious summer in the transfer window, were keen to bring him back. It was against David Moyes' own better judgement that he accepted his return as part of the deal that brought Iliman Ndiaye's unwelcome departure to Manchester City.

Moyes needed discipline in a thin squad where every player's contribution would count this season. It was an opportunity for the few star players to inspire and shine a light for the younger ones. And therein lies the tragedy of missed opportunity where Grealish is concerned.

He, the quintessential British maverick playmaker in the mould of George Best and Alan Hudson, could be a Goodison hero of these days, yet seems incapable of showing he is bothered, ridding himself of the acolytes and hangers on who are dragging him down, and appreciating what an opportunity football offers him.

Though he likes a drink, it's not so much booze as his attitude, and a struggle to turn down a good night out, which is contributing.

There is no doubt that he still has the skills to be a cherished player. That much was clear in the early stages of last season when he was providing more assists than any other Everton player until a broken foot requiring surgery brought a premature end to his season.

This season he has, as yet, no assists. He has perhaps been frustrated at the number of chances he has created not being converted, though not every winger has Erling Haaland as his support act.

Grealish's patchy attitude to a football life is affecting his game, as he is not taking his man on in the way he used to and does not emit such light on the wing

Look hard enough, though, and you'll see signs that his patchy attitude to a football life is affecting his game. He is not taking his man on in the way he used to and does not emit such light on the wing. Pep Guardiola, at Manchester City, was the first to see this and rapidly made it clear he wanted him gone.

It's not too late for the 31-year-old to become the totemic presence that so many fervently want him to be on Merseyside. Moyes, who sees the wasted potential, has given him abundant support and patience since City left him out in the cold, hoping that he can make him see the opportunity, here.

Thursday night's excellent Carabao Cup win over Newcastle United opens up the potential for an exciting Cup run, with Fleetwood Town awaiting in the quarter-finals. Everton have not won a trophy for 31 years.

The hope must be that the significantly public nature of Grealish's omission – very much a case of Moyes refusing to tolerate another breach – will shock him into action.

It was even the wish of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, present at Thursday night's match, that Grealish would be re-signed to Everton and the PM declared after meeting him at the Pride of Britain awards that the player was an example of the way people 'buy into Everton.'

The collective wish for him to thrive at the club could not be clearer. Only he can make that happen.

#1441. Stephen Robinson proud of his battling Dons but injury crisis deepens

Published: 17:30 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 14:43 EDT, 2 November 2026

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson has revealed his injury crisis has become even more catastrophic ahead of the weekend league visit of Hibernian that has the potential to make or break his reign.

The Dons manager saw his side put in a fine, disciplined display in going down 1-0 to Rangers in the Premier Sports Cup final, but lost Emmanuel Gyamfi within 15 minutes after he collided with Kim Min-su and also has Brad Lyons battling a knock.

Robinson admitted afterwards that there is no chance of longer-term absentees Chris Cadden, Mats Knoester and Lewis Mayo being available, with Dan Happe the only player likely to return for the Saturday night showdown with Premiership bottom dogs Hibs after being suspended last night.

‘Gyamfi will be out for a long period of time,’ reported Robinson. ‘It looked like it was maybe the other thigh that he’s had a problem with. It’s a heartbreaker for the boy.

‘Brad Lyons took a really bad knock. I’m not sure how serious that is. Hopefully, he’s got away with it.

‘Chris Cadden will be out for six weeks. Mats Knoester is four to six weeks.

Emmanuel Gyamfi limped off early with an injury in Aberdeen's semi-final defeat

‘The only plus point is Dan Happe. It’s very difficult because half the squad are not available. Any team that does well, there’s consistency and patience.

‘Over time, the last person that had prolonged success in Aberdeen was Derek (McInnes). He was given a lot of time and a lot of support, but we’ve not been able to put a consistent team, never mind a consistent shape, on the pitch.

‘It’s four changes every week at the moment.’

Robinson, however, stated his pride in the way his players performed and backed centre-back Jack Milne while taking a pop at the criticism he has come in for of late.

‘They rose against adversity this time. They put in a real performance,’ he said.

‘Rangers scored during our best spell in the game, which is unfortunate, but it’s been a tough week for us with injuries, really tough.

‘They showed great character and courage.

‘Jack’s a young man. Surprisingly, he’s from Aberdeen and he still gets an incredible amount of stick.

‘He’s had one full season and he’s a lovely boy that wants to learn. He’s just learning the game. I thought he showed real character.’

Dons boss Stephen Robinson on the touchline in the 1-0 defeat to Rangers

Robinson also refused to criticise captain Kevin Nisbet after seeing him pass up a couple of golden chances.

‘If you want chances to fall to anyone, it’s Kevin and he had the opportunity to play Mitchy Ntelo in with one of them when clean through,’ he reflected.

‘We had grown into the game. We were organised defensively despite not knowing what our team would be until Saturday morning.

‘I’m proud of the players because they gave me absolutely everything.

‘You’d need to ask the fans if they saw positive performances. I can only answer for myself. I saw a group of boys give everything in adversity.

‘Everyone expected us to roll over and get battered but that wasn’t the case. They’ve shown they have the character to play for Aberdeen in big games, no doubt.’

#1440. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

Liverpool have been aggressive and on the front foot, but we’re still waiting for a noteworthy chance to be created here at Anfield. City haven’t been spectacular, but they’ve done just about enough so far.

Kerkez fires in a cross and there’s a miscommunication between Guehi and Donnarumma, with the centre-back slicing a clearance instead of allowing the goalkeeper to gather the delivery. Barcola can’t capitalise on the loose ball and City get away with one there.

Let’s not kid ourselves about what we are seeing at the moment. There is a lot of noise but nothing has happened to light a fire and the onus has got to be on Liverpool’s players to step this up considerably. This occasion, more than anything, is crying out for someone to play how the supporters are feeling and it’s not there yet. It’s been tame and Manchester City are, accordingly, comfortable.

City motor forward on the counter through Cherki, whose delightful touch takes him away from Mac Allister. From inside his own half, the Frenchman dribbles to the edge of Liverpool’s penalty area. He attempts to play a one-two with Fernandez, but the pass is cut out by Jacquet.

Manchester City have not got going, as of yet. The defiant message from the club is they would not let the verdict affect them. They have defended well enough but have barely strung a passing sequence together against a Liverpool side who appear be playing off pure emotion.

Gravenberch is bossing this game in midfield. Another powerful run from deep results in a delightful nutmeg on Fernandez, who slips over. Liverpool’s energy has been really impressive. City need to ride out this early storm.

It’s getting heated at Anfield! Mac Allister and Anderson clash sparking a scuffle between both sets of players. It threatened to boil over for a second, but the drama quickly calms down and play resumes after the referee has a word with the two captains.

All fairly difficult to stomach, the Manchester City fans’ performance at kick-off. Inflatable bananas to signify nostalgia for the late 1980s, when these were all the rage after the club’s relegation to Division Two? The City of Sheikh Mansour are about as far removed from the era of Jimmy Frizzell as is possible to imagine, with their colossal wealth enabling cheating on an unprecedented scale. And as for the Poznan during You’ll Never Walk Alone? When Liam Gallagher asks Oasis fans to perform this backwards dance during next year’s tour, I suspect there will not be quite the same take-up.

There’s an early flashpoint as Koumas puts Guehi under serious pressure, causing the defender to fall to the ground and grab the ball with his hands. It’s not a foul and Liverpool are given a free kick. The hosts want Guehi booked and Araujo sprints over to the referee waving an imaginary yellow card, but gets one himself.

Amid all the build-up and backstory to this extraordinary fixture it is remarkable that 21-year-old Lewis Koumas is making his first Premier League start as Liverpool’s makeshift centre-forward. And he has started well.

A spell of Man City possession has slightly quelled the atmosphere. On paper, you would have to say the away side’s starting 11 is superior to Liverpool’s.

Liverpool make a fast start as Gravenberch effortlessly turns Fernandez and Munoz darts inside of O’Reilly. The winger’s shot is smothered by Guehi, but the early signs are encouraging for the hosts.

City get us under way at Anfield. This is one we’ve quite literally all been waiting for.

A roaring rendition of YNWA is bellowed by Anfield, which is in full voice. City players huddle together and go over to clap their fans in a show of solidarity.

In the corner of the stadium, where the Sir Kenny Dalglish Stand meets The Kop, there is a white banner with black paint proclaiming: “A generation of supporters cheated” - none of this is bothering the Manchester City fans, who are going back a generation and have a raft of inflatable bananas. (It was a craze in the 1980s, for you younger readers). Anyway, let’s get on with the game and what an opportunity this is for young Lewis Koumas, who has produced the individual performance of the season so far for Liverpool against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup. He needs to be a scampering, scurrying menace once again.

The Kop has now started a chant of “you cheating b-------” you know what you are. Doubt it will be the last time we hear that this afternoon. They are now singing “going down, going down, going down”.

No chance of hearing the names of the Manchester City players as the team is read out by the PA announcer. He is drowned out by the boos, jeers and whistles from the Liverpool fans. The atmosphere is certainly starting to build.

A re-imagining of Oasis’ Wonderwall at the front of the Kop. “And after all,” the banner reads, “you really robbed us all.”

Andoni Iraola told Sky Sports: “He came back from the international break with an overload. He felt a tight hamstring.

“He tried somehow pushing through training, but he was not feeling 100 per cent.

With just over 15 minutes until kick-off, here’s a recap of the two sides.

When asked if the mindset and mood are right for him to do his job, the City boss replied: “Yes. Absolutely. Yes.

“The mood is good, the mindset is good. Now it’s time to start the game - finally!

“It [togetherness] is very important; the mix between the players and the fans, everyone.

“We are away in a complicated environment, a complicated stadium, but we are going to do our best to try to win the game.”

The Manchester City players are out for their warm-up and, dare it be said, they were greeted with apathy by the Liverpool fans. Not even the murmur of a boo when Erling Haaland and Co emerged. It surely will be very different when kick off comes.

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England.

However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given how alleged City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool finished second in the 2018-19 season, accumulating a staggering 98 points, while winning 30 matches and losing just once. City incredibly pipped them to the Premier League trophy by one point. A strikingly similar scenario occurred in the 2021-22 campaign, with Liverpool placing as runners-up with 92 points. You guessed it, City had 93.

What’s done is done, and ultimately we are entering a territory of ifs, buts and maybes. However, if City’s appeal against the charges is unsuccessful and the guilty verdict is upheld, then Liverpool would have unfairly missed out on historic success and lifelong memories.

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1439. SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding1,2. Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types3. However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

The BAF complex remodels chromatin by repositioning or evicting nucleosomes, which enables transcription, transcription factor (TF) binding and DNA replication1,2,3,4. Genes encoding BAF subunits are among the most frequently mutated in cancer, with LOF alterations present in around 20% of patients across nearly every tumour type3,5,6. Despite the widespread involvement of BAF complexes across cancers, a unifying mechanism of how BAF LOF contributes to transformation across diverse tissue types has not been clearly established.

In mammals, BAF complexes are highly diverse and feature numerous non-catalytic auxiliary subunits. So far, three main BAF complexes have been characterized in mammalian cells: the cBAF complex, the polybromo-BAF complex (PBAF) and the non-canonical BAF complex (ncBAF). Each of these has distinct and overlapping biochemical properties, chromatin targets and roles in disease7,8,9,10,11. The mechanisms by which mutations in BAF complexes promote oncogenesis include impaired chromatin accessibility at key enhancers and promoters and altered dynamics of interactions between transcriptional co-activators and TFs3,4,12,13. However, it remains unclear whether BAF LOF affects chromatin structure beyond nucleosome positioning and whether different BAF subunits have distinct or shared functions across tissues.

Beyond nucleosome positioning, epigenetic and transcriptional programming is controlled through higher-order architectural remodelling of the genome. However, it is unclear whether BAF complexes regulate 3D genome organization, despite growing evidence that other chromatin remodellers have a role in higher-order chromatin folding14,15,16. Although architectural proteins such as CTCF and cohesin have been extensively studied17,18,19,20, how BAF influences higher-order chromatin structures and regulates chromatin topology has not been fully explored. BAF complexes have a crucial role in nucleosome remodelling, and emerging links have been identified between other chromatin remodellers and higher-order genome organization21,22,23. On the basis of these findings, here we propose that disruptions in BAF function converge on a unifying mechanism of 3D genome reorganization. This mechanism could explain how distinct BAF LOF mutations drive oncogenesis across multiple tissue types.

Because BAF mutations predominantly cause LOF5,6 and ARID1A is the most frequently mutated BAF subunit with recurrent truncating alterations24, we modelled BAF dysfunction through ARID1A deletion (cBAF LOF) and the compound FHD-286, a SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 inhibitor24,25,26,27,28,29. We treated 15 human cell lines—including cancer cells from diverse tissues, human embryonic stem (hES) cells and non-cancerous immortalized lines—with FHD-286 for 24 h (Fig. 1a,b). All treated cell lines were BAF wild-type (WT) except SHSY5Y, which carries a SMARCA4 missense variant of unknown function (p.R973W)30. We also generated six isogenic lines using RIVA (lymphoma), Raji (lymphoma) and SUM159 (breast cancer) cell lines with heterozygous ARID1A (ARID1AHet) or homozygous ARID1A (ARID1AHom) deletions or knockdown via short hairpin RNA, as well as WT ARID1A.

a, Schematic (top) and results (bottom) of motif analysis of gained ATAC–seq peaks after BAF inhibition across 15 human cell lines treated with DMSO (n = 3) or the pan-BAF inhibitor FHD-286 (red; n = 3) and 6 lines with ARID1A depletion (blue; n = 3 per genotype). TF motif enrichment was calculated using a previously published algorithm24,41. TFs classified as ‘multi-lineage shared BAF-dependent (closing)’ were closing in at least two cell lines and those classified as ‘common BAF-antagonistic (opening)’ were opening in at least two cell lines. ‘Enriched for tissue specificity TFs’ were selected from published tissue-specific enrichment data39,86,87,88,89,90. The dashed line highlights enrichment of tissue-specific TFs. All samples passed quality control (Supplementary Fig. 5). The colour key for treatments applied to cell lines is used throughout the figures. b, Single-locus genome browser example showing increased chromatin accessibility after FHD-286 treatment across tissues. Differences between FHD-286-treated and WT cells are shown as the coefficient difference of ATAC–seq accessibility of peaks containing the indicated TF motif. c, ATAC–seq peak overlap analysis across tissues comparing FHD-286 and DMSO treatments. Columns denote peaks ordered by the discrete pattern of each peak across all comparisons, classified in each comparison as significantly opening or closing, unchanged or absent. log2[FC], log2 fold change. d, Schematic (top) and results (bottom) of the ATAC–seq analysis of mouse cell lines treated with FHD-286, and primary germinal centre B cells from Arid1aHet mice and Arid1a WT mice. n = 3 per condition. mES, mouse embryonic stem cells. e, Representative locus for d. f, Baseline CTCF expression levels (transcripts per million; TPM) across malignant cells from DepMap. Inner box plots indicate the median and interquartile range (Q1–Q3). n provided in the Methods. g, Top TFs with altered motif accessibility for RIVA cells coloured by multivariate adjusted P value. Bars show robust multivariable linear model coefficients ±95% Wald confidence intervals (CI) and P values are from two-sided coefficient tests with Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment. Statistics calculated across accessible peaks, n of peaks shown in Supplementary Table 1. Peaks were derived from n = 3 technical replicates per condition. h, Same as g, but for SUM159 cells. n of peaks provided in Supplementary Table 1, and peaks were derived from n = 3 per condition. Icons in d created in BioRender; Debek, S. https://biorender.com/4tx6w5k (2026).

Using ATAC–seq to assess chromatin accessibility, we identified regions where chromatin either opened or closed following BAF complex loss or inhibition. Analyses of sites with reduced chromatin accessibility (in closing peaks) did not identify TFs common across cell types. Instead, TFs in closing regions were specific to the cell type (for example, SOX5 in skin, HNF4A in liver and SPI1 in lymphoid and myeloid cell lines; Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Many of these TFs interact with BAF complexes (for example, JUN, BATF, NFKB2, ETS1, SPI1, POU5F1 (also known as OCT4), SOX2 and SOX10)21,24. This result supports the notion that BAF complexes modulate cell-context-specific TF activity3,31,32,33,34,35,36,37,38. By contrast, opening peaks were enriched for CTCF motifs in 20 out of the 21 cell lines (Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Figs. 2, 3 and 5). Opening CTCF peaks showed significantly lower cross-cell-type variability than closing TF peaks, which indicated that there is cell-context-independent CTCF regulation by BAF (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Notably, the CTCF effect was not driven by a small number of loci. Instead, it was an intermediate but broad and coordinated shift across many sites. For example, in RIVA cells, a comparison between ARID1A knockdown and WT cells showed that CTCF motif peaks accounted for 47% of opening peaks and 5% of closing peaks in ARID1A-deficient cells (Cohen’s h = 1.30, Cramer’s V = 0.51; Extended Data Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 1).

These effects were conserved in mice. FHD-286-treated mouse cell lines and primary Arid1aHet B cells from Arid1a conditional knockout mice24 also showed the gain in CTCF-site accessibility (Fig. 1d,e). Overall, the strongest gains occurred in lymphoid and myeloid lines, which also show the highest baseline CTCF mRNA and protein expression across healthy tissues and cancers30,39,40 (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1d). An orthogonal TF motif enrichment method, HOMER, confirmed CTCF enrichment across cell lines, with lymphoid and myeloid tissues ranking the highest (Supplementary Fig. 6a). We focused our subsequent experiments on lymphoid (RIVA) and breast cancer (SUM159) models (Fig. 1g,h).

To directly measure occupancy, we performed CTCF chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) in ARID1AHet and WT cells. Chromatin regions that opened after ARID1A deletion showed increased CTCF binding in both lymphoma and breast cancer cells, with stronger gains in the lymphoid line (Fig. 2a,b). Because CTCF cooperates with cohesin at topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries18,41,42,43,44, we next profiled the core cohesin subunit SMC3. SMC3 occupancy increased globally, most prominently at sites with both enhanced accessibility and higher CTCF binding (Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Fig. 6b). Moreover, the majority of newly accessible CTCF sites overlapped with SMC3 peaks (Fig. 2c). mRNA levels of CTCF and subunits of cohesin and BAF complexes were unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 6c), as were CTCF protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 6d). This finding indicates that the CTCF gain reflects increased chromatin binding rather than protein abundance.

a, The log2 fold change in CTCF and SMC3 binding (ChIP–seq) between ARID1AHet and WT RIVA and SUM159 cells, ranked by accessibility changes identified by ATAC–seq. To test whether CTCF itself drives the gain in accessibility, we acutely depleted CTCF by CRISPR in WT and ARID1AHet lymphoma B cells and performed ATAC–seq 48 h after transfection with CTCF-targeting Cas9 ribonucleoprotein. During this window of time, CTCF loss does not lead to effects on viability or proliferation45,46 (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 3). Principal component analysis (PCA) separated samples by genotype (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Consistent with previous observations24, ARID1A mutations caused loss of accessibility at NF-KB2, NF-KB1, REL and RUNX1 motifs (Fig. 2f). Moreover, CTCF depletion in the ARID1AHet background restored accessibility at CTCF sites to WT levels without affecting other TFs (Fig. 2g,h). These results establish these peaks as bona fide CTCF sites and rule out CTCF as a driver of the other TF-related changes. Accessibility gains correlated genome-wide with the expression of nearby genes, which therefore links them to transcriptional output (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta-delta analysis revealed that 93.5% of peaks (1,971 out of 2,108) that opened at CTCF sites in ARID1AHet cells reverted towards WT when CTCF was depleted (Fig. 2i, Extended Data Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 6e,f). To test whether ARID1A heterozygosity acts as a LOF alteration, we compared chromatin accessibility profiles of ARID1AHet cells to those in which ARID1A was completely knocked out. Differential accessibility profiles in ARID1AHet cells strongly overlapped with those of ARID1AHom SUM159 cells and of ARID1A-knockdown RIVA cells, in which full knockout is not viable (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

To determine whether the increased accessibility at CTCF motifs reflects altered nucleosome positioning at the motif itself, we inferred nucleosome positions using nucleoATAC47. The analysis identified a subset of CTCF sites with a nucleosome positioned directly over the CTCF motif in WT cells. This motif-centred nucleosome was displaced in ARID1AHet cells and restored in ARID1AHet cells with CTCF also depleted. This result couples nucleosome displacement after cBAF loss to CTCF occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 1h).

As stronger CTCF sites drive loop extrusion48, we ranked CTCF ChIP–seq peaks by baseline WT intensity and observed that stronger peaks gained greater accessibility in ARID1A-deficient cells than weaker ones (Extended Data Fig. 1i and Supplementary Fig. 6g). These data suggest that ARID1A controls higher-order chromatin organization through CTCF and cohesin distribution.

To test whether the CTCF response occurs in non-transformed cells, we treated hES cells (MEL-1) with FHD-286 for 24 h. CTCF and SMC3 binding increased, although more weakly than in cancer lines (Supplementary Fig. 6h). This result probably reflects the dependence of pluripotent cells on SWI/SNF for stemness and differentiation that is triggered by prolonged pan-BAF inhibition. To uncouple the immediate chromatin response from differentiation, we engineered an ARID1A dTAG degron in hES cells and performed ATAC–seq, CTCF ChIP–seq and ARID1A ChIP–seq after rapid ARID1A depletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a). CTCF-site accessibility increased at both 6 h and 24 h, with strong enrichment already at 6 h (Extended Data Fig. 2b). ARID1A ChIP–seq confirmed loss of ARID1A occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 2c), and CTCF ChIP–seq showed a consistent, broadly distributed gain across more than 10,000 pre-existing CTCF peaks rather than de novo sites (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Furthermore, at the same regions that showed gain of CTCF, we observed a strong loss of ARID1A, which suggested that these loci were previously bound by ARID1A, which prevented CTCF binding (Extended Data Fig. 2c). To validate our findings in an independent setting, we performed a short FHD-286 treatment time course in RIVA cells. CTCF accessibility increased as early as 4 h after treatment, with a progressive increase at 12 h and 24 h, which indicated that CTCF responds rapidly to BAF inhibition. These results provide support for direct chromatin antagonism between BAF activity and CTCF occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 2e).

If CTCF functionally mediates the pathogenic consequences of cBAF loss, concurrent CTCF impairment should attenuate them. Consistent with this idea, patients with alterations in both ARID1A and CTCF showed significantly improved overall survival compared with those with an ARID1A alteration alone (Fig. 2j). To test whether this result reflects a deficit in the ARID1A-loss-driven proliferative advantage, we isolated primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from embryos carrying conditional floxed alleles of Arid1a, Ctcf or both. Deletion was induced by Cre–GFP transduction followed by sorting of GFP-positive cells, and efficient recombination was confirmed by genotyping (Supplementary Figs. 7 and 12a). Arid1a-deficient MEFs proliferated faster than empty-vector controls, and concurrent Ctcf deletion restored proliferation to near-WT levels (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g). This finding indicates that the fitness advantage due to cBAF loss depends on CTCF.

If CTCF gain drives the proliferative phenotype of ARID1A loss, CTCF overexpression alone should phenocopy it. In RIVA lines overexpressing CTCF in ARID1A WT and heterozygous backgrounds, CTCF overexpression in WT cells accelerated growth to ARID1AHet levels (Fig. 2k). High CTCF expression was also associated with more aggressive disease and worse clinical outcomes in patient data (Extended Data Fig. 2h).

CTCF works with the cohesin complex to form TAD boundaries that confine genomic interactions in specific regions42,49. To directly assess the impact of ARID1A deficiency on chromatin 3D architecture and CTCF-associated loop formation at high resolution, we performed Micro-C50,51 on ARID1AHet and WT lymphoma cells. Consistent with the gain of cohesin and CTCF occupancy, ARID1AHet cells showed increased intra-TAD contacts that were strengthened more than weakened (Fig. 3a), and a global shift towards intra-TAD over inter-TAD interactions (Fig. 3b). Moreover, in line with the gain in CTCF binding, ARID1AHet cells showed TAD splitting at higher frequency than merge, loss or complex rearrangements (Fig. 3c), with new boundaries visible in formerly continuous TADs on contact maps (Fig. 3d). To test whether CTCF gain drives this splitting, we examined insulation scores at sites of differential CTCF and SMC3 binding. Regions gaining CTCF showed increased insulation (a lower insulation score indicates fewer cross-boundary contacts; Fig. 3e), and boundaries overlapping CTCF peaks had higher CTCF binding in ARID1AHet cells than in WT cells (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 8a). Thus, enhanced CTCF occupancy drives TAD splitting and boundary insulation after cBAF loss.

Right, proportion of promoter loops in split TADs and TADs selected randomly (two-sided proportion test). h, Aggregate peak analysis plots anchored on Mustache-called loops in WT and ARID1AHet cells (bottom) and the connectivity difference (top) between the conditions. i, Schematic representation of the hypothesis. cBAF loss leads to stabilization of CTCF and cohesin binding and increased intra-TAD interactions at the expense of long-range inter-TAD interactions.

To test whether these structural changes are functional, we measured promoter connectivity in split TADs. Split TADs showed a higher proportion of promoters gaining connectivity than both WT counterparts and random unchanged TADs (Fig. 3g). This finding indicates that splitting reinforces local promoter interactions by limiting longer-range contacts. Indeed, genes in strengthened TADs had increased expression in ARID1AHet cells, whereas genes in weakened TADs were unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 8b,c).

One of the main functions of TADs is to enable connection and coordination between genes contained in their borders. Because genes in TADs tend to manifest coordinated epigenetic marks necessary for coordinated expression levels52,53,54, we asked whether splitting disrupts this coordination. We performed RNA-seq and ChIP–seq for H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me1 and H3.3 marks in ARID1AHet and WT cells, then compared concordance in split, single (preserved boundaries with altered strength) and stable (preserved boundaries and strength) TADs. Split TADs showed greater discordance in chromatin marks and transcription than stable or single TADs (Supplementary Fig. 8d–g), which indicated that splitting establishes distinct chromatin environments. Thus, cBAF normally maintains regulatory coordination by preventing CTCF from subdividing shared domains. Finally, structural loops showed increased connectivity in ARID1AHet cells (Fig. 3h), a result consistent with enhanced cohesin stalling at gained CTCF sites. Together, these results show that cBAF loss reshapes 3D chromatin architecture through increased CTCF and cohesin activity (Fig. 3i).

To test whether BAF insulator antagonism is conserved beyond mammals, we examined Drosophila S2 cells, which use a diversified insulator repertoire, including Ctcf, Beaf and Su(Hw). CRISPR depletion of osa, the Drosophila ARID1A orthologue and a core subunit of the BAP complex, increased chromatin accessibility not only at Ctcf motifs but also at Beaf and Su(Hw) motifs (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j). Thus, SWI/SNF loss broadly opens architectural protein-binding sites across metazoans, which indicates that cBAF normally restrains engagement of multiple insulator classes.

To identify CTCF cofactors that might mediate 3D architectural changes after cBAF loss, we performed immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry (IP–MS) for CTCF in lymphoid cells. CTCF co-precipitated ISWI subunits, consistent with its previously reported role in CTCF function21, and all PBAF-specific subunits (PBRM1, ARID2, PHF10 and BRD7) together with BAF-shared subunits (SMARCC1, SMARCC2, SMARCE1, SMARCB1, SMARCD1, SMARCD2, SMARCA4, SMARCA2 and BCL7A). By contrast, cBAF-specific and ncBAF-specific subunits were depleted relative to IgG (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 9a). Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments for BRD7 and PBRM1 recovered CTCF and the PBAF-specific subunit ARID2 but not the cBAF-specific subunit ARID1A (Fig. 4b). IP–MS for PBRM1 recovered all expected PBAF subunits and CTCF at levels comparable to PBAF core subunits (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 9b). These data reveal a previously unknown association between CTCF and all subunits of the PBAF complex.
