(a) Conserved chromatin opening at CTCF sites across tissues. Variability analysis of ATAC-seq peaks opened or closed by BAF loss across cell types. Newly opened CTCF-associated peaks are broadly shared and show lower inter-tissue variability than closed peaks. This indicates that BAF loss elicits a common, conserved chromatin opening at CTCF sites across diverse lineages. (b) Peak overlap analysis across cell lines with genetic deletion of ARID1A. Peaks at CTCF motif are generally shared across cell lines, and heterozygous loss of ARID1A results in a similar phenotype to homozygous deletion. (c) Occurrence of CTCF motif in opening, stable and closing chromatin regions after ARID1A deletion, or FHD-286 treatment, or after CTCF deletion. CTCF binding sites predominantly become open after cBAF loss/inhibition. Closing of the CTCF motif in CTCF CRISPR shows that the opening of the sites corresponds to binding. (d) Basal CTCF mRNA levels in cancer cell lines (top) and normal cell types (bottom) from the Human Protein Atlas single-cell dataset. Each violin represents the distribution of normalized TPM (nTPM) values across cell lines within a given primary disease group. Lymphoid and myeloid cells exhibit the highest CTCF expression among all tissue types. Inner boxplots indicate the median and interquartile range (Q1-Q3). N is indicated in the Methods. (e) Correlation of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq differential peaks in ARID1AHet vs. ARID1A-WT RIVA cells, showing high concordance between changes in gene expression and alterations in promoter chromatin accessibility. The top panel anchors expression changes on differentially accessible peaks, the bottom panel anchors accessibility changes on differentially expressed genes. n = 3 technical replicates per genotype. Center dot is the median and error bars show 25th–75th percentiles, p-value is from ANOVA. (f) Scatter plots showing that CTCF deletion reverses the chromatin accessibility gains triggered by ARID1A loss. Each dot represents a genomic region identified in ATAC-Seq of ARID1AHet, ARID1AHetCTCF CRISPR and WT. The position of each dot reflects accessibility change in ARID1AHet vs WT (x axis), or ARID1AHet CTCF CRISPR vs WT (y axis). The colour of the dots represents accessibility change of that region in CTCF CRISPR vs WT, with red indicating putative CTCF-binding sites, i.e. regions which lose accessibility after CTCF deletion in WT cells. The top panel includes all peaks from ARID1AHet, ARID1AHet CTCF CRISPR and WT ATAC-Seq, while the bottom panel focuses on putative CTCF-binding sites within those peaks. Dots that shift back toward zero on the y-axis (ARID1AHet CTCF CRISPR vs. WT) indicate that removing CTCF reverses the aberrant accessibility caused by ARID1A loss. (g) Peak overlap analysis across cell lines comparing opening and closing regions in cell lines treated with FHD-286, or with knock-out or knock-down of ARID1A. Loss of cBAF function, whether through pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion, results in concordant changes in chromatin accessibility, with the same peaks opening or closing in the same direction under both conditions. (h) Nucleosome occupancy profiles predicted from NucleoATAC shown over CTCF ChIP-seq peaks and centered on the CTCF motif. Profiles reveal reduced nucleosome occupancy at CTCF binding sites, accompanied by more clearly phased and organized nucleosomes flanking the motif in ARID1AHet compared to WT. This pattern is reversed with the addition of CTCF CRISPR to ARID1AHet background. Left: All CTCF peaks with the CTCF motif. Right: Increasing CTCF peaks in ARID1AHet vs WT. (i) Correlation between baseline CTCF-binding strength in WT cells (vertical axis, binned from strong to weak peaks) and the CTCF occupancy change for ARID1AHet vs. WT (horizontal axis). Stronger WT peaks show larger occupancy gains when ARID1A is lost, suggesting cBAF preferentially restrains high-affinity CTCF sites.

(a) Schematic representation of the experiment and immunoblots showing the efficiency of ARID1A degradation after 6 h or 24 h in hES cells, representative from 3 independent experiments. (b) Motif enrichment after 6 h or 24 h of ARID1A degradation in hES showing that CTCF sites opening is a direct effect of cBAF loss, as the changes are present already at 6 h. Bars show multivariable linear model coefficient estimates from modeling peak log2 fold-change as a function of motif presence and GC content. Error bars show 95% Wald confidence intervals using heteroskedasticity consistent standard errors, and p-values are BH adjusted two-sided robust coefficient tests. Peaks derived from n = 2 biological replicates per condition. (c) Heatmaps showing ChIP signals of all CTCF peaks, or ARID1A binding at the CTCF-bound regions in hES cells after 6 h of ARID1A degradation or in DMSO-treated control, and log2 fold change of CTCF binding between dTAG- and DMSO-treated cells, as well as density plots showing CTCF or ARID1A-HA ChIP signal in all sites (n = 2, two biological replicates for each condition). (d) Pie charts showing proportions of peaks occupied by CTCF, SMC3 (cohesin) or both. The majority of newly accessible sites are cohesin-bound insulator elements. (e) Schematics of the time-course experiment. RIVA cells were treated with FHD-286 and subjected to ATAC-seq after 4 h, 12 h and 24 h of treatment. Motif enrichment analysis shows that opening of CTCF-binding sites occurs as early as at 4 h of treatment and persists through 24 h, arguing that increased CTCF accessibility is a direct effect of BAF loss. Bars and error bars calculated as in (b). Peaks derived from n = 2 technical replicates per condition. (f) Schematic representation of the experimental design. Cells were isolated from mouse embryos and transduced with either a Cre-GFP-expressing vector to induce gene deletion or a GFP-only control vector. GFP-positive cells were sorted and subjected to a CellTiter-Glo proliferation assay. Proliferation at 24 h (relative to 0 h) is presented as the fold-change in luminescence signal of knockout cells compared to their corresponding control cells derived from the same embryo. Two independent embryos were analyzed per genotype, with data from different embryos indicated by distinct symbols (circles or triangles). n = 16 for Arid1aHet and Arid1aHetCtcfHet (2 embryos, 8 technical replicates each) and n = 8 for CtcfHet (2 embryos, 4 technical replicates each). Statistical significance was determined using two-way ANOVA. Error bars represent mean ± SD. (g) Representative proliferation curves of cells derived from a single embryo over 72 h (n = 4 technical replicates per genotype, experiment conducted 2 times, using different embryos of each genotype in each experiment). Statistical significance was assessed by two-way ANOVA, and the p-value for the genotype factor is indicated in each graph. Error bars represent mean ± SD. (h) Overall survival of patients in the pan-cancer TCGA cohort (PMID: 24071849) stratified by CTCF expression z-scores (n = 6,931). Hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated relative to the “Very High” CTCF expression group (> 4), and log-rank tests were performed in cBioPortal (PMID: 22588877). Kaplan–Meier curves are displayed through 90 months of follow-up. High CTCF expression is associated with poorer prognosis. (i) ATAC-seq performed 48 h post CRISPR in D. melanogaster cell line S2. Immunoblot confirming the reduction of Osa expression. PCA of ATAC-Seq shows clear separation of chromatin accessibility status between WT and osa knock out samples. n = 4, comprising 2 technical replicates from two independent CRISPR reactions targeting two different parts of osa gene. (j) ATAC-seq motif enrichment in osa-deleted samples shows opening of chromatin regions that contain binding motifs for fruit fly insulators Su(Hw), BEAF, CTCF and cohesin-associated (Pnr) proteins. Bars and error bars calculated as in (b). Peaks derived from n = 2 biological replicates per condition. Gel source data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1. Schematic in f created in BioRender; Debek, S. https://biorender.com/ejlfwm8 (2026).

(a) Left: Western blot analysis of CTCF immunoprecipitation with and without the addition of endonuclease (Benzonase). CTCF-PBRM1 interaction is preserved after the digestion of nucleic acids, supporting the suggested direct interaction between the proteins. Representative blot from two technical replicate runs using samples from a single experiment. Right: DNA concentration in the sample before and after endonuclease treatment measured by BioAnalyzer (Agilent). (b) Reciprocal immunoprecipitation of CTCF and PBRM1 in SUM159 cell line followed by immunoblot analysis, confirming that CTCF preferentially interacts with PBAF components. Representative blot from two independent experiments. (c) Same as in (b) for Raji cell line. Representative blot from two independent experiments. (d) CTCF does not co-fractionate with cBAF in wild-type cells. Glycerol gradient fractionation of nuclear extracts from SUM159 cells, and immunoblot analysis for the cBAF subunit ARID1A, the PBAF-specific subunit PBRM1, shared BAF components, cohesin (SMC3), and CTCF. In WT cells, both cBAF and PBAF subunits sediment in high-molecular-weight fractions (corresponding to higher glycerol percentages), consistent with their expected size (~1.5–2 MDa). In contrast, CTCF is predominantly detected in lower-molecular-weight fractions, separate from PBAF, while cohesin (SMC3) also distributes in distinct fractions. These data indicate that under basal conditions, CTCF does not stably associate with the PBAF complex. Representative blot analysis from two independent experiments. (e) cBAF loss enhances CTCF-PBAF association. Glycerol gradient profiles from ARID1A-Hom (cBAF-deficient) cells reveal a redistribution of CTCF toward higher-molecular-weight fractions that overlap with PBAF-containing fractions. The PBAF-specific subunit PBRM1 remains enriched in these heavy fractions, and CTCF abundance in these fractions is substantially increased compared to WT cells. This shift suggests that loss of cBAF promotes association between CTCF and PBAF-containing complexes. Representative blot analysis from two independent experiments. (f) Heatmaps showing ARID1A binding (ChIP-seq) in WT, ARID1AHet or WT FHD-286-treated SUM159 cells (n = 3 replicates for WT and ARID1AHet, and n = 2 for FHD-286-treated). (g) Same as (f), but or PBRM1. PBAF occupancy is increased after FHD-286 treatment, while cBAF shows a decrease. Peak order is identical to (f). (h) Proportion of ARID1A- or PBRM1-bound regions that close (ATAC Down) or open (ATAC Up) after pan-BAF inhibition with FHD-286. The closing peaks are predominantly occupied by cBAF (ARID1A), suggesting that FHD-286 primarily targets cBAF, which potentially enables PBAF to expand its activity. (i) Immunoprecipitation of CTCF followed by immunoblot analysis in RIVA and SUM159 cells treated with FHD-286, or DMSO. CTCF-PBAF interaction is not affected by BAF inhibition. Representative blot from an experiment performed in two clones for each cell line, in two technical western blot repetitions. (j) Western blot validation of selective BAF degraders, confirming on-target effects for PBAF and ncBAF inhibition. Representative blot from 3 independent experiments. Gel source data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1. (k) Heatmaps (top) and density plots (bottom) showing log2 fold change ATAC signal at summits overlapping with CTCF ChIP peaks in RIVA ARID1AHet (left) or WT (right) cells treated with PBRM1i or DMSO after 24 hours (n=3 for each condition).

(a) Multi-mark chromatin segmentation pipeline overview, showing the input for the model: accessibility (ATAC-seq), chromatin binding (CTCF and PBRM1 ChIP-seq) in WT, as well as their log2 fold change between ARID1AHet and WT. (b) Profile plots of input samples for the MMM model showing signal and log2 fold change. (c) Input datasets for the model. Upper panel: WT values for ATAC-seq, PBRM1, and CTCF ChIP-seq. Lower panel: log2 fold change comparison between ARID1AHet and WT, highlighting differential chromatin accessibility and binding patterns in response to BAF loss. (n = 4 per condition for ATAC, n = 3 for PBRM1, n = 6 for CTCF). Dashed outlines indicate top CTCF-gaining clusters with matched ATAC-seq gains in BAF inhibitor and cell line atlas data in the same regions. (d) Model readouts. RNA expression profiling of genomic clusters affected by BAF loss. CTCF-Increasing clusters (G1-G8) show transcriptional upregulation in their proximal genes, suggesting that increased CTCF accessibility corresponds with changes in gene activity. ChIP/CNR log2 fold-change readout includes BAF subunits (BRD7, SMARCA4, ARID1A), cohesin (SMC3), and active histone modifications (H3.3, H3K27ac). BRD7, a PBAF-specific subunit, is also enriched at CTCF-increasing cluster sites, along with increased cohesin (SMC3) and core BAF complex components, whereas ARID1A, a cBAF subunit, is depleted in most affected clusters. Also, analysis of histone modifications reveals that regions gaining CTCF binding exhibit a gain of H3K27ac and increased nucleosome turnover as indicated by H3.3 incorporation. (n = 6 per condition for RNA-seq, n = 4 for BRD7, n = 1 for SMARCA4, n = 3 for ARID1A, n = 2 for SMC3, n = 3 for H3.3, n = 3 for H3K27ac. In violin plot center dot is the median and error bars show 25th–75th percentiles). (e) ATAC-seq log2 fold change analysis comparing the effects of pan-BAF, and PBAF inhibition vs. DMSO. Loss of cBAF leads to increased chromatin accessibility at CTCF-associated loci, whereas PBAF inhibition reduces accessibility, highlighting a compensatory role for PBAF in the absence of cBAF (n = 3–4 for each condition and treatment). (f) Same analysis as (e) but across cell lines in the ATAC-seq dataset (Fig. 1). Most cell lines exhibit a general increase in CTCF accessibility. n = 3 to 6 per condition across the cell lines. (g) Distribution of CTCF motif abundance across clusters. CTCF-Increasing clusters show a strong enrichment of the M1 CTCF motif, consistent with the observation that high-occupancy CTCF sites are most affected by BAF loss. (h) Magnified inset of CTCF binding distribution in the segmented chromatin regions for the CTCF gain clusters. Left: Mean of WT CTCF signal for each cluster. Right: log2 fold change between ARID1AHet and WT. (Profiles shown are cluster center ±1 kb. n = 6 per condition). (i) Left: TAD Insulation Score analysis in WT cells, showing that CTCF-Increasing clusters from (h) exhibit higher insulation (lower scores), suggesting that these sites act as stronger insulators in the genome. Right: Delta TAD insulation between ARID1AHet and WT, highlighting that the largest gains in insulation (shaded red) occur within CTCF-Increasing clusters, further linking BAF loss to genome structural changes (Profiles shown are center +/− 100 kb, using 10 kb bins. n = 2 per condition for Micro-C, pooled).

(a-b) log2 fold change relative contact probability (HET/WT) across genomic distances for regions containing either differentially increased or stable CTCF (a) and SMC3 (b) peaks. Gray bands show 95% confidence interval. (c) Waterfall plot representing the delta connectivity score differences between ARID1AHet and ARID1A WT cells in single-cell multiome. (d) Expression of genes with the highest gain of connectivity due to ARID1A loss in ARID1A WT (left) and ARID1AHet (right) projected onto UMAP dimensionality reduction based on Harmony corrected RNA and ATAC. (e) Example genome track showing DORC (domains of regulatory chromatin) connectivity of peaks linked to gene expression in ARID1AHet and WT cells. (f) Expression of genes with DORCs. p value = 1e-300 by two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum. n = 12704 cells for ARID1A WT and n = 13940 cells for ARID1AHet. (g) DORC connectivity score of regions with increased CTCF binding (ChIP peaks) in ARID1AHet vs. WT cells. Significance of connectivity measured by two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test with a p-value = 1.9e-09. Number of DORCs identified in only WT, or only ARID1AHet cells. p-value = 1.4e-39 by fishers exact test. n is indicated in the right panel. (h) Expression of genes linked to regions with increased CTCF binding. p-value = 1e-300 by two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum. n = 543 genes. (i-j) Same as (g) and (h), but for PBRM1 peaks. p-values = 3.0e-12, 3.7e-46, and 1e-300 respectively. n = 442 genes. (k-l) Same as (g) and (h), but for BRD7 peaks. p-values = 1.5e-26, 1.4e-53 and 1e-300 respectively. n = 564 genes. For f, g, h, i, j, k, l center dot is the median and error bars show 25th–75th percentiles.

All panels show aggregated data from two clones for each genotype, in n = 3 technical replicates per clone. (a) Contour scatterplot showing log2 fold-change of intra-TAD vs. inter-TAD connectivity changes across the three genotypes, showing that BAF loss leads to increased intra-TAD interactions which are mostly reverted in ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells. (b) The inter-TAD vs intra-TAD connectivity ratios across all TADs. The decrease in the inter-/intra-TAD ratio observed in ARID1AHet cells gets reverted in ARID1AHetARID2Hom. p-values calculated with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Boxplots display median and IQR (Q1-Q3), with whiskers extending to values within 1.5 IQR. (c) Aggregate TAD analysis (ATA) plot on Micro-C matrix showing delta difference between WT and ARID1AHetARID2Hom compared to ARID1AHet in strengthening TADs (top) and weakening TADs (bottom). (d) Aggregate peak analysis (APA) plots centered on all TAD boundaries. Left: WT signal shown as enrichment of observed signal normalized to randomly shifted local background, indicating the insulation valley around the boundary separating the flanking TADs. Center: Loss of inter-TAD connectivity and increased insulation in ARID1AHet compared to WT. Right: Partial normalization of inter-TAD connection and reduction in insulation in ARID1AHetARID2Hom compared to ARID1AHet. (e) The example loci from Fig. 3d with the addition of ARID1AHetARID2Hom and delta comparison to ARID1AHet, indicating a partial reversal of connectivity changes and normalization of inter-TAD connection with ARID2 deletion on ARID1AHet background. In CTCF/SMC3 log2 fold change tracks, red and blue indicate positive and negative log2 fold change values, respectively, between ARID1AHet and WT ChIP-seq peaks. ChIP track display CPM signal plotted on a common scale.

(a) Waterfall plot representing the delta connectivity score differences between ARID1AHet and ARID1A WT cells, as well as ARID1AHetARID2Hom and ARID1AHet in single-cell multiome. Genes were ordered by the difference in connectivity between ARID1AHet and WT cells. (b) Expression of genes with the highest gain of connectivity due to ARID1A loss (ARID1AHet vs WT) in ARID1A WT (left) and ARID1AHet (middle) and ARID1AHetARID2Hom (right) projected onto UMAP dimensionality reduction based on Harmony corrected RNA and ATAC. (c) Violin plot (left) showing DORC connectivity scores of regions with significantly increased CTCF binding (ChIP peaks) in ARID1AHet vs WT, in WT, ARID1AHet or ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells. Indicated p-values for significance of connectivity were calculated by two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test. Bar plot (right) showing number of DORCs identified in WT, ARID1AHet or ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells. Indicated p-values were calculated by fisher exact test. n is indicated in the right panel. (d) Violin plot (left) showing DORC connectivity scores of regions with significantly decreased CTCF binding (ChIP peaks) ARID1AHetARID2Hom vs ARID1AHet, in WT, ARID1AHet or ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells. Indicated p-values for significance of connectivity were calculated by two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test. Bar plot (right) showing number of DORCs identified in WT, ARID1AHet or ARID1AHetARID2Hom cells. Indicated p-values were calculated by fisher exact test. n is indicated in the right panel. (e-h) Expression of genes gaining connectivity (e), or linked with BRD7 (f), CTCF (g) or PBRM1 (h). Indicated p-values were calculated by two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test. n = 2459, 748, 748, and 573 genes respectively. (i) Example loci showing increased connectivity in ARID1AHet cells, and its reduction after the deletion of ARID2 (ARID1AHetARID2Hom). For c, d, e, f, g, h center dot is the median and error bars show 25th–75th percentiles.

(a) Motif enrichment analysis of differentially accessible regions after the loss of cBAF (ARID1AHet), or cBAF and ISWI complexes (ARID1AHet, SMARCA5Hom) vs. WT RIVA cells. Deletion of SMARCA5, the catalytic subunit of ISWI, in ARID1AHet background results in widespread closure of CTCF sites, representing a reversal of the phenotype observed with ARID1A loss alone (n = 3 technical replicates from each of the 2 clones per genotype). Bars and error bars show multivariable linear model coefficient estimates and 95% Wald confidence intervals, and p-values are BH adjusted two-sided robust coefficient tests. Statistics were derived across n = 35,310 peaks. (b) Proliferation assay shows that the deletion of SMARCA5 eliminates the hyperproliferative phenotype of ARID1AHet cells. Data shown are from 4 independent experiments, with 3 technical replicates per clone in each experiment. Data from independent clones of the same genotype were pooled across independent experiments as biological replicates, yielding n = 4 for WT, n = 4 for ARID1AHet and n = 8 for ARID1AHetSMARCA5Hom. Two-way ANOVA p values for genotype × time interaction are indicated in the graph. Error bars represent mean ± SD. (c) Left: Venn diagram showing overlap of PBAF ChIP, CTCF ChIP, and ISWI-regulated ATAC sites. Right: Bar plot showing proportion of ISWI-regulated sites co-occupied by ISWI and CTCF, PBAF, both, or neither. Gel source data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

(a) Schematic representation of germinal center reaction (left) and the experiment (right) (b) Germinal center size is reduced by cBAF loss and not rescued by CTCF deletion. Flow cytometry quantification of germinal center B cell populations in conditional knockout mice (immunized with sheep red blood cells (SRBC). Mice with Arid1a haploinsufficiency in germinal center B cells show substantially smaller germinal centers compared to WT, indicating cBAF is required for normal GC formation (two-sided t-test). This GC size defect is not reversed in double-knockout (Arid1aHetCtcfHet) mice. The result suggests that while CTCF loss rescues the proliferative imbalance (dark zone expansion) caused by Arid1a loss, it does not restore overall GC size, consistent with other BAF-dependent factors (e.g., PU.1, NF-κB) controlling GC development. CTCF loss rescues dark zone expansion across immunization models (two-sided t-test). Phenotype of dark zone vs light zone composition in germinal centers after an independent antigen challenge (NP-KLH immunization). For SRBC immunization: WT n = 7 mice; Arid1aHet n = 9 mice; CtcfHet n = 3 mice; Arid1aHetCtcfHetn = 7 mice. For NP-KLH immunization: n = 7 mice from each genotype. Error bars represent mean ± SD. (c) PCA of chromatin accessibility in sorted DZ (CB, centroblasts) and LZ (CC, centrocytes) B cells, showing that the chromatin changes induced by Arid1a loss are reversed upon CTCF deletion. (d) Representation of PC1 values from (e). Boxplots display median and IQR (Q1-Q3), with whiskers extending to values within 1.5 IQR. (e) Top: Schematic representation of the experimental workflow. Bottom left: PCA of chromatin accessibility in sorted normal centroblast cells in WT, Arid1aHet, and Arid1aHom genotypes where PC1 separates the WT from cBAF loss. Bottom right: Projection of centroblast cells harvested from diseased Bcl2-Tg mouse on the same PCA space, showing that the tumour samples cluster with Arid1aHet samples in PC1. (f) Motif enrichment analysis of Bcl2-Tg+Arid1aHet mice compared to Bcl2-Tg background in pre-disease state (left) and after disease onset (center), showing an increase of Ctcf. Analysis performed as in Fig. 1a,g. Right: An example locus (proliferation marker Mki67) showing increased accessibility at CTCF motifs in the Bcl2-Tg+Arid1aHet samples. (g) CTCF motif enrichment calculated by comparing chromatin accessibility profiles of each individual mouse against healthy WT centroblasts. Bcl2-Tg+Arid1aHet tumors show similar levels of CTCF enrichment as Arid1aHet centroblasts on average, whereas Arid1a wild-type tumors show lower levels of enrichment. Center dot is the median and error bars show 25th–75th percentiles, p-values from two-sided t-test. (h) Flow cytometric analysis of germinal center dark zone phenotype in WT (n = 17), Arid1aHet (n = 10), Pbrm1Het (n = 14) and DKO (n = 17) mice, showing that loss of PBRM1 rescues the proliferative dark zone expansion phenotype caused by Arid1a deletion. Each dot represents a mouse used in phenotyping. Two-sided t-test, error bars represent mean ± SD. Panels e-g include n = 5 mice for WT and 3 for Arid1aHet in normals, n = 7 Bcl2-Tg, n = 13 Bcl2-Tg+Arid1aHet. Icons in b, e and h created in BioRender; Debek, S. https://biorender.com/wj90pea (2026).

#1438. Kevin Nisbet's lack of cool proved so costly for Aberdeen at Hampden... and underlines why he's not a man for the big occasion

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 18:27 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:32 EDT, 31 October 2026

In the build-up to this Premier Sports Cup semi-final, Aberdeen captain Kevin Nisbet spoke about the players needing to step up and deliver.

On a woeful run of form as they arrived at Hampden, and with huge pressure mounting on Stephen Robinson, Nisbet insisted the players owed the manager a performance and a result.

Just to take the heat off as much as anything else. With 76 minutes on the clock in this tense and cagey affair with Rangers, Nisbet had a golden opportunity.

With the score locked at 0-0, Stuart Armstrong fed a pass into Nisbet’s path and the ball was crying out to be struck first time.

Nisbet could probably see the whites of Ivor Pandur’s eyes. In the context of the game, it was as good a chance as Aberdeen could have hoped for.

But his finish was absolutely awful. Nisbet hesitated when he should have pulled the trigger straight away, allowing Olwethu Makhanya to make a block.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet reflects on a golden chance to fire Aberdeen ahead at Hampden

On such moments are cup semi-finals won and lost. Just seven minutes later, at the other end of the pitch, Ryan Naderi prodded home from close range to send Rangers through to the final.

Nisbet will surely be haunted by his miss. He has scored 13 goals this season. For all Aberdeen’s struggles, some have even touted him for a Scotland recall.

But he is not up to scratch at the top level. In some respects, he finds himself in the same boat as Lawrence Shankland.

Any time Shankland has been given an opportunity with Scotland, he hasn’t really taken it. Particularly in the World Cup in the summer.

Nisbet is a decent enough striker at Scottish Professional Football League level. But in the big moments in big games, he’s not good enough.

It was a chance he had to take. In the end, Aberdeen were left to rue what might have been as Rangers, who were poor for much of the game, edged through to the final.

All in all, this is a defeat which just piles more pressure on Stephen Robinson. His team did not play poorly but they did not win.

Nisbet took too long with the ball and allowed Olwethu Makhanya the chance to block his shot

There is no sense in trotting out excuses about being competitive and unlucky. Aberdeen were not unlucky.

They had a glorious chance to go in front late in the game and their captain wasted it. That is not misfortune. It is profligacy.

Robinson and his players now face a huge game against Hibs at Pittodrie next Saturday.

With the international break just around the corner, a time when clubs invariably change manager once the rot has set in, it could well be last-chance saloon for Robinson.

#1437. Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The N7-methylguanosine (m7G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex1,2,3,4. The m7G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m7G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

Over 150 RNA modifications have been described to date, with transfer RNA (tRNA) being one of the most highly modified RNA species5,6. tRNA modifications are critical for the folding, stability and function of tRNA2,7,8. One of the most prevalent tRNA modifications is m7G1,2. It is deposited at position 46 of tRNA (m7G46) by the METTL1–WDR4 heterodimeric protein complex, with METTL1 functioning as the catalytically active component of the complex, and WDR4 having a scaffolding and RNA-binding role2,3,4. The m7G modification on tRNA has been shown to have an important role in stabilizing the tRNA structure, regulating the translation of mRNA and influencing a number of cellular processes, including stress response and oncogenesis9,10,11,12,13. Recent studies have shown that METTL1 may also deposit the m7G modification on mRNAs and microRNA precursors14,15,16, although at a substantially lower rate compared with the m7G levels on the tRNA fraction.

Many studies have implicated the role of the epitranscriptome in the development and regulation of cancer17,18,19. An increasing amount of evidence shows that dysregulation of tRNA modifications and their pathways contributes to the pathogenesis of human disease, including cancer6,18. Notably, upregulation of METTL1 and its catalytic activity has been linked to oncogenic transformation as well as the initiation and maintenance of aggressive haematological and solid malignancies, including acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), melanoma, glioblastoma, liver and lung cancers11,20,21,22. Moreover, the non-catalytic function of METTL1 has recently been linked to the development of sarcomas through its interaction with the multi-tRNA synthetase complex23.

To date, epitranscriptomic drug discovery efforts have largely focused on the targeting of the m6A mRNA modification and its regulators24,25,26,27. Early prototype inhibitors of METTL1 have recently been described and support the feasibility of pharmacologically inhibiting METTL128,29. However, their limited potency and selectivity render them unsuitable as tools to assess the molecular and therapeutic impact of targeting METTL1 catalytic inhibition. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a potent and highly selective first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1 that demonstrates significant anti-tumour activity across diverse cancer types through the reduction in m7G on tRNA substrates of METTL1.

We performed a high-throughput screen of 250,000 diverse drug-like compounds. After initial hit triaging, STM4529 was identified as a singleton non-S-adenosyl methionine (non-SAM)-related hit that inhibited METTL1 with a half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) of around 15 μM (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed that STM4529 binding to METTL1 was competitive with the SAM analogue S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH), indicating its binding to the catalytic site of METTL1 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). After extensive chemical optimization of potency, selectivity and in vitro and in vivo absorption–distribution–metabolism–excretion properties, we identified STM9005 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Note 1a).

a, The chemical structure of STM9005. b, Representative biochemical activity assay showing inhibition of the METTL1–WDR4 enzyme complex using a concentration range of STM9005 and the less active analogue STM9001. c, Representative METTL1 cellular target engagement of STM9005 and STM9001 was assessed using the InCELL Pulse assay. For b and c, the geometric mean IC50 and s.d. indicated in brackets were derived from n = 13 (STM9005) and n = 3 (STM9001) independent experiments. d, STM9005 selectively inhibits METTL1–WDR4 in a methyltransferase profiling panel of 49 methyltransferases. The asterisk indicates less than 1% activity remaining. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 2 independent samples. e, The reduction in m7G modification on small-fraction RNA after treatment with vehicle, 0.6 or 1.2 µM of STM9005 was measured using RNA MS in the MOLM-13 and OCI-AML2 cell lines. Ratio of m7G to A, C, G and U nucleosides. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 independent samples. P values were calculated using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with multiple-comparison correction. f, Crystal structure of METTL1 (carbon atoms in green) in a complex with STM9005 (carbon atoms are shown in purple). The interactions between the compound and the protein or neighbouring water molecules (red spheres) are indicated (yellow dashed lines). PDB: 9RYL. g, The pharmacokinetic (PK) profile of STM9005 in vivo was measured in mouse plasma after a single i.p. dose of either 10 or 30 mg per kg. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 2 (12 h time point for 10 mg per kg cohort) and n = 3 (all other groups) mice. Compound exposure over time (area under the curve, AUC), maximal concentrations (Cmax) and half-life (t1/2) are indicated in the pharmacokinetics summary table. Pharmacokinetics values after oral dosing are shown for comparison. p.o., oral gavage.

STM9005 inhibited recombinant METTL1 enzyme activity with an IC50 < 13 nM, a value restricted by the lower detection limit of the assay (Fig. 1b). To use a more sensitive assay system and to verify binding to METTL1 in an orthogonal system, we performed SPR analysis, which demonstrated direct stoichiometric high-affinity binding of STM9005 to METTL1 with a Kd of 2 nM (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Moreover, using a cellular target engagement assay, we confirmed cell penetration and binding of STM9005 to METTL1 in cells with an IC50 of 13 nM (Fig. 1c). STM9005 was found to be highly specific to METTL1 as it had no effect on the activity of other RNA-methyltransferases (METTL3/14, METTL16, BCDIN3D, TSG1 and NSUN2) when used at comparable concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 1e), and exhibited greater than 10,000-fold selectivity for METTL1–WDR4 when tested against a broad panel of 49 RNA-, DNA- and protein-methyltransferases (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1). Moreover, no significant off-target toxicity liabilities were identified when STM9005 was tested in a broad panel of 97 kinases (KINOMEscan, Eurofins DiscoverX; Supplementary Table 2) and over 70 assays testing a range of receptors and enzymes commonly associated with drug toxicity (SAFETYscan 47, Eurofins DiscoverX; Supplementary Table 3).

To further investigate the cellular activity of STM9005, we applied RNA mass spectrometry (MS) to assess the specific effect of STM9005 on the m7G modification level of tRNA from the previously known METTL1-dependent AML cell lines MOLM-13 and OCI-AML211,30,31. We observed a significant decrease in m7G levels (Fig. 1e), but not in the levels of the m1A and m5C RNA modifications (Extended Data Fig. 1f). To further quantify the cellular effect of STM9005 on m7G-modified tRNA, we developed an antibody-based m7G detection assay (Meso Scale Discovery (MSD)), which enabled us to measure the effect of STM9005 on tRNA-Val. This demonstrated a concentration-dependent decrease in tRNA-Val-m7G after treatment with STM9005 with an IC50 of 34 nM (Extended Data Fig. 1g), confirming potent inhibition of tRNA modification by STM9005 in cells at nanomolar concentrations. Moreover, we confirmed STM9005 acts specifically on the METTL1–m7G tRNA axis, as we observed no significant effect on m7G modification of 18S ribosomal RNA (Extended Data Fig. 1h).

To characterize the binding of STM9005 to METTL1 further, we performed X-ray crystallography, confirming unequivocally that STM9005 binds to the SAM-binding site of METTL1 (Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 1i, Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1b). Notably, part of STM9005 binds in a pocket not previously observed in METTL1 crystal structures, where it forms molecular interactions such as the hydrogen bonds between Tyr184 and the central carbonyl moiety of STM9005, and a pi-carbon interaction between Phe159 and the tetrahydroisoquinoline methyl of STM9005, providing the basis for its high affinity and selectivity. In strong support of this, STM9001, a diastereomer of STM9005 in which the tetrahydroisoquinoline methyl is in an opposite orientation, is around 100-fold less active (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a,g), providing further evidence of the specificity and binding mode of STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 1i and Supplementary Table 1).

The observed binding of STM9005 to the catalytic pocket of METTL1 did not impact the RNA or protein levels of METTL1 after in vitro treatment (Extended Data Fig. 1j,k), in contrast to the significant and selective effect observed on the m7G tRNA modification levels (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). Finally, pharmacokinetic profiling of STM9005 in mice after a single intraperitoneal (i.p.) dose of either 10 or 30 mg per kg showed good bioavailability with maximal plasma exposures of 13 and 56 μM, respectively, and a half-life of around 1 h. Importantly, at the 12 h time point, STM9005 plasma levels remain above the METTL1 cellular IC50, indicating METTL1 inhibition in vivo over a period of at least 12 h (Fig. 1g).

Taken together, these data establish STM9005 as a potent, selective and bioavailable catalytic inhibitor of METTL1 that is suitable for both in vitro and in vivo investigations.

To investigate the anti-cancer potential of STM9005 in cellular models, we initially screened the impact of STM9005 treatment in three different cancer cell panels using colorimetric assays which measure metabolic activity (MTS assay). For these experiments, we used cancer cell models that were either previously reported to be sensitive to the genetic inhibition of METTL111,32,33, or their METTL1-dependency status (sensitivity or resistance) was validated here using CRISPR-based genetic disruption of METTL1/Mettl1 (human and mouse, respectively) in competitive co-culture assays (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We observed a dose-dependent reduction in the proliferation of human leukaemic cell lines (Fig. 2a), primary mouse AML models (Fig. 2b) and human and mouse solid cancer models (Fig. 2c) from different tissue origins (skin, lung, pancreas, colorectal, oesophageal and soft tissue). Investigating the direct effect of STM9005 on cell growth using a methylene blue assay, we observed highly potent, dose-dependent effects on the fitness and growth of a subset of these cell lines (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Additional reprofiling in proliferation assays using ATP quantitation under optimized culture conditions confirmed the anti-proliferative activity of STM9005 at submicromolar concentrations in these cells (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3b). By contrast, the diastereomer control compound STM9001 was significantly less potent in these systems, consistent with its reduced activity against the catalytic activity of METTL1, providing strong evidence that the anti-proliferative effects of STM9005 are due to METTL1 catalytic inhibition (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3b). There was also a significant dose-dependent negative effect seen in the colony forming potential of MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+-driven primary mouse AML cells after ex vivo treatment with STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Notably, the cancer models that appeared to be independent of METTL1 genetic loss (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) were also not significantly impacted after treatment with STM9005 (Fig. 2d). To confirm that the anti-proliferative effects of STM9005 are mediated specifically through METTL1, we assessed its impact in two insensitive (OE33, mPDAC2) and two sensitive (B16F10, mPDAC1) cancer cell lines with a loss of METTL1 or Mettl1 after CRISPR–Cas9 targeting. STM9005 treatment in both sensitive and insensitive cell lines resulted in no additional negative effect (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e) despite the absence of METTL1 protein (Extended Data Figs. 2a,b and 3a), consistent with the small molecule exerting its mechanism of action specifically through inhibition of METTL1’s catalytic activity.

In the context of haematological malignancies, pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 using STM9005 caused significant and dose-dependent myeloid differentiation in both human and primary mouse models of AML (Fig. 2f,g and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Moreover, we and others have previously shown that genetic inhibition of METTL1 negatively affected various cancer models by impacting their cell cycle status11,20. To examine whether the observed effect on cell cycle is dependent on the catalytic activity of METTL1 we analysed a panel of solid cancer cell lines with different tissues of origin and mutational background and showed that treatment with STM9005 causes a significant disruption of cell cycle, with a dose-dependent increase in cells in G0/G1 phase and a significantly decreased number of cells in S phase (Fig. 2h,i and Extended Data Fig. 3g,h) as the most common changes across the cell lines tested. Moreover, western blot analysis of cell-cycle-related markers confirmed the observed cell cycle dysregulation seen in the various cancer models tested here (Fig. 2j,k). Moreover, annexin V analysis showed no significant levels of apoptosis after treatment with STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 3i).

These data confirm the importance of METTL1’s methyltransferase activity in maintaining both haematological and solid cancers, and that pharmacological inhibition of its enzymatic activity is sufficient to elicit anti-cancer cellular effects.

To assess the molecular changes caused by treatment with STM9005, we analysed its impact across different layers of the transcriptome. We first performed modification-induced misincorporation tRNA sequencing (mim-tRNA-seq) to investigate the m7G modification status on tRNA fractions from B16F10 melanoma tumours and a primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+-driven AML. Analysis of the mim-tRNA-seq data revealed a highly specific and significant reduction in the m7G46 mark in known m7G-modified tRNAs—a result that was highly similar between both cancer models (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 4).

a,b, mim-tRNA-seq analysis of the mean (red) and individual replicate (grey) log2-transformed fold change (log2[FC]) in misincorporation at the m7G46 site of tRNAs (a) and the log2[FC] (grey) in tRNA levels (b) in B16F10 (left) and MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ (right) cells after 72 h treatment with vehicle or 2 µM STM9005. The purple asterisks represent a significant change (a; P < 0.01, unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests) or a significant decrease (b, Padj < 0.05, Wald test).
