#1407. Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1,2,3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative—growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials—has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb–OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm−3, mobility 124 cm2 V−1 s−1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors.

a, Calculated concentration of the growth-active species HPbO2− (black, left axis) and its differential response to hydroxide concentration, dCHPbO2−/dCOH− (red, right axis), as a function of pH at a total Pb concentration of 17.8 mM. b, Concentration of HPbO2− and its differential response to total Pb concentration, dCHPbO2−/dCPb, over a total Pb concentration range of 0.1–100 mM. c,d, Differential responses of the Pb–Cl complex (c) and Pb–acetate complex (d) to total Pb concentration at the indicated logarithmic ligand concentrations. The equilibrium calculations were performed using Visual MINTEQ. Together, these results identify an alkaline chemical window in which HPbO2− is abundant and comparatively buffered against variations in pH and precursor concentration, supporting stable control of supersaturation during aqueous PbS growth.

a, Texture factor of the PbS (200) reflection for films grown at pH values ranging from 11.0 to 11.4. Each point represents an independently prepared film and the distributions were obtained from seven independent measurements at each pH. The highest (200) texture factor was obtained at pH 11.2. b, Dynamic-light-scattering-derived particle counts as a function of reaction time at the indicated pH values. Solid lines represent the mean values and shaded regions indicate the variation across three repeated scans. The negligible particle signal at pH 11.2, together with the enhanced (200) texture factor, is consistent with the suppression of homogeneous nucleation and preferential PbS growth at the substrate interface.

a, Measured velocity spectra for applied vertical vibrations spanning 0.1–100 Hz. b, Enlarged velocity spectra near 40 Hz at the different driving amplitudes used in d; the peak velocity was taken as the vibration velocity amplitude. c, PbS (200) diffraction peak intensity (black, left axis) and FWHM (red, right axis) as functions of vibration frequency. The dashed lines indicate the corresponding values measured without externally applied vibration (0 Hz). d, PbS (200) peak intensity and FWHM as functions of vibration velocity amplitude at a fixed frequency of 40 Hz. Data in c and d are presented as mean ± standard deviation from n = 3 independently prepared films for each condition. The reduction in diffraction intensity and accompanying peak broadening at higher vibration frequencies and amplitudes are consistent with decreased crystallographic ordering under stronger mechanical perturbation.

a, Schematic illustration of the customized in situ synchrotron XRD configuration used to monitor aqueous PbS crystallization directly on a CMOS ROIC. b, Photograph of the experimental set-up, including the beamline configuration, sample holder and vibration-isolation platform; the growth cell is indicated by the red arrow. c, Representative one-dimensional radial intensity profiles obtained by integrating the two-dimensional diffraction patterns at selected reaction times. The PbS (002) peak near q ≈ 2.3 Å−1 increases progressively, whereas the reflections originating from the CMOS substrate remain detectable throughout the measurement. The PbS diffraction intensity increases continuously over the 200-min growth period, whereas the substrate signal gradually decreases. These time-resolved measurements directly reveal sustained PbS crystallization and film accumulation on the CMOS ROIC during aqueous growth.

a, Representative photographs of the substrate before and after aqueous PbS deposition, showing uniform film coverage over the full substrate area. b, Spatial distribution of the PbS film thickness measured by spectroscopic ellipsometry at the indicated sampling positions. The thickness variation across the wafer is limited to approximately 50 nm. c, Spatial distribution of the integrated intensity of the PbS (200) diffraction peak. d, Spatial distribution of the FWHM of the PbS (200) diffraction peak. Black points in b–d indicate the measurement positions and the continuous maps were generated by interpolation between these points. The colour scales represent film thickness in nm, diffraction intensity in arbitrary units and FWHM in degrees, respectively. Both the PbS (200) peak intensity and FWHM remain broadly uniform across the mapped region. Although minor localized variations are present, no systematic spatial degradation or large-scale gradients are observed, supporting well-controlled film growth and crystallographic uniformity over the inch-scale substrate.

a–c, Pole-figure maps of the PbS (220) (a), PbS (200) (b) and PbS (111) (c) reflections. The colour scales indicate diffraction intensity, whereas grey points denote positions with no detectable diffraction above the background. The (200) pole figure exhibits a strongly localized maximum at the centre, consistent with preferential alignment of the PbS (200) planes parallel to the substrate surface. The discrete symmetry-related maxima observed in the (220) and (111) pole figures, together with the absence of continuous diffraction rings, indicate a highly textured film with a limited population of randomly oriented grains. These measurements support the dominant out-of-plane orientation and low orientational dispersion of the MISI-grown PbS films.

a,e,i, Chemical-potential stability regions for In-doped, Sb-doped and Bi-doped PbS, respectively. Red points 1–3 denote S-rich, intermediate and Pb-rich conditions, respectively. b–d,f–h,j–l, Calculated defect-formation energies as functions of Fermi level under the corresponding chemical-potential conditions. Vertical dashed lines mark the equilibrium Fermi levels. Among the three dopants, substitutional SbPb exhibits the lowest formation energy and weakest competition from compensating acceptor defects, allowing the equilibrium Fermi level to approach or enter the conduction band. In-doped and Bi-doped PbS show comparatively higher donor-formation energies and stronger compensation, indicating narrower processing windows for stable n-type doping.

a–c, SEM image (a), high-resolution TEM image (b) and XRD pattern (c) of an undoped PbS film grown under optimized MISI conditions. d–f, Corresponding SEM image (d), high-resolution TEM image (e) and XRD (f) of an Sb-doped PbS film. The Sb-doped film retains a dense and continuous morphology without obvious pinholes or phase segregation. The measured lattice spacing decreases locally from 0.292 nm in the undoped film to 0.285 nm after Sb doping, consistent with local lattice contraction associated with Sb incorporation. The nearly unchanged position and intensity of the PbS (200) diffraction peak indicate that the average crystal structure and preferred orientation are preserved after doping.

a, Photograph of a PbSe film deposited directly on a CMOS ROIC substrate by the MISI process at room temperature. b, Surface SEM image of the on-chip PbSe film, showing dense and continuous crystalline coverage. c, XRD pattern of the PbSe film. The dominant PbSe reflections are indexed to the rock-salt phase, whereas the extra peaks originate from the Au and SiO2 layers of the CMOS ROIC; the reference PbSe diffraction pattern is shown at the bottom. d, Pole figure of the PbSe (200) reflection, indicating a pronounced preferred crystallographic orientation. e, Time-dependent current response of a PbSe photoconductive device under repeated on–off illumination from a 573-K blackbody source at a bias of 10 V and an incident power density of 0.1 mW cm−2. f, Normalized spectral photoresponse of the PbSe device, extending into the mid-wave infrared range. Together, the preserved film morphology, preferred crystallographic orientation and functional infrared photoresponse provide a proof-of-concept demonstration that the MISI strategy can be extended from PbS to PbSe.

#1406. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

Désiré Doué with a brilliant finish from range to give PSG an early lead in Manchester 😮‍💨 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/Uwilx7I37H

There is a certain irony that it was PSG who inflicted this defeat, ending City’s run of eight wins from eight in all competitions under Maresca.

It was a meeting of two clubs empowered more than any other by the riches of Gulf states: Abu Dhabi versus Qatar. Both have also had their run-ins over money. Both were sanctioned, but escaped full bans by Uefa for breaching financial fair play rules.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

So we should savour it and we did. That included Pep Guardiola on his first return to the Etihad – in a sign of solidarity – after quitting at the end of last season. Not that he savoured much of what he saw as PSG dominated City to such an extent that their fans adopted the “Poznan” celebration and the home supporters were silenced.

City could have gone in front before they conceded with the erratic Safonov – who was Gianluigi Donnarumma’s understudy and has become his unlikely replacement – punching a corner against his own crossbar before Antoine Semenyo shot the rebound over.

Then PSG ran all over City. They broke far too easily and scored far too easily. Not once, but twice, to go 2-0 up.

For the first, PSG countered, with City struggling to cover, and Doué caught out Donnarumma with a low shot inside his right-hand post from 22 yards.

Then PSG sliced through City’s defence with Ousmane Dembélé scooping the ball across the area to Doué who returned it back. Dembélé stooped to head home.

Ousmane Dembélé doubles PSG's lead just 2 minutes after they scored the first 🤯 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/MxhJ3oCWpC

After Achraf Hakimi headed against the inside of a post and City could not clear, the ball came back with Warren Zaïre-Emery flicking on Maghnes Akliouche’s cut-back. It ran to Vitinha who slammed in a first-time shot. It was the first time City had ever conceded three goals at home in the first half of this competition.

Vitinha with a BEAUTY to put PSG three up after just 30 minutes 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/vgqkI6kI3h

Maybe it was too easy. Maybe City could not continue to be so dominated but it was as if a switch was flicked when the teams returned. The chances came for City. Enzo Fernández should have scored from a close-range header and Haaland did, glancing in an inswinging Ndiaye cross.

Finally the City fans found their voices but then they were silenced. What a calamity for Donnarumma as he got a hand to Akliouche’s shot on the turn, but only palmed the ball up in the air before it bounced into the net.

But City did not stop. Nuno Mendes headed Josko Gvardiol’s flick off the line, Fernández hit a post before Bouaddi set up Haaland and he swept the ball past Safonov.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

There was time for PSG to miss a penalty, with Donnarumma comfortably saving Ferran Torres’s weak effort as City bravely continued to push. They lost, but it did not quite feel like that.

I think our start was quite good until the first goal. Then we conceded the second after one [more] minute and that created bad feelings so we struggled.

Second half we were much, much, much better and we probably deserved even something more.

It was strange to be honest because until the first goal we were in the game. We created things, didn’t concede and then the first goal led to the second one. When you concede two goals in two minutes it could [get] even worse.

At half-time we adjust something, didn’t lose our balance and in the second half we created enough to deserve something more. We adjusted the way we were pressing, something on the ball [too].

We lost the balance [by conceding the second goal]. Even at zero-three we created enough in the second half and Luis said afterwards that they had been quite lucky.

[A message for the fans?] We feel sorry for the first half but I think we’re quite happy now. Big game on Saturday [Ipswich at home at 3pm].

Both Arsenal and Barcelona had shorter prices than PSG to win the Champions League. Now it’s only Barcelona but I would say even they are not as good as PSG.

I doubt Guardiola will speak publicly but let’s wait and see.

FT: Manchester City 2-4 PSG #UCL | @bet365 | 18+ | #AD https://t.co/fPdGHP2OHp

Matheus Nunes, Bouaddi and Ndiaye were terrific. Small wonder that Luis Enrique and Maresca were exhaling hard as they embraced at the final whistle.

After a PSG performance in the first half that was as good as any I’ve seen in the past 10 years, Manchester City stiffened midfield in the second and went toe-to-toe to play their part in a basketball game with crosses and shots raining down on the PSG goal.

PSG have managed this last few minutes well, making important tackles and interceptions.

Pacho cuts out a pass to stop Semenyo pouncing.

City have had 27 attempts on goal, PSG 14.

PSG have dropped back in numbers and City are probing away.

Four minutes to come. O’Reilly replaces Enzo Fernandez.

Ferran Torres hit it low and not even halfway towards the right post. Terrible penalty, straightforward save.

His hand touched the sole of his boot as he slid in. Very soft.

Didn’t seen that Matheus Nunes touched Nuno Mendes from the replay.

Semenyo takes Haaland’s pass and his iffy control by the right of the penalty spot knocks it up. He does well to manipulate the defender out of the way but the ball won’t come down quick enough and he ends up stretching for it and lashes it over the bar.

Anderson, looking for Haaland from the left with a right-foot inswinger, overcooks it and Safonov comes off his line to catch.

Haaland meets Nunes daisycutter of a cross having been sent to the byline with his outstretched left leg as he slides in at the back post and Safonov sprawls to save on the goalline again. Should have scored but then again he was right at the extent of his reach when he made the connection.

Attempts on goal now number 36 after Kvaratskhelia’s tepid effort is saved by Donnarumma then Khusanov makes a last gasp tackle to stop Ferran Torres converting Joao Neves’s sensational pass.

This is a game for the ages. Too much action to chronicle fairly.

Ferran Torres → DembeleJoao Neves → Akliouche

Man City 2 PSG 4 (Haaland) Having just stuck an effort on to the top of the crossbar, Haaland sweeps a right-foot shot into the bottom left corner after terrific work from Bouaddi to win the ball, play a one-two with Fernandes and tee up the hit man.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

Now Anderson floods into space 20 yards out and runs on to a pass to shoot and Pacho again makes the block.

Ndiaye, who has been magic, fizzes a pass into Fernandez’s feet and the Argentina midfielder absolutely lashes a right foot shot into the angle of post and bar.

Mendes heads Gvardiol’s near-post flick from the free-kick off the line with Safonov stranded.

Ndiaye and Anderson combine and the latter’s tenacity is rearded with a free-kick out by the left corner flag when Zaire-Emery boots him.

Haaland blazes over with his left when put through down the inside-left channel by Fernandez’s fine pass. Maresca hops in frustration.

Semenyo does well to twist Pacho and Ruix but shoots into the side-netting.

Man City 1 PSG 4 (Akliouche) The winger receives the pass in the D facing the right touchline, spins and puts his laces through a left-foot piledriver. Donnarumma soars to his right, sticks up his top hand and tips it upwards but without enough power to push it over or wide and it drops behind the keeper and spins past the scrambling keeper.

Donnarumma is unable to keep out Akliouche's long range effort, and it's 4-1 to PSG 😳 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/u567943XOw

No doubt that PSG have been rattled by City’s ferocity in this half so far and have not been able to stop Bouaddi pulling the strings.

Bouaddi to Semenyo who sends Nunes on the underlap to the byline. The right-back fizzes over a cross and Ndiaye sticks out his right leg and just gets his toe to it but cannot hook it on target.

Fernandez drills a lofted pass from the right out to Ndiaye who burns past Hakimi down the outside and tries to but it back to Haaland but Marquinhos telescopes out a leg to knock it away. The crowd is now just electric having flat-lined in the first half.

City have turned the momentum around as they fly forward and create chances for Semenyo and then Haaland and Semenyo, the last two when the flag was poised to go up. Ndiaye is giving Hakimi a roasting.

Man City 1 PSG 3 (Haaland) Header from 12 yards, unstoppable, set up by Ndiaye with a superb cross moments after the substitute had drilled a shot straight at Safonov.

Erling Haaland pulls one back for City with a brilliant header 👀 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/piUSOy77PH

Erling Haaland is now Man City's all-time top goalscorer in the Champions League 👑 https://t.co/Od42nJxcKG

Enzo Fernandez should score with a header at the back post when he meets a cross from the right. He had run off Hakimi and was completely free but diverted it wide, helping it on its way,  rather than going back across Safonov.

Semenyo runs on to Haaland’s square pass and shoots with his left on the right of the box from 16 yards into a defender. Should have done better. City corner and Gvardiol, who had got away from his marker, pumps his header straight at Safonov.

Bouaddi immediately finds Ndiaye with a crossfield pass to the left and the winger drives towards the box but thrashes his rising shot over the bar.

Nunes → DiasNdiaye → DokuBouaddi → Cherki.

It would make sense to stiffen midfield by introducing Bouaddi and trying a different right-back though neither Rico Lewis or Matheus Nunes are defensively sound. Perhaps they should have done that at 2-0. Having said that, City have made four or five half-chances and, although they have been overwhelmed at times, the scoreline could be closer.

Anderson pings a pass out to Doku who dribbles in from the left, burns past Hakimi and then shoots low to Safonov’s left.

Marquinhos blocks Semenyo’s shot and then Fernandez is tackled as he tries to drive into the box.

Two minutes of stoppage time are signalled as Doku gives the ball away.

PSG corner as their fans sing their favourite Bonnie Tyler song. The ball rolled down Dias’s arm but he protests weirdly that it should be a goalkick. From the corner a deflection off Guehi forces Donnarumma into a save.

Chance for City with Gvardiol by the left post but he snatches at it.

City corner after Semenyo’s good run. PSG turn it behind at the near post and the second attempt, taken short, is worked to Haaland in the box but he makes a mess of his connection. Just before Hakimi, in acreshectares of free space has a dig and fires his shot straight at Donnarumma.

In the words of Barry Davies. Poor old Man City just don’t know what day it is. Hakimi whacks a right-foot shot inches past the left post.

City held a lengthy post-mortem after they conceded a third goal in the first half of a European match for the first time. They can’t cope with PSG’s three midfielders. Cherki is not built for this.

Man City 0 PSG 3 (Vitinha) A few seconds earlier Hakimi, evading his marker, hit the post with his header after Doué and Vitinha, one outside, inside, had Khusanov chasing shadows. Then PSG win the ball back and work it into the box from the right. Zaire-Emery’s backheel puts it perfectly in Vitinha’s path and he rockets a shot past Donnarumma and into the backboards behind the goal with a thud.

Vitinha with a BEAUTY to put PSG three up after just 30 minutes 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/vgqkI6kI3h

Donnarumma dives to his right to save Vitinha’s shot but can only parry it and back come PSG with such slick passing they manipulate space for their runners to glide into. It’s Zaire-Emery’s turn to have a shot and Guehi wears it flush in the face.

From the corner Doku has the vision to spot a gap for Anderson to burst into the box but Anderson isn’t on the same wavelength and is out of the blocks too late.

Doku, who is playing well, diddles Hakimi with an explosive start from a standstill to drive past him and ping a cross to the back post. Haaland, behind Pacho, can’t track the flight properly with the defender blocking his view. In the end he has a free header but saw it so late he can only head it back across goal. Safety firts from PSG who put it behind for a corner.

Haaland tries to force a shot past Pacho who is too close and makes a solid block. Moments later Semenyo, looking for Haaland at the back post, bends a left-foot cross from the right over his head and out for a goal-kick. Haaland shoots him an old-fashioned look.

#1404. Shambolic off the park, shambolic on it, dire defeat at Falkirk leaves O'Neill on thin ice

Published: 10:28 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 10:58 EDT, 1 November 2026

It took Celtic supporters the best part of half an hour on Sunday afternoon to belt out their now traditional rendition of ‘Sack the Board, Sack the Board’.

But as dysfunctional as this club may be off the park, there’s no doubt things are every bit as bad on it. This is an organisation that requires a rebuild from top to bottom. No one should be exempt.

Not the board members, not the management team, not the players. The whole thing is a shambles.

The table will show the champions are right on track to defend their crown. Indeed, the stats here will show this was a contest they dominated. But anyone with a set of eyes and any sort of common sense knows the real story.

Ahead of the match, Martin O’Neill insisted he is essentially oblivious to the outside noise around his team. Aye right.

Callum McGregor looks frustrated as Celtic go down in Falkirk

Scott Tanser celebrates his goal with Falkirk team-mate Owen Eames

Legend at the club though he may be, the Northern Irishman is surely on thin ice. Any other Celtic manager with three wins in his last 10 in all competitions certainly would be.

Frankly, he’s kidding himself on when he says he’s been satisfied with Celtic’s start to the season. The fans aren’t buying that nonsense any more. Does the man himself even believe it?

He continually talks about how his team need time to find their feet. More drivel. We’re now in November. Falkirk also signed 17 in the summer and they seem to be doing relatively well.

The football is just atrocious to watch. It has been all season. Such is the standard of the opposition in Scotland, they usually have just about enough quality to get away with it.

But that’s not a long-term solution to an increasingly worrying problem.

Falkirk, by the way, were outstanding here. They have now won four games on the bounce, each in a thoroughly un-Falkirk way.

Their success under John McGlynn has been built on the ability to pass teams off the park. This victory was far more to do with grit, determination and unity than anything else. Three qualities their opponents are lacking.

Falkirk play like a team. Celtic play like a bunch of individuals. And unless something changes pronto, things are going to get even uglier.

Just as they did in the 2-1 win over Hibernian at Easter Road last week, Celtic fell behind early doors.

Finley Barbrook picked up a loose ball midway inside the visitors’ half before finding Ryan Strain in acres of space on the right-hand side.

The full-back’s cross should have been blootered clear by Cameron Carter-Vickers at the back post with minimal fuss. Goodness knows what he actually tried to do, with the ball simply bouncing off the big American and right into the path of the grateful Ethan Ross, who couldn’t miss from five yards out.

Celtic winger Haissem Hassan gets involved in a scuffle with Falkirk players

Shocking stuff from a Celtic perspective. Carter-Vickers’ comments questioning Celtic’s ‘random’ style following defeats to Rangers in September were bang on the money. But he would do well to examine his own performances too. He’s not as good as some fans seem to think.

It took 10 minutes for Celtic to muster up a response. Liam Scales’ long ball found Camilo Duran in behind the Falkirk defence. His strike across goal from a tight angle beat Scott Bain, but not the far post.

Haissem Hassan’s curler from the follow-up was then brilliantly tipped round the post by the keeper.

Jacob Murrell is the country’s in-form striker with five goals in his last seven outings, but sclaffed a shot wide from the penalty spot at the end of a lovely move involving Owen Eames and Scott Tanser down at the corner flag.

Duran should have levelled things up on the half-hour mark after getting on the end of a wicked Hassan ball into the six-yard box, but headed straight at Bain. Anywhere else but right down the middle would have done the trick.

He was made to pay for that miss as Falkirk doubled their advantage with a wonderful team goal on 38 minutes. Eames was given far too much space on the Falkirk left, but take nothing away from the way he threaded an inch-perfect pass into the path of the underlapping Tanser.

He took one touch to set himself as he drove into the box before coolly slotting past Johnstone. It was the kind of football we’ve become accustomed to seeing on a weekly basis from this side under John McGlynn.

Yes, Celtic looked like they couldn’t even be bothered to try and stop them but that’s not Falkirk’s problem. Their execution was flawless.

Man-of-the-Match Bain was once again called into action as the break came into view, and he once again stepped up, tipping Duran’s left-footed strike from 18 yards around the post.

Martin O'Neill looks on in dismay as Celtic suffer in Falkirk

O’Neill could have taken off any one of his so-called big-name stars at half-time and there would have been no grounds for complaint. He settled for just the one, replacing Callum Osmand with James Forrest.

Osmand should never be playing on the wing anyway. In Yang Hyun-Jun’s absence – and with Jota still searching for fitness – he has had a run of games in that position. You suspect he won’t be holding on to it for long. Square pegs in round holes, and all that.

If O’Neill did give his players a boot up the backside at the interval, you wouldn’t have known it, conceding a shocking third through Murrell within minutes of the restart. Fortunately for the visitors, they got away with it, with VAR spotting that the ball was bundled in by the striker’s hand.

Forrest forced a comfortable stop from Bain on the half-turn, with Callum McGregor then blazing over from a promising position.

The captain has been a shadow of himself all season. In truth, he looks a yard or two off the pace.

For so long, we’ve heard that Celtic just can’t do without him. However, playing like this, he isn’t helping this team.

Bain’s stop to deny Forrest on 68 minutes was simple enough. The one which denied substitute Benjamin Nygren seconds later to seal the points was right out of the top drawer.

The Bairns hadn’t beaten Celtic in 19 years coming into this one. Given the state of this Celtic side, is anyone truly surprised that run has come to a halt?

#1402. Mikel Arteta's mission to conquer his Anfield demons: Why Arsenal boss must overcome psychological damage from his playing days and take the handbrake off as he plots first win at Liverpool, writes ISAAN KHAN

Published: 08:47 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 11:13 EDT, 1 November 2026

The word 'Anfield' still haunts Mikel Arteta.

It was there, 12 years ago, that the Spaniard suffered a chastening experience after losing 5-1 there as an Arsenal player in February 2014.

In a subsequent interview with Spanish newspaper Marca, Arteta used the term 'pajara' - a Spanish phrase com monly associated with cyclists who suddenly run out of energy - to describe a sensation mirroring mental paralysis. He had been caught up in an Anfield tornado.

'Suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around, the game is passing all over me and I cannot react,' Arteta reflected.

'Everyone is thinking, 'What is he doing?' I cannot react, emotionally, physical. I cannot cope, everything goes fast and I only had that feeling in my career once - and it was at Anfield.'

Such was the impact of that trauma that Arteta felt compelled to bring a slice of Anfield to Arsenal's London Colney base ahead of a league meeting in November 2021.

Mikel Arteta (right) has consistently found life tough when managing away at Anfield

Going to Anfield has become something akin to a hoodoo - and it shows no signs of abating

Arteta surrounded the training pitch with enormous speakers which blared out 'You'll Never Walk Alone' during a training session, in hope the noise would ready his players to tackle the very atmosphere he himself wilted in. It was to no avail.

The Gunners found themselves on the end of a 4-0 drubbing and Arteta on the end of mocking from critics for his alternative methods.

Five years later, Arsenal's away day hoodoo against the Reds has shown no signs of abating.

The north London club's league record against Liverpool away under Arteta reads: six games, three draws, three defeats. Arsenal's most recent league victory there was in September 2012, in which Arteta played in the 2-0 victory.

Their results against Manchester City at the Etihad - their other closest title rivals in recent years - under Arteta are no better either. Seven games have resulted in five defeats and two draws.

In fact, across the 27 Premier League teams Arteta's Arsenal have faced away from home during his seven-year reign, his lowest points-per-game ratios are against Man City (0.29) and Liverpool (0.50).

These matches are more than difficult away trips. They are a test of both Arteta's tactical flexibility and the psycho logical resilience of his team in the face of hostility.

Andoni Iraola's side have appeared to turn a corner in the league after beating the impressive Brighton last weekend. With a cloud of uncertainty hanging over Man City and whether their sanctions for breaching financial rules will be enacted before the season ends, Liverpool may well end up as Arsenal's closest challengers for the title.

Beating Arsenal on Sunday, certainly, would go some way to announcing themselves as true contenders.

Arsenal are champions but they have consistently struggled away against the very best teams

So where have Arteta's Arsenal gone wrong at Anfield and the Etihad Stadium? Well, Arteta's tactical approach has arguably been too cautious in these fixtures for a start.

The 1-0 defeat in August 2025 against Arne Slot's Liverpool smacked of restraint and a concession that a point would be good enough before Dominik Szoboszlai's stunning late free-kick winner.

Arsenal's defensive organisation has long been a major strength under Arteta. He has built his Arsenal from the backline, reinforcing it with excellent back-up options before assessing the forward positions.

Yet, in these high-profile away matches, the pursuit of defensive security can come at the expense of attacking ambition.

There's a big drop in attacking output between when Arsenal face Liverpool at Anfield under Arteta compared with when the Gunners face other league opponents on away turf across the last two seasons.

Possession drops from 56.3 to 43.2 per cent, expected goals from 1.6 to 1.1 and big chances created from 3.1 to 1.8.

The impact of the fervent Anfield atmosphere can't be ignored, either. Ray Parlour understands this better than most, making his Arsenal debut at Anfield in January 1992 aged 18.

The Gunners legend, part of Arsene Wenger's Invincibles side, has a word of advice for the current crop.

'I made my debut there, I know exactly how tough it is to play there. But mentally, you've got to get ready,' Parlour tells Daily Mail Sport.

'For me, the crowd in the first 15 to 20 minutes is always very important at Anfield, because you have to silence them if you can.

Arteta's attack routinely suffers as he seeks defensive solidity in the toughest away games

Arsenal are very strong when they score first but slow starts have proven their Achilles heel

'You've got to start on the front foot, put them under pressure, and I think they can leak goals, Liverpool. To try score that first goal is always important.

'We know defensively Arsenal are a very strong side, so if they go and get that first goal, then they might have a good afternoon there.'

Parlour raises a pertinent point. Arsenal's slow starts at Anfield have left themselves with a mountain to climb. Of the 26 league games Arsenal won last season, they scored first in 24 of those matches. Whereas in the six away matches against Liverpool under Arteta, the Gunners have taken time to getting going.

More shots (from 27 to 30) and an increased xG (from 3.2 to 3.5) were registered in the second period compared to the first half in those games.

Arsenal need to start quicker - and be more clinical, too. At the Emirates, Arteta's men have struck 10 goals against Liverpool, but just six at Anfield despite creating more big chances at Anfield (1.8 per away game vs 1.1 per home game).

Parlour references Arsenal's 3-0 pummelling at Brighton last month as a key example. Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler admitted telling his players to 'win the small battles first' and that's exactly what they did.

'Win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw in, win the first corner,' revealed Hurzeler when asked about his pre-match message to his players. The Gunners can use this as a lesson to overcome their bogey team.

'Look, they're champions. They've got to play in all different sort of atmospheres,' explains Parlour.

'There's a lot of experienced players out there, so you know what to expect.

Arteta played in Arsenal's last league win at Anfield - a 2-0 victory 14 years ago against Brendan Rodgers' Liverpool. He will look to end that streak as a manager on Sunday

Former Arsenal midfielder Ray Parlour wants to see a bravery that can help navigate the storm

'It's going to be a tough place to play, but you've just got to go there and play your game. Individuals win their battles, which is very important in football.

'You see Brighton when they turned over Arsenal, they won their battles that day, so you've got to make sure you get one over on the players you're playing against.

Ultimately, if Arteta is to banish the Anfield demons that have lingered for 12 years, Arsenal must arrive with the courage to impose themselves from the first whistle - and the resilience to withstand the inevitable storm. Only then can the Spaniard finally rewrite a story that has haunted him for so long.

#1401. Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea)1,2,3. The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia);6,7,8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales4,5. All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes9. Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis10, with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

Understanding how complex eukaryotic cells emerged from their prokaryotic ancestors is a fundamental challenge in biology. The widely discussed endosymbiotic theory posits that the last eukaryotic common ancestor was derived from a host cell that had taken up an alphaproteobacteria-related symbiont that later became the mitochondrion11,12,13,14. Although the identity of the putative host cell in this theory has long been enigmatic, recent metagenomic and phylogenetic analyses indicate that eukaryotes probably evolved from a lineage closely related to members of the archaeal group Asgard archaea2,6,7,15,16,17, which has now been formally classified as the phylum Promethearchaeota within the kingdom Promethearchaeati3. This relationship is further reflected in the presence of abundant eukaryotic signature proteins (ESPs) in their genomes15,16,18. Moreover, several of these ESPs exhibit structural and functional similarities to those found in eukaryotes19,20,21,22.

What has remained unclear was the cell structure and physiology of the archaeal group; both have important implications for how archaea may have transitioned towards eukaryotes. On the basis of the presence of abundant and diverse ESPs in these archaea, studies hypothesized that the archaeal ancestor to eukaryotes may have already evolved a complex internal cell structure (that is, an endomembrane system) before endosymbiosis of the alphaproteobacterial ancestor of mitochondria (that is, mito-intermediate or mito-late)1,23,24,25. Cultivation efforts yielded one isolate, Promethearchaeum syntrophicum strain MK-D13,4, as well as enrichment cultures predominated by ‘Candidatus Lokiarchaeum ossiferum’5 and ‘Candidatus Nerearchaeum marumarumayae’26, all revealing a typical prokaryotic internal structure without a persistent eukaryote-like endomembrane system4,5,26 and potential evidence for an actin-based cytoskeleton5,27. All of the Promethearchaeaceae strains gain energy from anaerobic degradation of peptides/amino acids (and/or sugars) through symbiotic metabolic (that is, syntrophic) interactions with H2-consuming methanogenic archaea or sulfate-reducing bacteria3,4,5,26. A metagenomic study also observed organotrophic H2 generation as a shared metabolic feature across four classes of Promethearchaeota23. Collectively, these data suggest that anaerobiosis, H2 generation and prokaryotic cell structure may have been relevant to the evolutionary transition between archaea and eukaryotes.

However, whether features found in these Promethearchaeia (formerly Lokiarchaeia) cultures are relevant to the origin of eukaryotes remains a matter of debate1,7,27. First, metagenomic predictions suggest a wide diversity of physiologies across Promethearchaeota (such as autotrophy, organotrophy and rhodopsin-based phototrophy)23,28,29,30,31. Second, according to recent phylogenetic analyses, the class ‘Candidatus Heimdallarchaeia’ or its order ‘Candidatus Hodarchaeales’ may branch as a sister group to eukaryotes6,7,8. On the basis of these observations, a variety of features, including complex internal cell structure4,7,8,23,24,25, have been proposed for the last archaea (specifically ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’) eukaryote common ancestor (LAECA). Another potential feature of this ancestor that has recently attracted attention is aerobic respiration7,23,30,32. If LAECA were capable of oxygen respiration, this would substantially alter some models of eukaryogenesis that posit an anaerobic archaeal host interacting syntrophically with an alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont capable of aerobic respiration. Studies find that some ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’ possess terminal oxidases (Cox)7,23 and further propose LAECA may have been aerobic30,32. These observations suggest that LAECA already had the beginnings of structural and respiratory features associated with eukaryotes. However, the cell structure of ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’ has yet to be elucidated and the simple presence of such enzymes cannot distinguish between aerotolerant anaerobes and (facultative) aerobes given that many obligately anaerobic organisms possess terminal oxidases for oxygen tolerance33,34. In light of this, cultivation of class ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’ from habitats exposed to oxygen is essential to identify how these archaea may interact with oxygen and determine the cell structures and physiologies that are potentially relevant to LAECA1.

Here we successfully cultured two strains of Heimdallarchaeia belonging to the order Hodarchaeales from a biofilm submerged in anoxic subsurface-derived brine water but exposed to air hourly. One was isolated in a pure syntrophic co-culture and another in a pure tri-culture with methanogenic partners. The strain in co-culture had terminal oxidases and yet exhibited strict dependence on anaerobic metabolism. We further report the cultivation procedures, cellular structures, physiological characteristics and genomic features of these strains, and their implications for the origin of eukaryotes.

To culture members of ‘Heimdallarchaeia’ and examine their potential relationship with oxygen, we capitalized on previous experience in cultivation of P. syntrophicum MK-D14,35. We attributed successful isolation of this strain to a long-term bioreactor-based increase in metabolic activity, acclimatization to artificial conditions and selection against other populations (that is, enrichment)3,4,35. Previous studies also hinted that the presence and activity of anaerobic methane-oxidizing microbial consortia were probably important in supporting the growth of Promethearchaeota members, presumably through the excretion of organic compounds35,36. Here we looked to a gas production well in the Boso Peninsula, Chiba Prefecture, Japan, which is operationally similar to our previous cultivation methane-fed bioreactor (Extended Data Fig. 1). Methane-bearing saline groundwater (that is, brine) upwells into the well and supports a biofilm on the walls containing populations identical or similar to those found in marine sediments, according to 16S rRNA gene tag-sequencing (iTag) analysis37. In contrast to our previous anoxic reactor, the biofilm is intermittently exposed to air (and therefore oxygen) due to periodic eruptions of brine, akin to geysers, that cause the water level to drop temporarily37. Enriched in these biofilms were small populations of Heimdallarchaeia, which we targeted for isolation (Supplementary Table 1).

We aimed to culture the biofilm microbial community in the laboratory while mimicking natural conditions. Filtered brine from the well was used as the basal medium and supplemented this with methane and magnetite to attempt co-enrichment of Promethearchaeota members with anaerobic methane-oxidizing archaea (Supplementary Note 1). While typical anaerobe cultivation procedures call for addition of reducing agents (such as sodium sulfide and/or cysteine) to the culture medium to scavenge oxygen, we omitted these to retain exposure to low concentrations of oxygen. After approximately 3 months, we detected several 16S rRNA gene sequences of Hodarchaeales, Heimdallarchaeales and Promethearchaeales (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). We implemented proteinaceous substrates, casamino acids and powdered milk (each 0.005%, w/v), as energy sources for subcultures to enhance the growth of these archaea, based on our previous observation that syntrophic degradation of amino acids/peptides is a widespread feature across the phylum4 (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Table 1). To also select against other organisms, we supplemented the medium with five antibiotics: ampicillin, vancomycin, kanamycin, streptomycin and erythromycin.

For cultures that sustained Promethearchaeota members according to iTag analysis, we subcultured twice in fresh medium of the same composition at roughly 100-day intervals; cultures that enriched one population of Hodarchaeales over other Promethearchaeota were further subcultured using a synthetic medium mimicking natural brine supplemented with casamino acids, powdered milk and five antibiotics (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). By omitting reducing agents, we were able to retain microoxic conditions (281 ± 123 nM dissolved oxygen, n = 5) that would possibly select for Hodarchaeales over Promethearchaeales members, each presumably associated with more oxidized and reduced lifestyles3,23. After four successive transfers under the same cultivation conditions, the culture retained aerobic bacteria (that is, Mariniphaga and Alcanivorax), contained a higher abundance of the Hodarchaeales population (1.8% in relative abundance) and lost the Promethearchaeales members (Supplementary Table 1). This suggested that the Hodarchaeales population can at least tolerate low-oxygen concentrations and is probably more adapted to oxic conditions compared with the Promethearchaeales members.

In subsequent subcultures, reducing agents were introduced and peptone was added as an additional energy source. The Hodarchaeales population reached up to 30% in relative abundance and maximum cell densities up to 106 16S rRNA gene copy numbers per ml. As for the other populations, only Mariniphaga, Alcanivorax and Methanocalculus remained (Supplementary Table 1). We isolated the Mariniphaga and Alcanivorax species, identified antibiotics that they are sensitive to (Supplementary Table 2) and applied these antibiotics (gentamycin, ciprofloxacin, cephalothin or ofloxacin) to the Hodarchaeales-dominated cultures (Supplementary Table 1). In parallel we also optimized the cultivation temperature and energy source types and concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Three years after the original sampling, we isolated Hodarchaeales in a purified co-culture with a single partnering methanogen population (Methanocalculus), each designated as strains HC1 and MC2, in an anaerobic medium supplemented with casamino acids, peptone and yeast extract (each 0.005%, w/v) at 30 °C (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Under these cultivation conditions, HC1 required 25–35 days to reach full growth with a doubling time of approximately 7–12 days, reaching a maximum cell density of 106 16S rRNA gene copies per ml (Fig. 1c). HC1 cells were morphologically similar to Promethearchaeales members3,4,5, with coccoid cells, albeit with larger diameters of 0.8–2.3 µm (1.3 µm on average; Supplementary Table 3) and multiple protrusions extending from the cell surface (Fig. 1b).

Using a cultivation strategy similar to that for HC1, we successfully isolated another Hodarchaeales strain and also enriched other Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeaceae members (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 2). One Hodarchaeales strain, designated SC1, was isolated in a purified tri-culture with Methanocalculus sp. strain MC3 and Methanolobus sp. strain MLB, with relative abundances of approximately 40%, 60% and <0.3%, respectively, based on iTag analysis (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1). The tri-culture is stably maintained in anaerobic medium supplemented with casamino acids, powdered milk, polypeptone peptone (0.01%, w/v) and yeast extract (0.05%, w/v). SC1 required approximately 60 days to reach maximum growth with a doubling time of approximately 14–20 days, reaching a maximum cell density of 106 16S rRNA gene copies per ml (Fig. 1e). The 16S rRNA gene sequence identity between SC1 and HC1 was 77.55% based on BLAST analysis. SC1 cells were morphologically similar to HC1 but with a smaller diameter, 0.6–1.2 µm (0.9 µm on average) (Fig. 1d).

We sequenced the genomes of both strains. HC1 and SC1 possess circular genomes 7.91 Mb and 6.75 Mb, respectively (Supplementary Tables 4–6). HC1 has a larger genome than all reported Heimdallarchaeia metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs)32. Phylogenetic analyses showed that both strains belonged to the family-level clade LC-3 in Hodarchaeales (Fig. 1a). We tentatively propose the names ‘Candidatus Margulisarchaeum peptidiphilum’ and ‘Candidatus Flexarchaeum multiprotrusionum’ for strains HC1 and SC1, respectively, under the family ‘Candidatus Margulisarchaeaceae’ (Supplementary Note 3).

According to our analyses, HC1 and SC1 each possess 27 and 29 types of ESPs (Supplementary Table 7), putting them in the top quartile of Heimdallarchaeia. Both strains have numbers of ESP types for each ESP category greater than or equal to the average among Heimdallarchaeia. As such, we propose that HC1 is a suitable representative of extant Heimdallarchaeia or Hodarchaeales for examining whether these lineages harbour any intracellular cell structures related to or resembling eukaryotic complexity.

Observation of HC1 and SC1 cells in late exponential and early stationary phases using electron microscopy (EM) revealed that both strains have signatures of typical prokaryotic cells (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3). Cells are coccoid and generally found as individuals, occasionally in aggregates (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Figs. 2c and 3c,d,s). Cells divide through binary fission and, during this, exhibit a ring-like structure (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3e). Both strains produced membrane vesicles (Extended Data Figs. 2o–s and 3w). On the basis of cryo-EM, the cytoplasm and protrusions contained actin-filament-like structures and ferritin-like membrane-less granules (Fig. 2j–n, Extended Data Figs. 2h–j,m, 3t–w, 4 and 5, Supplementary Tables 5 and 6, Supplementary Figs. 2–4, Supplementary Notes 4–6 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). On the cell surface, we observed regular S-layer-like structures under cryo-EM and quick-freeze deep-etch replica EM (QFDE-EM) (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Figs. 2g,l and 3r,s,v,w). A combination of protein multimer structure prediction using AlphaFold338 and glycoproteomics revealed S-layer proteins conserved across many Promethearchaeota lineages that form symmetric homotetramers with a central vertical pore and are N-glycosylated like S-layer proteins of other archaea39 (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 8). In addition to the S-layer, we observed that the cell body and protrusion surfaces of HC1 are covered with very thin filaments (around 55 nm in length and approximately 1 nm in diameter), although their function remains unclear (Extended Data Fig. 2i–k,m,n).

After mid-exponential phase, most cells possess multiple protrusions of uniform diameter (approximately 370 nm), varying lengths, branching and bulbous expansions (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3), morphologically similar to P. syntrophicum MK-D13,4 and ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5. Based on observations using scanning EM (SEM), protrusions were absent in all cells that appear to be undergoing cell division (cells that are in the middle of separating into two cocci with characteristic rings in both cocci marking where cell division probably began; Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3e), suggesting that protrusion generation and cell division are mutually exclusive processes. The protrusions often comprised more than half the volume of each cell (roughly 1.7 µm3 or 142% of the main cell body, on average; Supplementary Table 3), suggesting they have an important role in the physiology of these archaea. Notably, both protrusions and cells were flexible and were observed to sway by Brownian motion (Supplementary Videos 3 and 4). We found that fixation with formaldehyde tended to disconnect their protrusions (Supplementary Fig. 5), indicating that caution must be taken in defining morphology using fixed cells. The protrusions of all isolated and highly enriched Promethearchaeota3,4,5 were observed to physically attach to syntrophic partners. For HC1 and SC1, helical filaments on the protrusion surface tended to be found at the protrusion–partner interface (Fig. 2d,e, Extended Data Figs. 2e,f and 3g–j and Supplementary Note 7). Given the consistent presence of protrusions in Promethearchaeota cultures, we suspect that LAECA also probably possessed such structures.

We further microscopically investigated whether these Hodarchaeales strains have a complex eukaryote-like internal system. The eukaryote endomembrane system is characterized with universally conserved, physically persistent organelles (the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum) and structurally transient compartments (such as Golgi apparatus and lysosomes), all integrated by regulated membrane trafficking. Based on transmission EM (TEM) and cryo-EM, we did not observe any persistent internal membrane structures shared among all HC1 or SC1 cells (Fig. 2g,h,k,l, Extended Data Figs. 2h–j and 3k,l,t,u,w and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Meanwhile, although infrequent, low-electron-density intracellular vesicle-like structures were observed in some cells (Fig. 2m,n, Extended Data Fig. 3m,n,v and Supplementary Video 1). This indicates the absence of persistent eukaryote-like organelles and presence of transient internal structures. Consistent with this, a Heimdallarchaeales archaeon (‘Candidatus Yibarchaeum umbracryptum’) enriched by a recent study lacked persistent organelles and possessed transient intracellular vesicles of unknown function that appeared during early growth stages40. With current data, it is unclear whether the transient structures are related to ESPs, a primitive endomembrane system, or neither.

Despite the absence of conserved internal membrane structures, nearly all HC1 and SC1 cells showed spatial separation between DNA and rRNA based on fluorescence microscopy using DAPI and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) (Fig. 2i, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Video 5), as also previously observed in other Promethearchaeia and Heimdallarchaeia41,42. The reason for this spatial localization is not yet clear, but histones may mediate DNA compaction43. All microscopically studied Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeales—albeit three strains only—consistently lack conserved, persistent eukaryote-like organelles. Despite this cell architecture, HC1 and SC1 have a comparable number of ESPs associated with endosomal sorting and trafficking (11 and 10 out of 34 types) to other Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeia (10 ± 2 and 10 ± 2 types on average, respectively) (Supplementary Table 7). These suggest that other extant Heimdallarchaeia may also lack persistent internal structures. Given that only 9 out of 34 of the endosomal sorting and trafficking-related ESP types are moderately conserved across Heimdallarchaeia (found in at least 50% of the genomes associated with each order), LAECA may have also possessed few such ESPs. Although this suggests the possibility that LAECA also lacked persistent internal cell structure, the genomic composition of LAECA remains to be resolved.

The HC1 co-culture and SC1 tri-culture both contain H2-using methanogenic archaea, and addition of the methanogenesis inhibitor 2-bromoethanesulfonate (10 mM) to the cultures completely suppressed growth. This shows that both HC1 and SC1 depend on H2-mediated symbiosis with methanogens. Such a metabolic symbiosis is known as syntrophy, in which an organotroph performs a hydrogen and/or formate-yielding metabolism that is thermodynamically inhibited by these products and a partner organism scavenges these products to low non-inhibitory concentrations44. Accordingly, amending high concentrations of hydrogen gas or formate also suppressed the growth of both strains (Supplementary Table 9). In the SC1 tri-culture, we detected a methanogen that uses only methylated compounds, Methanolobus sp. MLB, and suspect that SC1 may generate methanol through formate reduction through the expressed aldehyde reductase and alcohol dehydrogenase (Supplementary Table 6), a recently discovered pathway and phenomenon45. Given that syntrophy and symbiosis have been hypothesized to be relevant to the origin of eukaryotes4,12,23, the identification of these features in Heimadallarchaeia has major evolutionary implications.

Both strains are clearly dependent on peptides, as supplementation with non-proteinaceous substrates did not stimulate growth of HC1 and SC1, and neither strain could grow when peptide substrates were replaced with a mixture of 20 proteinogenic amino acids (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 9). Ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC)-based analysis of macromolecule distributions in the cultures indicated clear consumption of higher-molecular-mass molecules (Fig. 3b,c, Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Note 8). Genome analyses revealed that both strains encode extracellular peptidases, peptide transporters, amino acid degradation pathways of glutamate, aspartate, threonine, methionine, glycine, serine, alanine and cysteine in both strains, and NiFe hydrogenases for syntrophic peptide degradation (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Energy is conserved through ATP synthesis through substrate-level phosphorylation and proton motive force generation coupled with ferredoxin-driven H2 generation (Fig. 4). Transcriptomic and proteomic data further confirmed their expression (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Glycoproteomics revealed that peptide/nickel transport system substrate-binding proteins of both strains were highly N-glycosylated like P. syntrophicum MK-D146 (Extended Data Fig. 8, Supplementary Table 8 and Supplementary Note 10), further evidencing the importance of peptides for the growth of these strains. Collectively, we demonstrate that both strains are obligately syntrophy-dependent peptidotrophic archaea.
