A similarly unexpected pattern emerged for the broader systems commonly used to distinguish emotion generation from regulation. The regulatory network was involved in both processes, as recently observed27 (d = 0.22 for emotion generation and d = 0.37 for emotion regulation). Notably, removing the outlying study 4 altered the pattern substantially, resulting in a stronger preference for emotion generation (d = 0.18) than for regulation (d = 0.08), the latter having an inconclusive Bayes factor (BF10 = 0.90). By contrast, the amygdala was selectively engaged during emotion generation (d = 0.16) and was not modulated during reappraisal (d = 0.01, BF10 = 0.03; detailed statistics are in Extended Data Table 2).

Despite extensive research on the neural basis of cognitive reappraisal, the assumption that brain activity during reappraisal reflects individual differences in regulatory capacity has rarely been tested at the scale needed for robust effects. Here we found a notable lack of convergence among three widely used indices of reappraisal capacity. Only the association between task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation was statistically significant, yet with an effect size (r = 0.08) so small that more than 1,000 participants would be needed for 80% power—far exceeding typical sample sizes in the field. Trait questionnaires showed no association with either index, with Bayes factors favouring the absence of effects. None of the three indices showed the expected relation with activity in canonical prefrontal emotion regulation circuits. These findings call for a fundamental reassessment of how reappraisal capacity is measured and interpreted across behavioural and neural levels of analysis.

The lack of convergence challenges a central assumption in affective neuroscience and clinical neuroimaging: that questionnaires, task-based affective change and neural responses provide complementary windows onto a shared underlying regulatory capacity, albeit with unique aspects. This matters because the extent to which common reappraisal task findings inform claims about emotion, psychopathology and intervention targets may be overstated if individual indices capture only distinct aspects of regulatory functioning. Indeed, research on emotional coherence shows that experiential, behavioural and physiological channels often diverge because they operate on different time scales and are shaped by different causal influences and biases28. Trait questionnaires reflect recollected beliefs about reappraisal habits and ability across diverse real-life contexts; task-based affective ratings capture momentary regulatory effects under constrained experimental conditions; and neural responses may additionally reflect processes outside conscious awareness29, while being shaped by neurovascular and scanner-related factors that are unrelated to regulation. The present findings therefore do not merely show weak measurement convergence; they suggest that common indices of reappraisal capacity, in fact, may carve the construct at different joints, without the widely assumed contribution of the prefrontal cortex.

For task-based affective ratings, we found associations in emotion-generative rather than prefrontal emotion-regulatory regions: the amygdala, the caudal pons, and—when excluding an outlier dataset from the early COVID-19 era—sensorimotor and dorso-parietal attention networks, outside of canonical emotion regulation regions. The role of the amygdala remains debated: although it tracks concurrent negative affect in well-powered studies30,31, it also responds to positive and otherwise salient stimuli4,32. We further confirmed with four large samples that it is not consistently modulated by reappraisal27. The amygdala is better understood as a neuromodulatory hub facilitating attention, memory encoding and consolidation33, and allostatic responding—processes that are relevant to emotion generation but not specific to it. One possibility is that reappraisal changes the quality or valence of an emotional response without proportionally reducing its salience.

Our finding of sensorimotor associations is consistent with extended process models that assign a role to sensorimotor cortices and the brainstem in the action phase of regulation27. Recent large-scale evidence indicates that even in the absence of overt motor responses, sensorimotor cortices carry rich information about emotion generation27, are modifiable by reappraisal strategies27, are related to individual differences in stress vulnerability12,34, and are a promising target for neuromodulation in depression35. Neurosynth decoding further indicated language-related activation, consistent with the verbal nature of reappraisal. Together, these patterns suggest that individual differences in affective down-regulation are more closely tied to salience-allostasis and perception–action-related processes than to canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits36. Notably, canonical regulatory circuits were similarly engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging the commonly assumed dichotomy between bottom-up excitation and top-down control in emotion regulation27.

The absence of associations between trait questionnaires and task-based or neural indices points to an explanatory gap that can be understood through process models of emotion regulation1,27. Most trait questionnaires capture habitual tendencies across multiple temporal stages, including encountering and recognizing reappraisable situations, deciding whether to regulate, and selecting reappraisal over competing strategies. From one angle, previous work showed associations between reappraisal habits, ability and neuro-behavioural implementation16,17,18, including causal evidence that neuromodulation affects reappraisal habits19. Similarly, we found a very strong correlation between habit and ability questionnaires, pointing towards a functional relation on a conceptual level. From another angle, standard fMRI tasks bypass much of the naturalistic reappraisal sequence: participants are instructed when and how to regulate, receive practice trials and respond to standardized stimuli optimized for reliable group-level effects. Therefore, individuals with higher reappraisal capacity might derive their real-world advantage less from universally superior neural implementation than from selecting, initiating and sustaining reappraisal in personally meaningful contexts, and from encountering environments that more readily afford successful reappraisal37. Relatedly, higher self-reported reappraisal tendency may partly reflect greater regulatory need rather than greater regulatory success: individuals experiencing stronger negative emotions may have more occasions to engage in reappraisal38. At the same time, highly intense negative emotions may render reappraisal less suitable than alternative regulation strategies39, relating reappraisal success to situational demands and individual differences in emotional reactivity4,12. This aligns with broader arguments that successful self-regulation reflects complex person-situation interactions rather than being governed by a context-general regulatory resource40. Future paradigms should therefore additionally engage other regulatory stages including strategy selection, personally relevant stimuli and spontaneous deployment.

The gap between task-based affective ratings and concurrent neural responses raises a different set of issues. Within persons, trial-by-trial affective ratings can be decoded from neural responses with large effect sizes, particularly with distributed multivariate neuro-affective signatures30. Even anatomically localized responses, such as the amygdala, track within-person fluctuations in affect with smaller but theoretically meaningful effect sizes30,31. This robust within-person correspondence demonstrates that brain–behaviour alignment is achievable and supports the value of process-oriented research for identifying neuromodulation targets.

Between persons, however, brain–behaviour associations are systematically much smaller12—a dissociation also observed for non-fMRI physiological markers of emotion28. Neural degeneracy provides one principled account: multiple neural configurations can support similar regulatory outcomes, and the specific configurations recruited may differ markedly across individuals41, particularly in higher-order association cortices where anatomical variability is substantial42. Yet degeneracy alone cannot explain the magnitude of the within–between discrepancy. Process-oriented fMRI studies routinely identify replicable regional response patterns, as reflected in meta-analyses of reappraisal2, and population-level models trained to decode within-person affective states generalize well to unseen healthy and clinical cohorts43. This indicates substantial representational overlap between individuals on a process level.

Three additional factors are likely to contribute. First, we demonstrated that established multivariate neuro-affective signatures can produce large effect sizes (dmax = 0.69) while conflating emotion generation and regulation, limiting their psychological interpretability and showing no association with reappraisal capacity. Second, standard reappraisal tasks were designed for process-based research and may not elicit the stable individual differences needed for strong brain–behaviour associations26. In support of this, we found little variance on the between-person level in task-based affective ratings (7–8%), even in two large samples with population-representative variance on affective traits12. Third, we found that between-person fMRI responses are strongly shaped by person-level whole-brain responsivity—potentially owing to factors such as neurovascular variation22—producing highly correlated regional responses that limit anatomical specificity. This extends to canonical resting-state networks, where correlations reached 0.50 to 0.80 across multiple task domains. This complicates efforts to interpret individual differences in task–fMRI responses through influential clinical models, including the triple-network model, suggesting antagonistic relations between canonical networks44. These global effects are not removed by calculating contrasts between conditions. As a result, most between-person variance in neural responses likely reflects confounded individual differences, in stark contrast to task-based affective responses. This highlights a fundamental misalignment, potentially alleviated by tasks designed to specifically induce individual differences while accounting for whole-brain responsivity12,45.

These findings might have direct implications for how neural correlates are used to guide clinical inference and neuromodulatory interventions. The absence of prefrontal individual-difference associations does not invalidate process-oriented findings: the neural systems identified in within-person reappraisal research could remain viable targets for neuromodulation, as they reflect the implementation of reappraisal regardless of between-person variation. However, our results support caution against inferring individual regulatory capacity from regional brain activation—whether in the prefrontal cortex, amygdala or elsewhere—as is common in clinical neuroimaging models of emotion dysregulation4,5. The success of neuromodulatory interventions targeting these regions8,19 may reflect distributed network reorganization rather than correction of a specific regional deficit35,46, consistent with evidence that different stimulation sites can achieve similar clinical outcomes. This fits a systems neuroscience perspective where single regions cannot be interpreted in isolation. Supporting this, recent well-powered studies linked individual differences in affective functioning with reappraisal-contingent connectivity between the amygdala and prefrontal areas (ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), dlPFC and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC))47, as well as shifts along primary gradients of macroscale neurofunctional organization48. Further testing these approaches represents a natural next step for the NIDER consortium and individual-difference neuroimaging of emotion regulation more broadly.

Our sample comprised non-clinical populations, limiting generalizability to groups with greater symptom severity and variability. A population-representative sample would show 1.3–1.5 times greater variance in reappraisal habits49, potentially enabling slightly larger effect sizes. More importantly, transdiagnostic samples covering the full range of clinical dimensions could reveal meaningful individual-difference associations that are absent in non-clinical adult individuals, while also introducing potential confounders. Most included studies used habit-oriented questionnaires,although the small number of studies with additional ability-focused measures still had sufficient power for most small effect sizes in fixed-effects analyses. Finally, whereas our meta-analytic approach is statistically equivalent to mega-analysis for voxel-outcome correlations, subject-level data would enable person-specific decoding models—a promising direction for future work on neural heterogeneity.

Together, our findings challenge the assumption that prefrontal activation during reappraisal reflects individual differences in regulatory capacity. The three most commonly used indices of reappraisal capacity do not converge, and none relates to canonical emotion regulation circuits in the expected direction. More broadly, person-level whole-brain responsivity represents a pervasive methodological challenge for task-based fMRI research on individual differences—one that extends across emotional, cognitive and pain domains. Large-scale resting-state studies with sample sizes in the thousands have similarly failed to identify replicable neural correlates of emotion-related traits13, underscoring the need for better alignment between theoretical constructs, behavioural tasks, and neural measures12. Progress will require methodological refinements—including connectivity and gradient-based approaches—as well as a conceptual re-framing of what reappraisal capacity means, how its multiple components are best measured, and the level of analysis at which each measure is expected to predict real-world emotional well-being. Until then, strong claims about a person’s emotion regulation capacity based on any specific brain region should be made with considerable caution.

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they measured (1) task-based fMRI (2) during a cognitive reappraisal task, (3) using negative stimuli, (4) to compare a down-regulation condition with a view-without-regulation condition, and (5) included a trait-like questionnaire measure for cognitive reappraisal (6) in a healthy sample. The latter criterion was used to avoid excessive heterogeneity in disorder presentation and medications (see ‘Towards transdiagnostic neural systems’).

Contributing research groups were invited using two strategies. First, we conducted a systematic literature search, contacting 64 authors via e-mail or Researchgate. Second, we used mailing lists of academic societies to advertise the consortium. In total, this led to 32 contributing research teams with 40 datasets comprising up to 2,175 participants. For an overview of study characteristics see Supplementary Table 1. Nine studies were unpublished. For 31 studies (77.5%), teams indicated they had not performed any of the targeted main analyses of the present paper. There were no further assessments of selection bias. Most papers used the emotion regulation questionnaire (ERQ)51 to measure reappraisal, while six used the cognitive emotion regulation questionnaire (CERQ)52, and only one study used a different questionnaire (FEEL-E)53. The majority of studies used pictorial stimuli. Two studies used videos, one study used autobiographical memory cues, one study used Cyberball, and one study used a different game task.

We conducted a systematic literature search of articles using the PubMed, Web of Science and PsychINFO databases. See Supplementary Fig. 2 for a flow chart depiction of the screening and selection of studies via literature search. We searched for the following keywords: ‘emotion regulation’ cross referenced with ‘fMRI’ or ‘neuroimaging’ or ‘functional magnetic resonance imaging’ or ‘functional MRI’. This search process yielded a total of 2,633 potentially relevant articles on 7 July 2021 (after duplicates were removed). Two independent reviewers (J.Z. and M. Schweizer) systematically examined titles and relevant abstracts using the Rayyan website54 to determine whether an article fulfills the criteria to be screened. The following criteria were applied: The study included original empirical results, was written in English or German, included adult healthy participants, and assessed an explicit emotion regulation paradigm during fMRI measurement. In a next step, for all remaining studies full texts were screened by three independent reviewers (J.Z., M. Boll and D. Lang) and they were included if (1) participants were told to use reappraisal strategies to modulate a negative emotion, (2) an emotion regulation questionnaire was assessed (for example, ERQ), (3) a control condition was included in which participants were confronted with emotional stimuli but did not regulate their emotions, and (4) negative stimuli were used in the emotion regulation task. Finally, a total of k = 61 studies fulfilled all inclusion criteria. Relevant articles in the authors’ library were also reviewed for titles that might have been missed by our literature search. Studies identified in this manner (k = 3) were collected for inclusion. Of the k = 64 studies, k = 17 reported the correlation between fMRI BOLD activation (‘reappraise negative’) and emotion regulation questionnaire data. The authors of all 64 studies were contacted.

Research groups prepared up to three unthresholded group-level statistical images, containing voxel-wise t-statistics for the between-person correlation of the whole-brain neural response in the [reappraise negative – view negative] contrast and the three outcomes of interest. These outcomes were (1) trait questionnaires of cognitive reappraisal, (2) the person-wise averaged decrease of task-based affective ratings during ‘reappraise negative’ versus ‘view negative’ conditions, and (3) and person-wise averaged decrease of amygdala responses during ‘reappraise negative’ versus ‘view negative’ conditions.

A homepage with detailed instructions and a Matlab example analysis script was provided to support analyses. Contributors were instructed to compute the three measures of reappraisal capacity so that higher values correspond to better reappraisal capacity. For task-based affective ratings, this entailed (re-)coding for higher values to correspond to a more negative emotional response and calculating person-wise averaged down-regulation of affect from the contrast [view negative – reappraise negative]; thus, a greater reduction in negative affect via reappraisal leads to higher values. Similarly, for amygdala down-regulation, average activity was extracted from the [view negative – reappraise negative] contrast, as higher values correspond to a better down-regulation of the amygdala for sign congruence with the other two outcomes. A standardized amygdala mask was provided for all research groups based on the intersection of an anatomical amygdala mask (SPM anatomy toolbox v2.2b) and a functional emotion-generating network from an emotion regulation meta-analysis2, which ensures the anatomical and functional specificity of the amygdala region of interest.

Furthermore, contributors provided direct bivariate correlations between the three reappraisal outcomes (for example, trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings) as well as demographic and other study information (Supplementary Table 1).

Images were quality controlled individually by plotting t-values on a brain template, histograms, and performing brain-wide thresholding at false discovery rate (FDR) = 0.05 to check for plausibility. Collectively, quality was controlled by checking for outlier studies within the same emotion regulation outcome category (for example, mean whole-brain activation, Mahalanobis distance, and covariance matrices). Two images were removed from whole-brain analyses due to insufficient coverage55,56. Effective sample sizes for tests are reported in the results section.

Study-level estimates were aggregated within a random-effects meta-analytic framework. Under standard assumptions, this approach closely approximates subject-level mega-analysis for the associations examined here, while reducing barriers to data sharing57 and potentially increasing the number of includable studies and overall precision58,59 (see Supplementary Methods, ‘Meta- vs mega-analytic approaches’ for details).

First, we assessed the concordance between the three outcome measures (trait questionnaires, task-based ratings, amygdala down-regulation) using random-effects meta-analysis implemented in the R package meta using the DerSimonian and Laird approach to estimate between-study heterogeneity60.

Second, we tested associations between the three outcomes and two neural emotion regulation networks based on a recent process-based meta-analysis on emotion regulation2; networks 1 and 2 (Fig. 2). These networks are thought to be predominantly implicated in the cognitive control (versus emotion-generating) aspects of emotion regulation and mostly include regions in the prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortex. Images were resampled to the same spatial resolution of 2 × 2 × 2 mm³. The statistical core procedure was done in three preregistered stages. In the first stage, we tested the correlation between average activity in the two networks of interest, respectively, and reappraisal capacity, with Bonferroni corrections for two tests. In the second stage, we performed voxel-wise tests in the combined two networks with FDR correction based on the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (FDR = 0.05, approximately 10,000 voxels). In a third stage, we repeated the second-stage analysis on the whole brain (approximately 180,000 voxels). Between-study heterogeneity was tested for statistical significance based on whole-brain data and corrected with the same FDR procedure.

To perform the image-based fMRI meta-analysis, we developed custom Matlab code which interfaces with the fMRI-specific functionality of the CanlabCore toolbox23. Our procedure converts study-wise unthresholded t-maps to correlation maps and therefore, together with sample size information, offers voxel-wise estimates of effect size, statistical significance, and between-study heterogeneity via the DerSimonian and Laird approach61,62. The code was validated by testing congruence with meta-analytic packages in R as well as performing a small meta-analysis on six openly available group-level images of physical pain, which detected typically involved brain regions and was successfully decoded as ‘pain’ using Neurosynth63 (Supplementary Methods, ‘Testing the custom meta-analytic functions’). Neurosynth decoding was performed analogously as described in the main text.

We calculated Bayesian posterior odds for focal effects to quantify the relative evidence for the null hypothesis (that is, no effect exists) against the alternative hypothesis (that is, an effect exists) based on established interpretational thresholds64. These analyses were performed using Bayesian model-averaged meta-analysis65. We used objective literature-based prior distributions for effect sizes and between-study heterogeneity. For effect sizes, we used a normal moment prior66 approximating the empirical distribution of meta-analytic correlations across individual-difference research67, with a mode at r = 0.20 (Supplementary Fig 3). For between-study heterogeneity (τ), we used a one-sided t-distribution (scale factor = 0.15, df = 1), approximating the empirical distribution found for over 700 meta-analyses68 (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Bayesian posterior odds were not corrected for multiple comparisons in the three preregistered overlap tests (see ‘Divergence of capacity indices’) and the preregistered tests on average network activation. Therein, the null and alternative hypothesis are assumed to be equally likely (prior odds = 1:1), making the Bayesian posterior odds identical to the Bayes factor. For voxel-wise tests, we calculated Bayes factors across all four canonical networks involved in emotion regulation, including both aspects of emotion regulation and generation2, consisting of about 20,000 voxels. Due to this large number of comparisons belonging to the same global hypothesis, we performed Bayesian corrections for multiple comparisons by adjusting the prior odds to be equal for the global null (no effect across all voxels) versus the alternative hypothesis (an effect in at least one voxel) using Jeffrey’s method69. Like Bonferroni correction, this method is conservative when tests are not independent. Therefore, we calculated the number of effective independent tests based on the spatial correlation structure70, indicating 53 independent tests as a basis for multiplicity correction.

Anatomical regions were defined using the CANlab 2018 combined atlas in MNI152 space, which integrates cortical and subcortical regions from several established parcellations23. The full set of 489 regions, including atlas labels, anatomical or network descriptions and references to source parcellations, is provided in the Supplementary Atlas File. For each pair of regions, between-person Pearson correlations were calculated across participants using region-wise activation estimates. Correlations were then summarized across all region pairs to characterize the overall degree of shared between-person variation in regional activation.

To obtain trial-level neural responses, additional first-level general linear models (GLMs) were estimated using a beta-series approach in which each trial’s (n = 45) viewing epoch was modelled with a separate regressor, yielding 45 trial-specific parameter estimates for subsequent ROI analyses. Additional regressors in the beta-series GLM included a regressor reflecting all rating periods (to account for motor responses) as well as the six realignment parameters (to account for head motion-related activation). Subsequently, each trial-specific beta map was used to extract mean amygdala and regulatory network response scores for each trial and used for the variance decomposition, parallel to the task-based affective ratings.

To stabilize variance estimates for all three outcomes, we first removed outlier observations outside 3-times the interquartile range within each participant (9–113 out of 16,155 observations). Then, we removed whole outlier participants outside 3-times the interquartile range based on their average ratings (1–4 out of 359 participants). Next, we fit intercept-only linear mixed models to decompose variance between (random intercept) and within (residual) individuals.

Analyses included three candidate signatures: a negative affect decoder trained to predict task-based affective ratings (affective state)30, a decoder discriminating reappraisal from other competing processes (reappraisal state)71, and a decoder trained to predict individual differences in reappraisal success from task-based affective ratings (affective trait)72. All three were developed in relatively large samples, while the first two were additionally validated in multiple independent samples. Generally, these neural signatures consist of brain images containing regression weights. For each decoder, person, and condition, we calculated the signature expression by taking the dot product between the respective contrast (beta) image and the signature image. Pattern-expression scores, as well as the amygdala and regulatory network responses, were z-standardized within studies to transform them from the arbitrary site-specific fMRI metric to a comparable Cohen’s d metric. Specifically, for differences between conditions, values were standardized on the pooled within-condition variance separately for each study. Then, a linear mixed model was calculated with condition, study, and their interaction as fixed effects and a random intercept for each participant. Aggregate estimates and confidence intervals were obtained from estimated marginal means averaged equally across studies73. For correlations with reappraisal capacity, pattern-expression scores were calculated for the contrast [reappraise negative – view negative]. Pattern-expression scores and reappraisal capacity measures were z-standardized within studies and then analysed using pooled individual-level linear regressions across studies. These approaches equate to fixed-effects mega-analysis (that is, without study-specific random intercepts and slopes), as modelling between-study heterogeneity is severely limited with only four studies.

For model-derived contrasts, approximate Bayes factors were calculated from the corresponding t-statistics and denominator degrees of freedom using the default Cauchy prior for standardized mean differences implemented in the BayesFactor package74.

Aims, literature search strategy, and statistical analyses were preregistered on PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42021243155. A notable error in the preregistration was the statement that only studies using pictures as stimuli are included. Rather, the meta-analysis included all types of stimuli, which we stated correctly on the accompanying homepage and the mailing list advertisements. Regardless of this error, the overwhelming majority of studies used pictures as stimuli (88%) and the low, statistically non-significant between-study heterogeneities as well as the jackknife procedures indicate that stimulus type does not influence the results.

The participating studies followed their respective institutional approval processes at the time of data collection, including applicable ethical approval and informed consent procedures. For the present meta-analysis, participant-level analyses were performed locally by the contributing research groups, and only study-level summary statistics and group-level statistical images were shared. No new data were collected and no participant-level or identifiable information was accessed by the meta-analysis team. Therefore, no separate institutional review board approval or formal exemption was sought for the present secondary analysis.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The 40 primary task–fMRI datasets contributing to the consortium are listed individually, together with their study references and sample characteristics, in Supplementary Table 1. Participant-level data were not centrally collected as part of the present study and remain under the governance of the respective contributing research groups. Study-level summary statistics and group-level statistical images used for the meta-analyses are available at https://github.com/MaurizioSicorello/NIDER_project. The repository has been archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22084628 (ref. 75)). The systematic literature search was conducted using PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), Web of Science (https://www.webofscience.com/) and PsycINFO (https://www.apa.org/pubs/databases/psycinfo). Neurosynth was used for automated meta-analytic decoding (https://neurosynth.org/). Publicly available group-level statistical images used for validation of the image-based meta-analytic procedure were obtained from NeuroVault (https://neurovault.org/); permanent image identifiers are provided in the accompanying studyInfo_neurovault.xlsx file in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/MaurizioSicorello/NIDER_project). Source data are provided with this paper.

Custom MATLAB and R code used for the analyses is available on GitHub (https://github.com/MaurizioSicorello/NIDER_project) and has been archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22084628 (ref. 75)). The custom code is released under the MIT License (https://opensource.org/license/mit).

#1386. Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin desperate to end his trophy drought by lifting the Premier Sports Cup

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 14:23 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:23 EDT, 1 November 2026

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin insists he is desperate to finally end his own personal trophy drought after reaching the Premier Sports Cup final.

Raskin has been at Rangers for almost four years but is yet to actually lift any silverware, something which he does not seek to shy away from.

The Belgian midfielder missed the final of this competition in December 2023 due to injury as Rangers beat Aberdeen 1-0 – and therefore did not collect a winner’s medal.

After beating the Dons by the same scoreline at Hampden last night, Rangers are now through to next month’s final against Hibs as they aim to secure the first trophy of the season.

Raskin freely admits that the fact his trophy cabinet is still bare after almost four years is something which annoys him. But it is something he is determined to rectify.

‘I just want to go and win it,’ said the 25-year-old. ‘My family tell me I’ve won one (trophy), but I tell them I haven’t.

Rangers star Nico Raskin wants to make up for missing the 2023 Premier Sports Cup final

Manager Derek McInnes joins Raskin and his Rangers team-mates after their semi-final victory

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi celebrates scoring the winner against Aberdeen at Hampden

‘When we won this competition previously, I got rested for the first two games - and injured for the next two.

‘So that’s not me winning it. Yeah (it annoys me). I think I’ve been here a long time and we’ve worked so hard.

‘Not having that is difficult, but hopefully next month we’ll win one. I’m just happy to get to this final with full belief and I want to win that cup.

‘It’s top. It’s really good for the team. But now we want to win it and there’s one game to go. Now we go full force to win the cup.’

After almost leaving Rangers at various points over the past year, Raskin insists he is now fully focused on delivering success over the rest of this campaign.

He was made captain yesterday by Derek McInnes and was glad to repay the manager’s faith with a hard-fought victory.

Despite toiling to break down a stubborn Aberdeen side, Rangers finally broke through when Ryan Naderi stabbed home from close range with only seven minutes remaining.

If Rangers can go on and lift the cup in next month’s final, Raskin believes it could pave the way for further success this season.

‘Listen, it’s not going to be an easy season. It’s a long season,’ he said. ‘But the main thing is to keep focused and keep working towards the goal.

‘We need to keep believing in the manager and what we’re doing, then we’ll be there.

‘Things happen for a reason (in terms of what happened with transfer interest) and I’m looking forward to that game next month in the final.

‘Hopefully we can achieve something good this season that will lead us to a more exciting season.

‘Aberdeen gave us a difficult game. If you think you’re going to have an easy game, coming out and winning 4-0, you’re wrong.

‘The other team is coming with a plan and it’s a big game for them, also. It’s not easy to win football games. So you go out and give the best performance you can.

‘We won, so we’re very happy. In terms of the manager, he breathes Rangers and he gives that to us.

‘It’s so good to have someone like him driving us every day and on the pitch. I’m delighted for him and hopefully we can win it for him too.

‘He told us that it wasn’t going to be easy. That if we turn up and do everything we have to do, then we’d win the game.

‘We couldn’t come out with complacency and think it would be easy to score four goals. It’s a hard game that isn’t easy to win, so we have to enjoy it when we do.’

#1384. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

Barcola hits the woodwork! The Frenchman attempts to lob Kelleher off the second phase of a corner but his effort comes off the crossbar.

Manchester City 4 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Ndiaye’s effort crashes off the crossbar and the ball falls to the feet of Enzo, who picks out Haaland and the Norwegian does the rest. What a finish. That’s his 13th City hat-trick.

Huge chance for Brentford! Anthony flashes a threatening ball across the face of goal and there Thiago is waiting and surely should score! He cannot arrange his feet quickly enough and Alisson is able to gather the ball with ease.

Liverpool’s front four have taken some criticism this season, and rightly so, but they have turned up in this second half. Wirtz assisted Munoz for the equaliser, and now Barcola has assisted Isak for the second.

The red card was the turning point in this game but the £400m frontline have delivered what was expected of them since the break.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 2 (Isak) The Swede is only just back from injury, and in all fairness has not looked great for much of this afternoon, but he’s put Liverpool infront here. Mac Allister plays a one-two with Wirtz down the right and the ball is worked to Barcola at the far post. The France winger nods it into the path of Isak who composes himself before spearing the ball beyond Kelleher.

Hull haven’t given up the ghost at Craven Cottage, knowing how easily Fulham crumbled last time out. Belloumi tries his luck from distance but cannot find the target.

Superb finish by Victor Munoz to level the scores here. Brentford were caught upfield and they were in trouble from the moment Florian Wirtz was able to slide the ball in behind for the Spanish winger. It comes as Liverpool were just starting to make their numerical advantage count.

Manchester City 3 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Ndiaye does well to play in Haaland who breezes past Outtara before lacing the ball into the bottom corner.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 1 (Munoz) Ngumoha plays the ball infield to Wirtz on the half-way line, and the German threads a ball in behind for the rapid Munoz to gallop on to, he cuts inside Lewis-Potter and fires the ball beyond Kelleher with his left foot.

Iwobi goes close. His curled effort has Tzolakis scrambling but zips just wide of the mark.

Fernandez, on as a second-half substitute, tries his luck with a free-kick from 25 yards out, but he cannot get the requisite dip on the ball to bring it down and it flies over.

Fulham are still dominating the ball and have been by far the better side. Their possession share remains in the high seventies. They’ve completed 476 passes to Hull’s 94.

A second goal would surely put this one to bed.

Liverpool brought on Jeremie Frimpong as a half-time substitute but he’s already limped off. That’s the second injury they have picked up today, after Dominik Szoboszlai.

This is a proper test of Liverpool’s creative ability now. Ten-man Brentford are going to sit deep for most of this second half, I am sure. Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola... time to deliver some game-changing quality.

Jacquet goes into the book. A loose pass out from the back is picked off my Brentford substitute Schade and Jacquet snaps in too enthusiastically and receives a yellow.

Chance! Will Fulham rue all these missed chances? King is involved once more, standing up a cross to the back post where Garcia nods down for Iwobi to stroke goalwards near the penalty spot, but Tzolakis does well to get down low to his left and keep Fulham’s advantage to just one goal.

Mateo Kovacic comes off injured for City. It is probably just a knock as he’s sat on the bench rather than heading down the tunnel. Was a standout player in the first half.

Close! Ajayi’s clearance comes straight back and Charles works the ball to King on the right, but with just the keeper to beat, the midfielder’s effort is saved by Tzolakis with his feet. King really should be scoring there.

Still some time before the Liverpool game resumes given the time added on at the end of the first half.

Following his clash of heads with Jarrad Branthwaite in the lunchtime kick-off at the Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Chelsea goalkeeper has now been taken to hospital to undergo precautionary tests.

Brentford lead Liverpool thanks to Keane Lewis-Potter's header, but the second half could be tricky for the Bees after Yehor Yarmoliuk was sent off just before half-time. Liverpool are yet to have a shot on target despite having seven shots in the first half. #BRELIV https://t.co/o9HE2Fh8qb

Andrews will be furious with how that first half ended. His side had done brilliantly to establish a lead, but will have their work cut out keeping Liverpool out after the break with the visitors a man to the good.

With half-time fast approaching and Brentford in front, this is absolute madness. Yarmoliuk looks to have butted Jacquet in an incident that reminds of Bentacur’s red card at Old Trafford last weekend.

The referee is sent to the pitchside monitor after a lengthy delay and Yarmoliuk is off!

We’ve had the second VAR review in just a few minutes here, and this one has resulted in a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk for a “headbutting action”. I have to say, this feels harsh. It’s pretty tame. There is a tiny movement towards Jacquet, who collapsed to the turf in dramatic fashion, but he’s hardly caused the Liverpool defender any damage. That will change the dynamic of this game.

Haaland restores City’s lead after Maeda had cancelled out Foden’s opener.

Arbeloa’s side are in front and could have been ahead by a wider margin, but we’ve been here before...

Gary Neville is a w-----, is a w-----.....is quite a loud chant here at City. Fans in a good mood here after Erling Haaland scored in his eighth game in a row.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 0 (Lewis-Potter) Outtara curls in a wonderful cross and Lewis-Potter steals in to head the ball beyond Alisson from 10 yards out.

Brentford take the lead, and it’s a lead they probably just about deserve on the run of play. It’s an absolutely superb header by Keane Lewis-Potter, up from left-back, as he thumps Igor Thiago’s cross into the top corner of Liverpool’s net. Textbook technique.

Just after Wirtz was denied a penalty of his own, Mac Allister looks to have won a spot-kick for real off a challenge from Outtara. The referee gives it, but is then sent to the monitor and the decision is reversed. Correct decision. Outtara clearly got a piece of the ball first.

Liverpool have been awarded a penalty but I don’t think this will stand. It shouldn’t stand. Dango Ouattara got a touch on the ball when he lunged in on Alexis Mac Allister.

Yep, the penalty has been overturned. Referee John Brooks missed Outtara’s touch on first viewing but the replays were pretty conclusive.

Manchester City 2 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Kovacic wriggles free of his markers and darts to the by-line. He’s able to stand up a cross and Haaland heads the ball forcefully downwards - just as your grassroots football coach always told you to - and Walton is unable to keep it out. Probably should have done better.

Fulham 1 Hull City 0 (Iwobi) A big, big goal for Fulham and Arbeloa. They are finally able to convert their overwhelming dominance with the ball into something material. This goal comes at the end of a sweeping move, with Iwobi stroking the ball beyond Tzolakis, who probably should have done better.

Bradley Barcola may not be justifying his fee at Liverpool yet but another Frenchman, Jeremy Jacquet, certainly is. The centre-back has been excellent all season and he has just produced a goal-saving challenge on Brentford’s Igor Thiago. A sliding tackle, perfectly timed, just as Thiago was about to score.

Brentford are getting the ball forward quickly, and Kelleher is the one to initiate the latest move. He finds Thiago on the halfway line, who gets the ball back off Outtara, but the Brazilian’s effort is well blocked by Van Dijk.

Some bad news for Liverpool, though, as Szoboszlai sits on the turf. It looks like his afternoon might already be over.

Daizen Maeda showed good strength to hold off Marc Guehi’s challenge before scoring his first goal for Ipswich since signing from Celtic. City will be disappointed with the defending there - it was a straightforward ball down the channel from Abdoul Ouattara.

Before that Phil Foden sent a message to Thomas Tuchel with the opening goal. Foden, playing in central midfield, was left out of the last England squad and has seen Alex Scott climb above him in the pecking order. But Scott is injured for next month’s international which may give Foden a chance.

Was Bradley Barcola’s midweek hat-trick the start of a great run of form for the £123m forward? Not on this evidence. A defensive mix-up allowed the Frenchman a clear run at goal, one-on-one with Brentford’s Caoimhin Kelleher, but his finish was woeful. An attempted dink that bobbled harmlessly wide. “What a waste of money,” comes the cry from the Brentford fans.

Manchester City 1 Ipswich Town 1 (Maeda) Woah, barely a minute between these two goals at the Etihad. Guehi relinquishes possession to Maeda and, left alone in the box, he stears the ball into the far bottom corner.

Manchester City 1 Ipswich Town 0 (Foden) While Foden has scored, huge credit must go to Doku, who did brilliantly down the left, working the ball on to his right foot before squaring to Foden who gets a shot away - Walton does well to get a hand on the ball, but he cannot keep it out.

Liverpool are looking bright, with Barcola and Wirtz combining well - just as they did in midweek - to force a corner. The ball is worked to Mac Allister on the edge of the box but his effort sails well over.

“You’re going down with the City,” sing the home fans at the Ipswich travelling support.

Arbeloa’s side have dominated the ball thus far, claiming an 87 per cent share of the ball. Hull have completed a grand total of 14 passes. But this has been the story of their season so far, lots of the ball but very little incision. Let’s see if they can be more productive this afternoon.

Bright start by Brentford here, although Liverpool have just created their first chance of the game as Szoboszlai shoots over from the edge of the box.

Thiago is putting himself about in Liverpool’s box, winning a corner which is headed behind for another by Van Dijk, but it comes to nothing.

Liverpool break and their sweeping move up the field comes to Wirtz whose cut-back picks out Szoboszlai perfectly but the midfielder miscues and his effort does not trouble Kelleher.

Ipswich centre-back Issa Diop did not take the knee like the other players on the pitch just before kick-off here at the Etihad Stadium. The Premier League’s ‘No Room For Racism’ initiative is this weekend and players have been invited to kneel on the pitch. Some players believe taking the knee has lost its meaning and impact.

As expected, Ipswich have dropped into a deep five-man block with very little space between their lines. It will be up to City’s creative players to fashion chances this afternoon.

Fulham simply need to win today and they get off to a good start. Iwobi goes close with an early effort which is turned behind by Tzolakis.

Huge boos and whistles for the Premier League anthem at the Etihad Stadium, with the final part of it drowned out by chants of “City, City, City.” Fans have made their feelings clear after the guilty verdict from the competition’s independent commission, with the club appealing the decision.

The anthem never gets a warm reception here - but that is the loudest I’ve heard the dissent.

Brentford-Liverpool is the first game to get going... Good luck one and all.

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1383. Hearts 1 Hibs 2: Reedijk's first victory is one to remember as spirited Leith men battle back to see off rivals and reach Premier Sports Cup final

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:25 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:33 EDT, 1 November 2026

If you are going to keep your supporters waiting until your fifth match in charge to record your first victory, best to make it a good one.

For Marink Reedijk and the Hibs fans, this pulsating triumph over their great rivals proved to be a classic case of better late than never.

By the end of a remarkable weekend, the fact the Easter Road side had dropped to the foot of the Premiership table wasn’t even so much as a mild concern.

Hibernian will return to Hampden in December 13 to face off against Rangers for the first major trophy of the season.

Just as significantly, they got there with a performance which was brave and brilliant.

After a difficult start to life in Leith, Reedijk belatedly announced his arrival with a storied victory.

McGrath fires home a rebound to put Hibs in front just before half time

Reedijk embraces goalscorer Boyle as he is substituted in the second half

Whatever happens next month against Derek McInnes’ side, Hibs have created history just by getting this far.

Their four previous jousts with Hearts at Hampden stretching back to 2006 had all ended in failure.

How those witnesses to those disappointments milked the moment at time up here as Sunshine on Leith echoed around the arena.

Reedjik’s men did not make life easy for themselves. They were behind inside four minutes when Claudio Braga struck.

Given how poor their league form has been of late, you wondered if it might get ugly. What did we know?

Hibs were scintillating until the interval, on the front foot and turning the game on its head through Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

While they defended like their lives depended on it when Hearts came at them in the second half, they spurned chances to put the game to bed.

Not that they’ll care a jot about that now. Under Reedijk, they finally have lift-off.

This was a painful episode for Wouter Vrancken, the Hearts manager.

It was as if the dream start startled his players. They were never in control of the contest the minute Hibs dusted themselves down and got to work.

Braga faded from view and he was not the only one. There was an air of desperation to Hearts’ efforts long before referee David Dickinson put them out of their misery.

The truth is that all the best players on the day - Joe Newell, Owen Elding and Boyle chief among them - wore the green of Hibernian.

Accordingly, Hearts’ wait for a first League Cup since 1962 goes on.

The bookmakers had predicted a win for the Tynecastle side. The form book pointed towards it. And, after just four minutes, so did the scoreline.

Calvin Miller won and took a corner at the Hibs end which swung in viciously. Braga timed his run to perfection, ghosted into space and planted a header beyond Raphael Sallinger.

Braga gets free at a corner to head Hearts into an early lead at Hampden

After two own goals in his past two matches, Jason Kerr could have lived without the finger of blame pointing towards him.

On the sidelines, Reedijk looked on impassively. How would his side respond? In the best way imaginable, as it happened.

Rather than going into their shells, Hibs went on the attack and completely dictated the minutes up until the half-time whistle. To a man, they were simply outstanding.

Newell was at the heart of everything, demanding the ball in tight areas, finding passing angles which no one else could.

He played a cute pass to Felix Passlack. Goal-side of Malachi Fagan-Walcott, he forced Beau Reus into a low save.

Hearts’ cause certainly wasn’t helped by a couple of early withdrawals through injury.

Tomas Magnusson never recovered from a head knock he sustained in a clash with Kerr. Yan Dhanda shed his tracksuit.

Miller tried to run off a muscular injury that required treatment but was eventually replaced by Sabri Guendouz.

But there was more to the change in the game’s flow than just the personnel.

Hibs were far more secure in possession. They were more inventive. They looked more dangerous.

Adam Mayor’s pace took him to the line. His cut-back ended with Elding blazing over. But it encouraged the men in green and white.

Their equaliser on 19 minutes came after a period of control.

Newell’s pass into Elding was played with the perfect pace and direction. Elding’s flick around the corner was precise.

Running off Fagan-Walcott’s shoulder, Boyle got enough on his shot to prevent Reus’ touch keeping it out of the net.

Boyle squeezes his shot through Hearts goalkeeper Reus to bring Hibs level

Any concern among the Hibs fans that their celebrations would be cut short by VAR were ended when a still image showed Jordi Altena playing Boyle on by a couple of inches.

Hibs’ determination to stay on top extended to deserved bookings for Kerr and Josh Mulligan for taking out Dhanda and Stephen Kingsley. Altena was also carded for clipping Boyle.

Newell clipped the top of the crossbar with a drive through a packed penalty box.

Three minutes from the break, Newell was instrumental in the move which saw his side deservedly go up the tunnel ahead.

Boyle’s corner was headed clear by Jamie McCart. Newell took a brilliant touch to take Braga out of the game. His fizzing shot was blocked on the line by Fagan-Walcott. McGrath kept his nerve from four yards to stab the ball home.

Hearts had started well but completely dropped their levels. Braga did flash a header from a Josh McPake cross narrowly wide in injury time but an equaliser was ill-deserved at that point.

You sensed Vrancken would go through his players in the dressing room.

They were better after the turnaround. Laurent Mendy curled a shout just over while Braga raced clear and forced Sallinger to make a solid stop at his near post.

While Boyle did dart in from the left and force Reus to save, Hearts were asking more of the questions.

When Reedijk’s men came up for air, Elding’s hopes of nicking a third were thwarted by McCart’s slide tackle. Kerr also headed straight at Reus.

Sallinger did well to prevent Guendouz’s net-bound strike creeping in under his bar.

The Easter Road side take the acclaim of supporters after booking their spot in the final

With the game increasingly stretched, Kingsley made up the ground to deny Passlack.

What Hibs fans would have given for a third to seal the deal.

Thibault Klidje should have done so when he burst clear with seven minutes remaining. With better options to his right, he took the wrong one and fired harmlessly over. At least he worked the keeper with his next attempt.

Hibs battened down the hatches. Grant Hanley came on and, this week, there was no debate about what end of the field he’d be stationed.

When Braga headed a chance from a free-kick wide with a couple of minutes remaining, the maroon exodus began.

Wild horses couldn’t have dragged the Hibs supporters from the arena. How they savoured this.

#1382. Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated ‘pseudobulk’ counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have revealed hundreds of thousands of association signals between genetic variants and human diseases and traits4, but the modes of action by which most of these variants affect phenotypes remain to be characterized, especially non-coding variants. The characterization of the impact of genetic variants on gene expression—known as expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) mapping—can help linking variants to the putative genes they regulate1,5,6,7,8,9, thus identifying the genes and pathways involved in disease pathogenesis, which is a critical step in identifying opportunities for therapeutic intervention10.

However, important limitations remain. First, eQTL mapping has traditionally been limited to common genetic variation (minor allele frequency (MAF)) greater than 1–5%) due to relatively small sample sizes and the widespread use of genotyping arrays, which do not accurately genotype most rare variants and complex structural variants11, compared with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) approaches. Second, eQTLs are extremely context specific, with many studies demonstrating that genetic variants frequently affect gene expression levels in ways detectable only in specific tissues3, sorted cell types6,10,12,13 or on stimulation14,15. Single-cell eQTL mapping has further demonstrated that the effects of many genetic variants on gene expression can only be detected within specific cell types and even transient cellular states3,16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23.

Here we introduce phase 1 of the TenK10K (up to 10,000 cells for 10,000 individuals) study, encompassing 5.4 million cells from 1,925 individuals of European ancestry selected from a broader cohort of 2,103 individuals. In accompanying papers, we leverage the same dataset to investigate the effect of tandem repeat variation on gene expression24 and the putative causal links between gene expression measurements and human diseases and traits25, and an overlapping set of samples to explore the impact of genetic variation on chromatin accessibility26.

Here we use an association method we recently developed, SAIGE-QTL27, to map common-variant and rare-variant single-cell eQTLs across immune cell types. We identify more than 150,000 common-variant effects and more than 30,000 rare-variant effects on gene expression, including signals for nearly 5,000 genes (roughly 25%) with no previously reported eQTLs in a large blood eQTL study5. We propose a framework for quantifying the extent of cell-type specificity or sharedness of eQTLs and show that about half of the effects are found in only one or a few cell types, and almost none are ubiquitous across all. We perform statistical colocalization between our eQTLs and 60 disease phenotypes and blood traits, identifying more than 60,000 colocalization events for more than 5,000 genes, providing potential molecular mechanisms in almost 900 genes associated with human phenotypic variation. We use a biologically driven deep learning method, scDeepID, to identify continuous cell states related to cell function and map more than 15,000 eQTLs that vary dynamically along those states. Finally, we identify 164 independent genetic variants that regulate the abundance of cell states.

After quality control, a total of 5,438,679 peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 1,925 donors were considered for analysis (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Methods). We collected and sequenced PBMCs from all individuals, yielding an average of 2,825 cells per individual after quality control (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 and Methods).

Each cell was assigned to their donor of origin by means of demultiplexing and to an immune cell type using a combined approach of reference-based classification and hierarchical clustering as recommended by the single-cell eQTLGen Consortium28 (Methods). Each cell was assigned to one of 28 different cell types, spanning the key expected immune lineages (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 2).

In addition, we generated WGS data for all 1,925 individuals, which was processed and quality-controlled using established pipelines (Methods). We called 66,658,242 sites across single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and insertions and deletions (indels), of which 53,784,018 (80.6%) were rare (MAF < 1%), roughly 4.5 times as many as from SNP array data (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 4).

To assess the effects of common genetic variation on gene expression changes, we mapped cis eQTLs, testing for the effects of common (MAF > 1%) variant sites within ±100 kilobases (kb) of the gene body on single-cell expression profiles (testing all sufficiently expressed genes; Methods). We used SAIGE-QTL27 to map eQTL effects using single-cell profiles modelled as Poisson counts, rather than relying on ‘pseudobulk’ aggregation. We mapped eQTLs separately in each of the 28 cell types and confirmed the type I error was controlled using permutations (Fig. 2a). At a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 5%, we identified 154,932 eQTLs in at least one cell type from 17,674 unique eGenes (83% of all genes tested; Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 5). The number of eQTLs identified varied substantially across cell types, largely due to the number of cells available for each cell type and the resulting number of individuals tested affecting statistical power, as previously shown in refs. 16,27 (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2).

For representative cell types, the percentage of eGenes compared to the total number of genes tested is highlighted.
