#1327. Puzzling Liverpool are not ready for the title, why Cole Palmer may have to leave Chelsea and Lisandro Martinez should have lost his spot long ago: IAN LADYMAN on My Football Weekend

Published: 07:09 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:20 EDT, 2 November 2026

In terms of points gathered, the Premier League title winner this season will be either Arsenal or Manchester City.

It's a two-horse race in which one of the horses has a bullet with its name on it sitting somewhere in a locked cabinet at Premier League headquarters.

We can presume, then, that Arsenal will win the title for the second season running.

Some are entertaining the idea that Brighton can have a go on our behalf. They have beaten Arsenal already at the Amex Stadium and now, after another brilliantly brave display at the Etihad on Saturday, they have beaten City too.

Fabian Hurzeler's team will not win the Premier League, though. Injuries, fluctuations in form and the fact they are playing in Europe will see to that.

Brighton have just played back-to-back games at City – the first in the Carabao Cup last week – and are off to Getafe in the Conference League on Thursday before facing Brentford back in Sussex on Sunday.

Liverpool are not ready to challenge for the Premier League title - and that is OK

It's exciting and it's fun but it's also a schedule that will get them in the end.

As for Liverpool, they are simply not ready. Not yet.

That was apparent before yesterday's home defeat to Arsenal, in which they played well.

Andoni Iraola's team also played nicely at home to City last month but lost that one too.

In fact, Liverpool have lost at home to both their rivals without scoring a goal. They don't score many against anybody, as it happens. Just 11 in the league which is three fewer than Ipswich and only one more than Manchester United.

So, no, Liverpool will not challenge for the title and that should be viewed as perfectly OK on Merseyside.

Liverpool have spent a lot of money since lifting the trophy under Arne Slot in 2025 but some of it has not been spent awfully well and last season was so very bad that they are coming from a long way back under their new manager.

There has been progress. Liverpool have recruited two sound defenders in Jeremy Jacquet and Ronaldo Araujo and are starting to see a return on Alexander Isak and, to a lesser degree, on Florian Wirtz, who has been nowhere near as bad this season as some people seem so keen to claim.

But Liverpool remain a puzzle in the final third. They play with nowhere near the structure and balance of Arsenal or the imagination and pace of City. Yesterday at Anfield was rather typical of how they can be. Possession, promise and power but a lack of calm intelligence and threat just when it really matters.

It may yet come. It is possible to see Iraola's influence. They would appear to have hired the right man to succeed Slot and that is half the battle.

But a third-placed finish, a journey to the last eight of the Champions League and a tilt at a domestic cup would represent progress for Liverpool.

As such – unless City escape their Premier League charges via appeal – this is Arsenal's title already and if that feels rather ho-hum and disappointing, it's for the rest of the competition to ask themselves how it has come to be this way.

Liverpool deserved to get something from the game at Anfield but warrant little sympathy for the manner in which they fell behind.

The home team's problems began when Virgil van Dijk took a goal kick and passed the ball a yard to his right to his goalkeeper Alisson Becker, who proceeded to give it away.

This is a common modern trend but no less confusing for it.

How have we reached a point where so many Premier League clubs seem happier for a goalkeeper to have the ball at his feet than they do an outfield player?

Van Dijk can pass the ball perfectly well. Let him do it!

Brighton are the league's top scorers with 24 and have had 11 different players on target so far.

That's more scorers than half the 20 Premier League clubs have scored goals.

Brighton celebrate a brilliant victory away at Man City - but they won't win the league

Nottingham Forest have to break free from their boom and bust cycle if they are ever to make serious Premier League progress and it feels as though that time is now.

Forest and their owner Evangelos Marinakis are on their fifth manager in the last 14 months. If normal rules apply, Oliver Glasner is in serious trouble after starting the season with just one win in nine games.

But Glasner was the manager Marinakis had wanted for quite some time. He first asked him to join in early 2024 at a time when Nuno Espirito Santo was struggling for results.

So now is the time for the Forest owner to look back at the churn of managers, players and indeed recruitment executives that has characterised his time at the City Ground and realise that something must change.

Glasner was unsparing in his criticism of the Forest players after Saturday's defeat at Brentford. In the same breath, he almost invited Marinakis to sack him.

But Forest's players could be forgiven for being confused and a little demotivated after so much change. Every time they lose back-to-back games, they must expect the manager to be sacked.

So it's time to shift that culture of uncertainty at Forest. Time to behave like a grown-up football club.

Glasner is extremely well paid by Marinakis. His annual salary is north of £10million a season and puts him up near the top of the list.

If Marinakis believes he has a manager of that standing, he should take his hands off the wheel and let him get on with it.

Oliver Glasner invited the sack from Nottingham Forest - but they should stick with him

Michael Carrick will do well to get much more time at Manchester United and there was a certain irony in Lisandro Martinez being the latest player to let him down as his team lost 2-0 at Chelsea.

Martinez – sent off after conceding a ludicrous penalty at Stamford Bridged – moaned publicly last month that United's recruitment hasn't been good enough in recent times.

Had it been any better, a seriously limited and unreliable central defender would have lost his place in the United first team a long time ago.

Carrick knows how this ends but what changes?

United actually played very well in the first half on Saturday and could easily have been two or three goals up by half-time, none of which will be of any comfort to their manager.

We have seen this movie before at Old Trafford.

Carrick will go, United's bunch of semi-serious footballers will raise their levels for a new manager and the club will start telling everyone they have cracked the code – again.

All of which goes to prove what we have known for a long time. Until the quality and indeed the mentality of the players changes at United then nothing else does.

Lisandro Martinez was the latest player to let Michael Carrick down away at Chelsea

Jamie Carragher believes Unai Emery is ready for a step up from Aston Villa to manage a club like United but has upset the Midlands club by saying so.

A Villa statement threatening to sue Carragher for his comments was simply embarrassing.

Carragher's language on the Stick to Football podcast was coarse and he may regret that but it was hard to take issue with his view that Villa sit below United in terms of profile and status.

Villa have made fabulous progress under Emery but part of becoming a really big club is learning how to behave like one.

Cole Palmer now has 50 Premier League goals in 105 games for Chelsea. Only Diego Costa and Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink reached that milestone more quickly.

Time will tell, however, whether Chelsea really will provide him with the platform for success his elite level of talent really deserves.

For all that they seem to be moving in the right direction under Xabi Alonso, Saturday's performance against a team waiting to be beaten was still some way below the level a team needs if it is to launch a credible title challenge.

Can Chelsea provide the platform for Cole Palmer that his talent really deserves?

Palmer will be lucky to find his way into Thomas Tuchel's England squad that will be announced on Friday.

His form perhaps warrants it but Tuchel was unimpressed by his withdrawal from the last international gathering and is unlikely to have forgotten.

What, meanwhile, of Trent Alexander-Arnold?

With Reece James and Tino Livramento still injured, the return to fitness of Ben White and Djed Spence has nevertheless given Tuchel some options at right-back for big Nations League games at home to Croatia and away in Spain.

Jarell Quansah can expect to start in Madrid for the game that matters leaving Alexander-Arnold to yet again consider the wisdom of his switch from Liverpool to Real in the summer of 2025.

Alexander-Arnold actually started for Jose Mourinho as Real won 3-0 at Racing yesterday but it was only the fourth time he has done so this season.

At some stage, Alexander-Arnold is going to have to make a decision regarding his future.

Anyone who has seen Tottenham play this season could or should have told you that the improvement on last term was obvious, even when early results were poor.

The London club may well have paid top-heavy prices for new players such as Sandro Tonali and the Manchester City duo of Savio and Omar Marmoush and the value of those deals will become apparent over time.

But Roberto de Zerbi's squad has more depth and balance to it and is benefitting in particular from the improvement in players he inherited from Thomas Frank.

We all remember Antonin Kinsky's Champions League horror show as Spurs collapsed at Atletico Madrid last March but the 23-year-old goalkeeper has been excellent this term.

So, meanwhile, has former England international Conor Gallagher who looked like he had forgotten how to play on arrival last season but was impressive once again in Saturday's win over Crystal Palace, this time as a second-half substitute for Dominic Solanke.

The fuss made about some clubs failing to sell out every single home game is ridiculous given the financial strains currently being placed on families across the country.

Still, it's strange to note pockets of empty blue seats at Coventry matches given how long the club have waited for a top-flight return.

Home games are listed as sold out yet rarely seem to be. Fans say it's because it's too difficult to pass a season ticket on to a friend on days they can't make it.

It's not a good look for Coventry and feels like a problem that needs solving.

There have been regular pockets of empty blue seats at Coventry matches at home this season

Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka called on his players to show courage and play as they train after their defeat at Coventry pinned them to the foot of the table.

But the uncomfortable truth is that nobody in Regis le Bris's team has struggled for form more than the experienced midfielder in recent weeks.

Xhaka was a success story last season as Sunderland stunned the Premier League but needs to find some of that Player of the Year form quickly.

#1326. Van Bronckhorst warns Feyenoord: ‘Win over Como guarantees nothing against Inter’

Giovanni van Bronckhorst has warned that Feyenoord’s home win over Como counts for little ahead of Tuesday’s Champions League clash with Inter in Rotterdam.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, citing FCInter1908, the Feyenoord coach spoke at his pre-match press conference before the game at De Kuip. It kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT] and will be refereed by Sweden’s Glenn Nyberg.

“Getting a result against an Italian team doesn’t mathematically mean we’ll win again,” Van Bronckhorst said. “Of course, we watched the Como game too, but tomorrow the opponent will be different. Como are in the Champions League for the first time, Inter have a different status. Every team has its vulnerabilities, though.”

Inter arrive in the Netherlands after their first league defeat of the season, a 3-1 loss to Milan in Saturday’s derby, which leaves them three points behind leaders Lazio. Cristian Chivu is also short of players, with Lautaro Martínez, Benjamin Pavard, John Stones, Curtis Jones and Luis Henrique all out injured.

Van Bronckhorst played as a left-back for Barcelona and Arsenal. He confirmed that Shaqueel van Persie and Reiss Nelson have trained and will be available.

“I’ve watched several Inter games, including the last one against Milan,” Van Bronckhorst said. “Playing against them is difficult, they play football similar to ours. They have a lot of injuries, but also a lot of quality and experience.

“Inter aren’t afraid to sit in a low block and then press high, they bring a lot of players forward, and they’re a complete team. They’re missing some players, and we’ll have our chances to win the game, as has always been the case.

“Tomorrow’s Inter will be different from the one we saw against Barcelona, but they know what to do in the Champions League to go through and be successful. Tomorrow we need to play our cards well and try to get a great result. We’ve struggled away from home, while we’ve already won at home against Como. Let’s hope we can do it again.”

Feyenoord are without a win in three games, and van Bronckhorst wants his side to repeat what worked against Como. “The group has energy. It knows it’s come from three games without a win and wants to show tomorrow that it wants to turn the page,” he said. “We don’t need to run more, but to be compact at certain moments of the game. We managed that against Como, and we need to do it again so we don’t leave Inter dangerous spaces.”

He also played down the derby result. “I didn’t look at the result, but at the way they played. They’re a top team, and not just this year. They have players who know what to do in the Champions League. I have to focus on their strengths, not on the result of their last game.”

#1325. One Everton Man Higher Than Dewsbury-Hall: Players Rated and Slated vs Newcastle

Everton secured a 1-0 victory over Newcastle at St James' Park, making it two wins against the Magpies in just four days.

It was a bright first half for Everton, and David Moyes will be wondering how his side weren't in front heading into half-time.

The ball fell to Thierno Barry from just a few yards out in the first half, but he failed to connect properly with the ball after taking a wild swing at it.

Later in the half, another big chance fell Everton's way. A smart run and pass from Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall helped find Harrison Armstrong, but he somehow missed the target with his first-time effort.

Shortly after the break, Everton found themselves in front. A smart set-piece routine allowed Dewsbury-Hall to find Tyrique George with a superb pass. He fired an effort at goal that went through goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, allowing Barry to tap home the opener.

It was a deserved opener for the Toffees after their missed chances in the first half, and Newcastle could have no complaints as Everton went 1-0 up.

Always an interesting game for Jordan Pickford, being a Sunderland lad. The Newcastle supporters certainly let him know!

Pickford was anonymous in the first half, which is everything Moyes would have wanted, with Newcastle barely testing the goalkeeper.

After another fairly quiet half, Pickford, one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League right now, made a crucial save in the final seconds with his feet, denying Yoane Wissa from close range.

Jake O’Brien hasn’t been given too many opportunities by David Moyes so far this season, but he came in at right-back vs Newcastle. The Republic of Ireland international kept Harvey Barnes quiet, while he was also a threat in both boxes aerially.

It was a comfortable start to the evening for both centre-backs in the first half, with Newcastle showing minimal threat. As per usual, James Tarkowski was winning everything.

When paired with Jarrad Branthwaite, Everton are more often than not an incredibly solid side at the back. The Newcastle game was no different.

It’s a similar story for Jarrad Branthwaite as it was for Tarkowski. He was incredibly solid at the back, and his inclusion allowed Everton to play a high line due to his pace. Newcastle tried to get in behind regularly, particularly in the first half, but Branthwaite was always there to snuff it out.

Further reports about Grealish have come to light after he was left out of Everton's squad to face Newcastle.

Vitalii Mykolenko has had plenty of criticism since his move to Everton, but he’s looked a different player this season. That was no different against Newcastle, with another solid display. Never anything outlandish or crazy in terms of performance levels, but solid.

James Garner, as he always does, showed plenty of energy in the middle of the park for Everton. Sitting in front of the back four allowed his midfield partners the freedom to get forward.

Sometimes Garner’s influence on the team isn’t too noticeable due to it being mostly off-the-ball work, but he was a key figure in the middle nonetheless.

Harrison Armstrong showed plenty of energy in the first half, and he should have got himself on the scoresheet. One of the best chances of the game fell to him after some good work by Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, but his right-footed strike from around 12 yards out was comfortably wide, when he should have scored.

Perhaps one of the surprise inclusions, starting at right-wing like he did against Chelsea. The German showed plenty of energy on the right-hand side in the first half, causing Lewis Hall problems.

Rohl was clearly used as an outlet for Everton, using his pace to get in behind in transition. He also tracked back well to help the Toffees out defensively.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was playing in his usual advanced midfield role. In the first half, Dewsbury-Hall was finding himself in lots of space in between the lines, and was undoubtedly Everton’s most creative threat.

That showed as Everton opened the scoring, finding George with a superb pass before his shot was palmed away and tapped in by Barry.

Overall, a faultless performance from the former Chelsea midfielder. He was everywhere, and played a crucial role in the goal.

It was a quiet first half for Tyrique George, who struggled to get himself involved.

Shortly after the break, however, George made a clever run from a set-piece to fire at Lukas Hornicek, with the goalkeeper spilling it before Barry fired home.

Fairly quiet overall, but didn't do an awful lot wrong.

Thierno Barry had an excellent chance to open the scoring for Everton in the first half, taking a wild swipe at the ball from close range, but he failed to connect properly.

Barry did make up for his missed chance, though, scoring the opening goal of the game as he tapped home from close range just after the break.

Barry struggled to get involved in the game outside of his opportunities in front of goal, but ultimately, scored the winner for the Toffees.

Further reports about Grealish have come to light after he was left out of Everton's squad to face Newcastle.

Although Dewsbury-Hall was the best performer on the pitch, David Moyes has to be given his flowers.

The Everton manager has taken a lot of criticism in recent weeks, but he answered those critics with a fantastic 1-0 away victory.

Moyes made some bold decisions to take Hayden Hackney and Tyler Dibling out of the team, while also starting Merlin Rohl at right wing.

When you make decisions like that, they have to work out, and no one can question Moyes for the decisions he made against Newcastle.

The team looked incredibly balanced and fully deserved their victory.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Barry is a nice guy but a dreadful footballer, I know we have to wait till January to bring in an alternative, but, in the interim, shortly we can fine a deputy from within the squad. Dibling may not be a striker, but he might be able to control the ball when played up to him, but I'm open to suggestions.

#1324. Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

#1323. Harry Kane Names the Major Trophy He'd Happily 'Trade' His Ballon d'Or For

It's been a fantastic few seasons for Harry Kane, culminating in his 2026 Ballon d'Or win.

The English striker scored goal after goal for Tottenham Hotspur, but never managed to get his hands on a major trophy with Spurs. In the pursuit of glory, he made the move to Bayern Munich in 2023, and that has proved to be a sensible transfer.

The 33-year-old, one of the oldest Ballon d'Or winners, has now won two Bundesliga titles and the DFB-Pokal, while continuing to score at an electrifying rate. Indeed, Kane scored 73 goals for club and country in 2025/26, which helped him win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Lamine Yamal may have won, but some former Ballon d'Or winners didn't even include him in their top three.

Having been named the world's best player, the Englishman could not hide his delight, saying he was 'speechless' as he claimed the award in London. However, in the short time since that historic night, Kane has revealed that he would swap the Ballon d'Or for one major honour.

Speaking to reporters via Goal, he claimed that he'd happily 'trade' his prize if it meant winning the Champions League with Bayern. Kane explained:

"Team trophies are why we play football. The team aspect of our sport is really, really important. The Ballon d'Or last week was one of the best feelings I've had in my life and my career... but to have moments with the team, celebrations with the club, to be able to lift the Champions League with Bayern would be an incredible feeling.

"Of course the Ballon d'Or is a highlight, it puts me on an even bigger level, but you want to have these big finals, the Champions League, having that feeling of emotion with your teammates as well. I would choose the Champions League, but I have the opportunity to do both, let's see what happens."

That's not to say Kane isn't appreciating the value of his award, as he went on to add: "Winning the Ballon d'Or was a huge achievement for me. I've had to overcome many challenges in my career, some people didn't think I'd get this far..."

Kane most notably made it all the way to the Champions League final with Spurs in 2018/19, but was unable to get across the line, as his team lost 2-0 to Liverpool. At the time, he dejectedly said:

“It was a tough one to take. It’s probably one of the biggest games we’ll ever play in our careers and to let it slide by is always a tough one to take. It’s an experience we need to learn from."

At Bayern, Kane then made it to the semis twice, and the quarters once, but still hasn't been able to make another final. He's also suffered more disappointment in cup competitions with England.

Once again, his goalscoring record at that level has never been questioned – he is the Three Lions' all-time top scorer after all – but he's lost two finals with his country, suffering defeat at both Euro 2020 and Euro 2024. He also made it to the semis with England this summer at the 2026 World Cup, but once again fell short when it came to pushing for glory.

With all that disappointment in mind, it's little wonder Kane would happily give up his Ballon d'Or if it meant finally getting his hands on a major team honour such as the Champions League.

#1322. Aston Villa drop legal action threat against Jamie Carragher after Sky Sports pundit's apology for telling fans to 'shut the f*** up'

Published: 08:46 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:30 EDT, 2 November 2026

Aston Villa have dropped their threat of legal action against Jamie Carragher after the pundit apologised for telling the club's fans to 'shut the f*** up'.

The Premier League club hit out at the former Liverpool defender for making what they labelled as 'unacceptable insults' on the Overlap podcast last week.

The row had centred on comments made by Carragher in which he pushed the idea of Aston Villa boss Unai Emery becoming the next Manchester United manager.

It escalated further when Carragher doubled down, telling Villa fans to 'shut the f*** up' as he claimed that Emery would be interested in managing a 'giant' again and declared 'There is a chain in football.'

On Friday, Aston Villa shared a statement on club channels carrying the name of co-owner Nassef Sawiris, reading: 'Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the Club and its fans.

'Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, Chairman.'

Aston Villa have dropped their threat of legal action against pundit Jamie Carragher

Carragher had been pushing Unai Emery towards the Manchester United job on The Overlap podcast and claimed that Villa 'will never be' United. (Source: TheOverlap/YouTube)

Aston Villa had threatened legal action on Friday, with Carragher apologising the following day

Carragher issued an apology on Saturday afternoon in an attempt to defuse the situation.

'I'd like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners & their fans,' Carragher wrote on social media.

'My language this week was clumsy & wrong. I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it's not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV!'

Fans were left stunned at the response by Villa to Carragher's comments, seemingly innocuous linking Emery, who is admired at Old Trafford, to the Manchester United job, which may soon be available with immense pressure on Michael Carrick.

‘I think Unai Emery is unbelievable with what he does year after year. That amount of change, players needing time to settle and he does it year after year,' Carragher had said.

'But the reason I’m going to go back at Villa fans is I can’t believe that a manager who is so successful in the Europa League, take a player, if you’d won the Europa League three or four times (Emery has won it five times) surely you’ll then want to go for the Champions League.

‘Aston Villa will never be Manchester United. I just think he didn’t do well at PSG or Arsenal, and maybe that’s because of egos in the dressing room and that sort of thing.

'But surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again. There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.’

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1320. Roma coach Gasperini before Manchester United: ‘Everyone has the right to dream, but we’re short in midfield’

Gian Piero Gasperini says Roma will treat struggling Manchester United as if they were at their best, and he admitted his side are short of bodies in midfield before Tuesday’s Champions League clash at Old Trafford.

With quotes via the Corriere dello Sport, the Roma coach spoke at his pre-match press conference in Manchester. Roma travel in high spirits after Saturday’s 5-2 win at Udinese, which left them third, a point off the top. United lost 2-0 at Chelsea that same day, piling more pressure on Michael Carrick.

“In the league they’re going through a difficult period for results, but we can’t let ourselves be distracted,” Gasperini said. “United are still a strong team, they have players of absolute quality, and it’s a hot, difficult environment. We’re preparing as if we’re facing the best Manchester United.”

Asked whether Old Trafford is the “Theatre of Dreams”, he replied: “Everyone has the right to dream. I try to have dreams that can come true soon, starting tomorrow, in a fantastic stadium that’s famous all over the world. I hope it can come true.”

Gasperini is without Lorenzo Pellegrini, Paulo Dybala and Manu Koné. Primavera youngsters were called up at the weekend to fill out the squad.

“We’re missing Pellegrini, Dybala and Koné in the same departments, so we try to adapt a bit at certain moments. We have Castro as an alternative with Malen, but in midfield we’re short. I hope it’s just a passing phase,” he said.

“We’ve played these seven games on a knife-edge, but we’ve always had well-prepared players who recovered quickly. Mora? He’s fine, the 17 players we have are all ready. After the international break we hope to have everyone back. It’s difficult this week.”

He also praised his wing-backs. “Lulli? Wesley is also doing very well in that position. Molina needed to play, and Rensch has done very well too. It’s draining for them, they cover a lot of ground with acceleration and speed.”

On how hard it is to be perfect: “Perfection doesn’t exist, not for the big teams and not for us. Our quality is that we always try to improve. We know our characteristics, but we know we can do better in some situations.”

Asked about Carrick’s difficult spell, and whether it compared with his short stay at Inter in 2011, Gasperini said: “Every situation is different. I don’t know United’s exactly, but I know they have strong players. You can suffer for a certain period, but then you manage to restart. Hopefully from the day after tomorrow!

“The comparison with me at Inter? I really wasn’t there long, three games, so I wouldn’t make that comparison.”

#1319. Exclusive: Nick Montgomery On Managing In China And Working Under Postecoglou

Beijing Guoan are unbeaten in 21 games in all competitions, and last month's trip to Henan showed exactly why. Three goals down at half-time, Nick Montgomery’s side scored four times after the break. Zhang Yuning got the 81st-minute winner. It was the first time in Guoan's 33-year history they had ever won from three goals down.

It caps a superb first season in China for 44-year-old head coach Nick Montgomery. He won the Chinese FA Super Cup – China’s version of the Community Shield – in his first competitive game in March, and Guoan are also unbeaten through three games in the AFC Champions League Elite tournament. Thai side Port FC are up next on Tuesday.

Only a five-point deduction for historical breaches, handed down after Montgomery arrived, has kept Guoan out of the title race. Without it, they would go into the final-day fixture on November 8 against Chongqing Tonglianglong top of the table, ahead of current leaders Chengdu Rongcheng on goal difference. Instead, they are third, two points behind Dalian Yingbo, with a Chinese FA Cup semi-final against Shanghai Port to come on November 20.

A former Sheffield United midfielder, Montgomery won the A-League as a head coach with Central Coast Mariners and the Europa League as Postecoglou’s assistant at Tottenham. Now he is making his name in China.

Montgomery did not need much convincing. He had played in Beijing with the Mariners, and the memory never left him.

“If we’re talking about Beijing Guoan, we’re talking about one of the biggest clubs in Asian football, and it’s a club I know well because of my time playing in the A-League,” he told GIVEMESPORT. “I played in the Asian Champions League, and I remember, I think it was a Wednesday night, playing in Beijing. There were 40,000 fans, and that always stuck in my mind.”

After leaving Nottingham Forest, where he was Ange Postecoglou's assistant, Montgomery had plenty of offers but was waiting for the right one. It came from Matthias Brosamer, the German who had just been appointed Guoan’s new sporting director.

"He is a great guy, very intelligent. He speaks fluent Chinese, and we had some amazing football conversations," said Montgomery, who was appointed on 8 January. “He told me about the project. He was looking for a head coach with experience in Asia, and he really loved my profile. Things moved forward quickly, and probably within a week or two we’d agreed to take on the project. I was landing in Beijing in wintertime – I think it was minus 20 when I arrived – and that was the start of such an exciting journey.”

Working largely through translators, Montgomery knew his first job was to win people over. It didn't take him long.

“When you come into a new country, you’ve got to be brave to start with,” he said. “You’ve got to know there’s a period where you’ll have to get everybody to buy in – to you as a person, forget the football – because you’re coming into their culture. If they see you’re committed and believe in your style of football, then they’re going to support you. I have created a real family environment, which is important.”

The start could hardly have gone better. Guoan’s Super Cup triumph came against Shanghai Port, winners of the last three Chinese Super League titles, who were beaten 2-0 in Nanjing.

“We beat Shanghai Port, who were the benchmark team. They had players picking up ridiculous salaries over the years, the best squads,” said Montgomery, who knows Port boss Kevin Muscat from their days in Australia. “That was the first real game, so to win a trophy was a great start.”

Injuries soon took their toll, though, and Guoan won just four of their first 14 league games, the last of those a 2-1 home defeat by Henan on 23 May. They have not lost since.

“People said you can’t play like this in China, that the players are not resilient enough, and I never believed that,” he said. “The players showed me on the training ground every day. We don’t speak about being 21 games unbeaten. We just focus on the process.”

The biggest change has come up front, where Montgomery has paired China captain Zhang Yuning with Angola international Fábio Abreu.

“I always played in Australia with two strikers, and I play in China with two strikers, which I was told no one did before,” he said. “I was told they couldn’t play together. The previous season, only one of them played and the other was on the bench. Now they’re both top scorers in the team.”

Unfortunately, Guoan lost Abreu in mid-October after he broke his leg in a 1-0 win against Qingdao West Coast.

"We were very sad," said Montgomery. "He will miss the rest of the season. Most of our injuries have been contact ones, which is very unlucky. We have had to deal with many challenges this season, and that makes our form even more satisfying."

Guoan's numbers speak for themselves. They are also at or near the top of the league for possession, forward passes and touches in the opposition box.

“If the players don’t want to run for you, you’re never going to have those statistics,” Montgomery said. “That tells you Chinese players are honest. If they believe in you, they’ll do everything you ask.”

It is all the more impressive given Guoan started on minus five points – a deduction neither Montgomery nor Brosamer knew about when they took over.

“It was a bit of a shock to everybody. You’re on minus points before you even get to zero,” he said. “If we’d started on a level playing field, we’d be top of the league."

The title may be out of reach, but Montgomery will feel encouraged that, without the deduction, Beijing Guoan would be top. Second place is still possible if Guoan win their last league game againstChongqing Tonglianglong and Dalian Yingbo lose or draw. And there is the chance to defend the Chinese FA Cup, which Gooan won for the sixth time last season when they beat Henan 3-0 under former coach Quique Setien.

“We can’t win the league because of what happened, which is a shame, but we can still finish second,” Montgomery said. “In the cup, we’ve got a difficult game against Shanghai Port. They were the Galácticos of the Chinese Super League for the last couple of years. Players like Oscar and Hulk – all the big names – loved playing in China.”

In the AFC Champions League, Guoan beat Pohang Steelers 3-1 in the first Asian Champions League game at the Workers’ Stadium for seven years, before winning 1-0 at Buriram United – “a very difficult place to go”, according to Montgomery. They drew 2-2 with Jeonbuk Hyundai Motors on October 27 and are currently fifth in the league phase.

Montgomery is clearly relishing life in China, where Guoan have drawn crowds of more than 60,000 at the rebuilt Workers’ Stadium this season.

“What the Western world thinks of China is the total opposite of the reality. It’s so advanced,” he said. “The infrastructure in football is unbelievable. Our home games get 50,000 to 65,000 on a weekly basis. There aren’t many Premier League teams that can match that attendance. It is one of the best stadiums in the world – very similar to the Tottenham stadium, which I know very well.

“And there is the belief, moving forward, that the club can bring a championship back to Beijing for the first time since 2009, which is a long time ago.”

Montgomery made the decision that he wanted to return to work as a No.1 again after spending time as Ange Postecoglou's assistant at both Tottenham Hotspur (2024-2025) and Nottingham Forest (2025).

“It’s not like I would be an assistant for any manager,” he said. “I did get asked about being an assistant to another manager, but it wasn’t for me. I knew I was waiting for the right opportunity to get back into management.”

His route to Tottenham began with a message from Postecoglou, who was among the first to congratulate him when the Mariners won the A-League in 2023. A year later, Postecoglou’s assistant Chris Davies left to become Birmingham City manager.

“As with anything in life, it’s about timing,” Montgomery said. “Ange contacted me, we jumped on a call, and he said, ‘I’m going to win a trophy at Tottenham. I want you to come and help me.’ To be honest, I didn’t really need to think about it much. It was a pretty quick decision, and one I definitely don’t regret. Seeing the Tottenham fans at the parade with the trophy was something you can never forget.”

That parade followed Brennan Johnson’s winner against Manchester United in the Europa League final in Bilbao in May 2025, which ended Spurs’ 17-year wait for a trophy – even as an injury-ravaged side finished 17th in the Premier League.

“There was an unbelievable amount of injuries, and the squad was very, very thin,” said Montgomery, who joined in June 2024 with his long-time assistant Sergio Raimundo. “We had some big results, beating Man City 4-0 away and Man United 3-0, but after the injuries came, it was difficult. Winning the Europa League would get the club Champions League football, so you put all your eggs in one basket. As a staff, that’s what we all did. We believed we could win it, and that’s what we did.

“I think only now, or years after, will people look back and think what an amazing achievement that was, because it’s been a difficult ride since then – when you look at the amount of money they’ve spent.”

Even that was not enough to save Postecoglou, who was sacked 16 days after the final. Montgomery admits the staff saw it coming.

“Ange came out and said it in an interview, so for sure – everyone knew there was going to be a change no matter what happened,” he said. “So you have that laser focus on what you can control, and that was winning the Europa League. It was amazing for the club to get Champions League football the following season – it’s just a shame they didn’t give Ange and us that chance. But that’s football. You move on.”

When Postecoglou took over at Nottingham Forest in September 2025, Montgomery went with him, alongside Raimundo and fellow Spurs assistant Mile Jedinak. The Australian was sacked after 39 days and eight games without a win.

Asked what went wrong, Montgomery chose his words carefully.

“Probably the least I say, the better on that one,” he said. “It’s a club with a passionate owner [Evangelos Marinakis] that wants instant success, and it’s a club that is renowned for making changes – a lot of changes, as we’ve seen. So you’re never going to go in thinking, ‘This is a stable environment.’

“I was literally about to take an offer of a head coach role, and Ange said: ‘I think it’s a young squad, we can play good football, and I’d love you to come in with me again.’ It was a big boost, because we’d just come off the back of winning the Europa League. We all went in there wanting to do something, but there wasn’t much time.”

Forest have since been through Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira, with Oliver Glasner appointed in July as their fifth head coach in less than a year.

“A lot of the performances were very good, but the results didn’t match them,” Montgomery added. “These type of projects depend on how much time people are willing to give you, and in the end, you’re not in control of that.”

One player he loved briefly working with was Elliot Anderson, who joined Manchester City for a reported £116m this summer.

“Elliot is a magnificent player, and I still keep in touch with him now. He literally never stops running and is brave on the ball – he just wants it all the time,” said Montgomery. “I think he’s definitely one of the best English midfielders I’ve seen, because he can do everything.”

Before Tottenham came Hibernian. Montgomery left Central Coast for Easter Road in September 2023, taking over a side who had lost their opening three league games.

“I had a lot of offers to go to Japan and other places, but I’ve got Scottish heritage in my family, and Hibs is a big club that hasn't had much success in a long time,” he said. “I was promised a rebuild. The club was bottom of the league and in a bit of a mess. I started well and took the team into the top three at one point. Then there was the Africa Cup of Nations and the Asian Cup, and we lost half the starting players.

“I felt I was building something really good, but we just missed out on the top six with the last kick of the ball. Then I had differences of opinion with the club over what had been promised in terms of the rebuild. You have the owner who wants his way, and in the end we chose to part ways. I moved on, went to Tottenham and won the Europa League. Everything happens for a reason.”

That last kick was Shane Blaney’s stoppage-time equaliser for Motherwell in April 2024, which let Dundee pip Hibs to the final top-six place. Hibs finished eighth, and Montgomery departed the following month – but he holds no grudges.

“I always believe every experience is a good experience – good, bad or indifferent,” he said. “Trust is a big thing for me. If you lose that trust, it’s difficult. But you grow from every experience.”

Montgomery’s methods were forged down under. After 12 years at Sheffield United, he joined Central Coast Mariners in 2012 and helped them win their first A-League Championship a year later. He made 133 appearances in all competitions and captained the club, then coached its academy side before stepping up to the top job in 2021. Two years later, he delivered the Mariners’ first title since his playing days.

“There were big teams spending a lot of money, like Sydney FC, Melbourne Victory and Melbourne City, and we were, comparatively, a small club,” he said. “As a coach, the club had suffered a lot of bottom-of-the-table finishes, with no budget compared to the other teams. I always believed I would take over the youth team, develop the players and push them into the first team when I got the opportunity for the job, and that came within two years.

“In my second season, we brought a lot more young players through and recruited some good foreign players. Jason Cummings, who many people will know in Scotland, was our top scorer. We beat Melbourne City 6-1 in the final with the youngest squad and lowest budget in history to win the championship, which was a massive achievement, and it made me really believe in myself as a coach.”

Cummings, the former Hibs striker, scored a hat-trick in that 2023 Grand Final, delivering the Mariners’ first title since Montgomery’s playing days a decade earlier.

“I never look too far ahead. One thing I remember Ange saying is: ‘They’ll only ever remember the people who win silverware.’ I think that’s true,” he said. “If you don’t win silverware, nobody really remembers your stint there. So making history with the three trophies I’ve been involved in, in such a short period of time as a young manager, makes you cherish those moments, because a lot of players and coaches go through their whole career without ever winning a trophy."

The excellent job Montgomery is currently doing is sure to catch the eye of other clubs around the world, including back in England. He is settled, and solely focused on some big games ahead to close this season with Guoan. Yet in the long run, the chance to manage in the Premier League would be hard to turn down.

“For me, I just take each day as it comes," he said. "For sure, maybe one day I would love to manage in the Premier League. But for now, being China is huge for me. I can't think of a better job right now for me, to be honest. I have a great sporting director [Brosamer] and president, Zhou Jinhui. They both support me and really believe in what I am doing.”

Once the domestic campaign ends, the AFC Champions League continues and will run on into next season. Should Guoan go deep, the finals are due to be held in Saudi Arabia next spring – where Postecoglou’s Al Nassr could be waiting.

“For me to represent Beijing, the capital of China, and get through to the knockout stage would be a huge moment for Chinese football,” he said. “There’s a long way to go, but who knows? It would definitely be good to see Ange if that happened.”

Almost two years on from Bilbao, it would be quite the reunion.

Tottenham Hotspur are flying high currently in the Premier League after finding their feet with three consecutive victories, and Roberto De Zerbi can do no wrong.

Spurs claimed a dominant 2-0 win over ten-man Crystal Palace this past weekend thanks to goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke in either half, moving them up to eighth in the table, and a win in the next game against Leeds could see them move up to fifth ahead of other games taking place over the weekend.

The north London club are even finding themselves in a position to hand young talents some minutes, with the Italian boss able to hand 18-year-old winger Luca Williams-Barnett an opportunity in the win over Palace.

Savio has been dealing with injury issues so far during his time at the club, while Omar Marmoush has struggled massively with his form playing across the forward line, and Dominic Solanke seemingly doesn't fit the way the manager wants to play too well.

That has seen many people clamour for the teenage sensation to be handed a rare start against Leeds, with the short cameo he had in the most recent game enough to ignite the excitement among the fan base.

It would be a huge opportunity for the youngster, but it's also worth noting that he is getting these opportunities because of injury issues within the squad currently.

Savio remains sidelined until after the international break, while James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski continue to deal with their own fitness issues following long-term injury problems. But another forgotten member of the squad is Chelsea loanee Mykhailo Mudryk, who is yet to feature after suffering a muscle problem back in September, and played for just 16 minutes prior to that issue.

De Zerbi has recently confirmed that he expects the Ukraine international to return to contention after the international break, and that could be a major issue for Williams-Barnett's chances of becoming a regular in the team.

"When the war started, we were together. And when I spoke about the Ballon d'Or, I was very clear. Maybe my English is not so good, but I was very clear because I was speaking about the potential of the player. The potential of the player can be the same and can respect the prediction or not.

"Until now, he has had many problems. The last problem, the suspension for whatever was the problem, but the [outcome] is clear. And now his challenge is to respect all his qualities because he's a great player. He has to leave this season in a right way, not too [much] pressure, but it is the right moment for him to show [his ability] because if Chelsea paid €100m four years ago ... I think they brought a lot of big, big players and to spend €100m, I think they thought very well about the qualities of Mudryk."

Having brought him into the club to strengthen the attack, it seems highly unlikely that when he's fit he won't be involved in the first-team picture more often than the teenager.

That may halt his development and also anger fans who want to see one of their own come through, especially ahead of a Chelsea player who didn't cut it at Stamford Bridge. It's something that De Zerbi will have to juggle with once the decision needs to be made, and the youngster may have the chance to ensure the decision is a difficult one against Leeds.

#1317. Mikel Arteta convinced his Arsenal players he could read their minds before north London derby win - before revealing the truth behind bizarre stunt

Published: 12:31 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:35 EDT, 2 November 2026

Mikel Arteta convinced his Arsenal squad that he could read their minds in what proved to be a successful strategy ahead of the north London derby four years ago.

Revealed in Daily Telegraph reporter Sam Dean's book Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal's Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta, the Spanish head coach played the trick on his players in the team hotel ahead of the 3-1 win at the Emirates on October 1, 2022.

Arteta, who is notorious for his use of offbeat coaching methods, reportedly asked the players to hide an object in one of their shoes and told them that he would be able to guess whose it was simply by looking into their eyes and reading their body language.

He promised the team that if he failed to guess the player he would take them and their families out for dinner, but if he managed to figure it out, they would be paying for him.

After he and his coaches left the room to let the players hide the object, he returned and studied each of the players, and 'even checked their pulses, supposedly to see which one of them was panicking the most', Dean writes.

When he guessed correctly that it was Brazilian defender Gabriel, the team reportedly 'went mental', a source in the book said.

Arteta convinced his players that he could read their minds ahead of their 3-1 win against Tottenham at the Emirates on October 1, 2022

Arteta is notorious for his use of offbeat coaching methods in order to gain an edge over rivals

Later that day, after goals from Thomas Partey, Gabriel Jesus and Granit Xhaka secured the three points against their north London rivals, Arteta and his staff revealed that they had seen them pick the player through CCTV cameras at the hotel.

This wasn't the first time that Arteta has deployed an unusual tactic with the hope of gaining an edge over his rivals.

Ahead of a game against Liverpool at Anfield during the 2021-22 season, Arteta blasted 'You'll Never Walk Alone' over speakers during training to prepare his players for the boisterous atmosphere.

In the summer of 2024, he hired a pickpocket to steal from the squad during an evening meal.

The pickpocket was disguised as a waiter during the meal and, after the dinner, Arteta held a pre-match team meeting where, at the end of it, he presented his players' stolen items at the front of the room.

That ploy was in preparation for a match against a team who tried every possible tactic to gain an edge, and Arteta wanted to adopt a 'pickpocket mentality', to always be aware of people trying to steal advantages from them.

For another game, Arteta did a pre-match team talk involving a lightbulb, as he wanted his players to shine and emit energy and light to one another.

As Arsenal pushed to end their long wait for a Premier League title, the club also installed the outline of the trophy in the entrance of their main building at the training ground. It was finally lit up in May, when the feat was achieved.

And during pre-season just past, Arteta revealed that he deliberately made his team late for matches by changing their route or meal times, as well as making the changing room hotter and reducing the number of massage beds in the hope of preparing the squad for difficulties on the road.

After signing new terms last month, Arteta revealed that his quirky practices began on his very first day on the job back in December 2019.

The then 37-year-old claimed he 'destroyed' an education centre at Arsenal's training centre, throwing 'the computers, the laptops, the cables' on the floor. He then requested his staff to reorganise the office in no time at all in order to prove their togetherness.

As Arsenal pushed to end their long wait for a Premier League title, the club also installed the outline of the trophy in the entrance of their main building at the training ground

In an interview with The Athletic, Arteta explained: 'I said, "Listen, this is what I heard. I don’t know if it’s true. But from a lot of different people, the sentiment is that this is how they feel about working in the organisation.

'I’m here to help you enjoy your profession and your life and the passion that we all share. If you want me to help you to do that, you have two minutes to put this in order and at least to be ready to work together’. And I left.

'That could have been my managerial career because if that would have stayed the same way, I had no job anymore!'

Arteta then outlined how he came back moments later and everything was 'immaculate'.

'Everyone was silent and had their eyes open and they were ready to listen. I said, "This is just the start. It’s something that we have to be in daily. Whatever we want to accomplish, we’re going to have to do it together. I cannot do it by myself. The issue that we have is much deeper than that, but the opportunity is infinite".'

Since taking charge in 2019, Arteta has overseen a notable improvement in Arsenal's fortunes, transforming them from a side floundering in mid-table to Premier League champions. He also took them to their first Champions League final in 20 years in May.

#1315. Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3,4,5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

NEC remains a major cause of mortality and long-term morbidity in preterm infants1,2. NEC pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving the complex interplay of immature intestinal development, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut dysbiosis and excessive inflammatory response3,4,5,6. The specific triggers of NEC and the mechanisms driving its rapid progression remain poorly understood.

The impact of NEC extends beyond the intestine. More than half of postoperative survivors develop brain injury and neurodevelopmental impairment7,8, with TLR4 inflammatory pathways implicated in this pathology9,10. Many insights are derived from experimental models that use hypoxia, cold stress and hyperosmolar formula feeding to increase intestinal vulnerability11,12. Although these models have been valuable for mapping inflammatory pathways, they may be less well suited to interrogating microbiome-driven early initiating events.

Gut microbiota are implicated in NEC susceptibility: NEC is associated with dysbiosis3,4,5, germ-free mice are resistant to NEC-like injury13 and microbiota-modifying interventions are protective14,15. Several studies identified enrichment of toxin-producing C. perfringens in NEC16,17,18, but causal virulence factors remain undefined.

C. perfringens is a ubiquitous, Gram-positive anaerobe producing diverse toxins19,20. Strains are classified into seven toxin types (A–G) based on toxin repertoire19. Type C strains produce Beta and Delta toxins, which are both pore-forming toxins (PFTs) that induce cell death by forming transmembrane pores21,22,23. While Beta toxin is well characterized, Delta toxin remains understudied. Here we identify C. perfringens Delta toxin as a virulence factor that drives intestinal necrosis and brain injury in a subset of NEC, providing an avenue for targeted therapeutic intervention.

To investigate the role of gut microbiota in NEC, we profiled faecal samples from 28 preterm infants without NEC and 16 preterm infants with NEC. 16S rRNA-sequencing analysis revealed an enrichment of C. perfringens in NEC samples (Fig. 1a), consistent with previous reports16,17. Two fatal cases of NEC showed high C. perfringens abundance (Extended Data Fig. 1a). To validate this finding, we performed anaerobic culture of faecal samples from 49 individuals without NEC and 17 patients with NEC (Supplementary Table 1). C. perfringens-positive cultures showed visible gas production and were confirmed by selective tryptose sulfite cycloserine (TSC) agar isolation and PCR targeting of C. perfringens-specific genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d). Overall, C. perfringens was more prevalent in patients with NEC compared with in infants without NEC (56% versus 18%), supporting its association with NEC (Fig. 1b,c).

C. perfringens produces a repertoire of toxins, including Alpha, Beta, Epsilon, Iota toxin, enterotoxin (CPE), necrotic enteritis β-like toxin (NetB) and perfringolysin O (Pfo)19. We next examined whether specific toxin profiles correlated with severe outcomes. PCR-based toxin typing identified isolates from two deceased patients as type C C. perfringens strains containing the delta toxin gene (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens clinical-03 and clinical-15) (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta toxin production was further confirmed by western blot analysis of culture supernatants (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). We further detected anti-Delta toxin antibodies in two patients with severe surgical NEC whose stool cultures were negative, probably due to antibiotic treatment, indicating previous infection with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens strains. Expanded serological analysis of ten additional patients with severe surgical NEC identified five anti-Delta toxin antibody-positive cases (Supplementary Table 2). Thus, 7 of 12 (58%) patients with severe NEC showed serological evidence of Delta toxin exposure, whereas Delta toxin was not detected in any infant without NEC by faecal isolate PCR or serology (Fig. 1b–d).

Clinically, Delta toxin+ infants showed more prominent systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and brain injury, compared with Delta toxin− cases characterized by elevated C-reactive protein and D-dimer, decreased monocytes, platelets and haemoglobin (Fig. 1e). Importantly, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in these patients indicated more severe injury, including lateral ventricular enlargement (Fig. 1f,g).

To assess Delta toxin pathogenicity, we selected representative clinical isolates, the Delta toxin+ strain C. perfringens clinical-03 and the Delta toxin− strain C. perfringens clinical-01 for genomic analysis and animal infection studies (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the clinical-03 strain clustered with NCTC3181 (a known Delta toxin+ type C strain24), whereas clinical-01 clustered with CVCC1160 (a Delta toxin− type C strain), with the two clinical isolates sharing around 96% DNA identity (Extended Data Fig. 1h). Neonatal mice orally gavaged with these strains and formula for 4 days developed severe NEC-like intestinal pathology only after Delta toxin+ infection, including disrupted intestinal architecture, villus and crypt damage, inflammatory infiltration and mucosal fibrin clots, accompanied by increased mortality (Fig. 1h–k). During infection with the clinical-03 strain, Delta toxin was detected predominantly in the intestine, with lower levels in the kidney and lung, but was undetectable in the brain based on western blotting and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Extended Data Fig. 1i,j). Nevertheless, infected mice developed severe brain abnormalities, including lateral ventricular enlargement and ependymal cell damage (Fig. 1l,m). Reference strain comparison using NCTC3181 and CVCC1160 (around 99% identity) confirmed that Delta toxin+ infection caused more severe intestinal, brain and lung injury (Extended Data Fig. 1k–m). Finally, culture supernatants from Delta toxin+ strains induced cytotoxicity in HeLa cells, HT29 cells and intestinal organoids, which was neutralized by a Delta-toxin-specific polyclonal antibody (Extended Data Fig. 1n–p). These results support Delta toxin as a key secreted virulence factor responsible for cell damage.

Owing to technical challenges in performing some assays in postnatal day 7 (P7) neonatal mice, we included 4-week-old weanling mice for subsequent experiments. Intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration of purified Delta toxin caused dose-dependent lethality in both age groups, with neonates showing greater sensitivity (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). We next quantified Delta toxin distribution in neonatal mice 4 h after i.p. injection of 10 μg toxin. Consistent with the infection model, toxin levels were highest in the intestine (around 61 μg per g), followed by kidney (approximately 15 μg per g) and lung (about 7 μg per g), with barely detectable toxin in the brain (Extended Data Fig. 2b). These levels were comparable to those in infected pups, supporting the physiological relevance of the toxin injection model.

We next challenged P7 neonates and 4-week-old mice using either an acute high-dose model to mimic fulminant infection, analysed at 4 h, or a single low-dose challenge with prolonged follow-up to approximate residual toxin activity after antibiotic clearance, analysed at days 5–7. Across both age groups and dosing strategies, Delta toxin induced a severe NEC-like multiorgan pathology. Intestines showed mucosal disruption, villus destruction, epithelial detachment and oedema (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Concurrently, the brain exhibited haemorrhage, ependymal disorganization, periventricular oedema, ventricular dilation (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 2e,f), neuronal shrinkage and degeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2g–i). We also observed intravascular coagulation within the cerebral microvasculature in the hippocampal region (Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). In 4-week-old mice, brain MRI further confirmed that Delta toxin caused brain injury and ventricle dilation (Fig. 2i,j), mirroring the neuropathology observed in patients with NEC. In vivo photoacoustic imaging of brains showed a significant reduction in cerebral blood flow, vascular density and branching index, indicating Delta-toxin-associated hypoxic–ischaemic injury and cognitive impairment (Fig. 2k,l).

Beyond the brain, Delta toxin induced widespread multiorgan pathology, with particularly severe injury observed in the kidney and lung. These tissues exhibited distinct signs of coagulopathy, haemorrhage and inflammatory cell infiltration, notably affecting the renal medulla, glomeruli and pulmonary parenchyma in both age groups (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o). Moreover, toxin-treated mice showed dilated ear vessels and increased Evans blue extravasation in the peritoneal lavage fluid, indicating vascular damage25 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Delta toxin further induced systemic coagulation abnormalities, including elevated red blood cell counts, reduced platelets and altered coagulation parameters, including prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time,  and reduced fibrinogen (Extended Data Fig. 3c–h). These findings recapitulate the severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) observed in Delta-toxin-positive patients with NEC (Fig. 1e). Inflammasome activation is known to drive coagulation through macrophage-mediated release of tissue factor26. Consistently, Delta toxin promoted tissue factor release from macrophages and Caco2 intestinal epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 3i), suggesting that both cell types contribute to toxin-induced coagulopathy.

To define the specific contribution of Delta toxin to neurological injury, we evaluated the effects of Beta toxin, which has been implicated in type C C. perfringens enteritis27. Beta toxin exhibited selective cytotoxicity for endothelial HUVECs but notably spared HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells and organoids (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c), aligning with a previous report that Beta toxin preferentially targets CD31+ vascular endothelial cells28. In vivo, it induced rapid, dose-dependent mortality (Extended Data Fig. 4d), but did not induce brain pathology at any dose tested (Extended Data Fig. 4e). These data demonstrate the specific pathogenic role of Delta toxin as a driver of NEC-like multiorgan pathology.

We next examined whether Delta-toxin-induced brain injury is associated with blood–brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and neuroinflammation. In 4-week-old mice, Evans blue extravasation revealed dose-dependent BBB leakage after Delta toxin challenge, with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)29 as a positive control (Fig. 2m–o). Acute high-dose Delta toxin (100 μg, 8 h) caused more-severe BBB disruption than either prolonged low-dose Delta toxin (20 μg, analysed at day 7) or acute LPS (1 mg, 8 h), indicating that Delta toxin rapidly disrupts BBB integrity. ZO-1 immunofluorescence in the hippocampus confirmed structural damage with localized disorganization and reduced signal intensity (Fig. 2p,q).

BBB disruption is often accompanied by neuroinflammation30,31 and intestinal CD4+ T cells migrate across the BBB into the brain, where they accumulate with microglia to trigger neuroinflammation32,33. We next characterized brain immune cell populations after exposure to Delta toxin. In both age groups, acute high-dose Delta toxin triggered an increase in total CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a). This increase was largely attributable to a marked expansion of the microglial population, predominantly reflecting microglial expansion (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), confirmed by increased IBA1+ immunostaining (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). Three-dimensional analysis revealed a shift of microglia from ramified to amoeboid morphology, characterized by shorter branch lengths and attenuated processes (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). GFAP+ astrocytes also increased, with increased branching and cell volume (Extended Data Fig. 5h–k), indicating pro-inflammatory activation34. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells remained at similar levels at this timepoint (Extended Data Fig. 5l). In neonates after low-dose prolonged challenge, microglial expansion and activation (Extended Data Fig. 5m–r) were accompanied by increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Extended Data Fig. 5s,t), consistent with T cell recruitment 4 days after NEC induction32.

As patients with NEC exhibit a pronounced systemic and central nervous system inflammatory response1, we analysed cytokine profiles in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NEC positive for C. perfringens Delta toxin. The results revealed abnormally high cytokine levels, including IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-1β (Fig. 3a,b). To examine whether Delta toxin contributes to this inflammatory activation, we administered Delta toxin to 4-week-old mice through i.p. injection and observed a significant increase in IL-1β levels in both the serum and peritoneal fluid (Fig. 3c), along with a dose-dependent upregulation of Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA levels in peritoneal lavage cells (Fig. 3d). IL-1β and IL-18 are major effector cytokines released after NLRP3 inflammasome activation35, and activated macrophages represent the principal cellular source of mature IL-1β36. The specific NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 suppressed Delta-toxin-induced Il1b and Il18 in peritoneal macrophages (Fig. 3e), improved survival rates (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6a) and mitigated Delta-toxin-induced BBB disruption, as evidenced by reduced Evans blue extravasation (Fig. 3g,h). These findings suggest that Delta toxin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome to drive local and systemic inflammation as well as BBB damage.
